An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ has been made with the use of 37 inverse picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measurement allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was determined to be 1.440 picoseconds ($\pm 0.025$ statistical $\pm 0.018$ systematic) with a $p$-value of $0.775$, indicating consistency with the known value of 1.506 picoseconds obtained from transitions of the $B^0_s$ to its massless meson counterpart. With an accuracy of 3.7%, this measurement surpasses previous records from BaBar and CDF, and like those, shows the $B^0_s$ decay into $K^+K^-$ occurs before it can transition into two photons. Additionally, LHCb was able to determine the branching fraction of this decay at $(8.2\pm0.4\pm0.3)\times 10^{-5}$ and the total cross-sectional area for $pp$ to be $(6.7\pm0.4\pm0.3)\times 10^{-7}$ nanobarns. Furthermore, LHCb was able to measure the angular distribution of this decay with an accuracy of 1.1%, and in doing so, discovered the alignment of the $K^+\bar{K}^-$ system with an accuracy of 0.5%, and the alignment of the decay plane with an accuracy of 0.4%. These discoveries were made possible by determining the side-ways component of the $K^+\bar{K}^-$ system with an accuracy of 0.3%. These results were achieved by employing a method of event reconstruction known as "flavor-tagging" which involves identifying the semileptonic decay of either the $B^0$ or $\bar{B}^0$ meson into electrons to determine the initial state of the $B^0_s$ system. With this information, LHCb was able to obtain an estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^0\bar{K}^0$ decay time by comparing the observed $K^+K^-$ decays to those expected from the known $B^0\rightarrow K^0\pi^0$ transition. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our detected energy range, a specific anisotropy pattern is evident - one that deviates from the random distribution seen in lower-energy cosmic rays. This deviation, known as the "Octopus" structure, was first identified in our previous research extending up to 4 EeV, and in this study, we expand this finding to energies as high as 8 EeV. Furthermore, we discovered that the direction and intensity of the "Octopus" anisotropy remain relatively consistent across various energy levels, suggesting a connection to the source of these extremely energetic cosmic rays. It is also observed that the orientation of the "Octopus" anisotropy corresponds to the large-scale distribution of cosmic rays at lower energies, specifically in the Northern Hemisphere, and is linked to a particular morphological feature of the Auger Surface Detector. Additionally, we identified a periodic pattern in the "Octopus" anisotropy at 300 million years, although this periodicity may be an artifact influenced by the Earth's movement. In our study, we also explored whether the "Octopus" anisotropy is a transient phenomenon or a persistent feature of the cosmic ray sky by examining its orientation in discrete time frames. Our findings indicate that the "Octopus" anisotropy exhibits a steady pattern of orientation across these time frames, suggesting that it may be a long-lasting aspect of the cosmos. In our research, we also considered various external factors that could contribute to the "Octopus" anisotropy, including large-scale structures in the cosmos, magnetic fields, and peculiar velocity distributions. While our analysis suggests that these factors may contribute to the directionality of the "Octopus" anisotropy, they do not fully account for its intensity. Consequently, we propose that the "Octopus" anisotropy may be a manifestation of anisotropic particle distributions within ultra-high-energy cosmic rays themselves, potentially originating from sources located along specific jet-like paths as observed in gamma-ray data. In this scenario, the connection between the "Octopus" anisotropy and the large-scale distribution of cosmic rays at lower energies, specifically in the Northern Hemisphere, may be attributed to the prevalence of these jet-like sources in that region. All research was conducted using the R programming language for both estimation and forecasting, as well as data analysis, in line with the recommendations of the Journal of Statistical Software. The results indicate that TV-PARX outperforms the benchmark models in the short term but performs similarly to them in the long term. Furthermore, the study reveals that changes in model specifications have a limited impact on the accuracy of forecasts. The implementation of TV-PARX is made available to the research community through an R package called "tvparx". This package can be utilized for both estimation and forecasting with a time-varying Poisson auto-regressive model, as well as for diagnosing and addressing potential issues with the model. Additionally, the package includes an illustrative example based on the research presented in this paper. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
maintains detailed information about an object's shape and positional relationship
with other objects, even in the absence of collision. This representation is
defined over the space surrounding an object and is structured by a coordinate
system, facilitating efficient computation of objects' spatial relationships. To
utilize NDFs in real-world applications, we develop an object manipulation method
called 3D co-architectural learning, allowing two Neural Descriptor Fields to
communicate and influence each other through an exchange of messages. This allows
us to model complex objects' interactions, such as those involving deformation and
the influence of materials, without needing to solve partial differential
equations. We also enhance NDFs' performance through the use of spatially
organized self-attention modules and a specially designed graph architecture.
Evaluating our approach on multiple datasets, including those containing both
synthetic and real-world objects, shows that NDFs surpass current object
representations in tasks like object detection, segmentation, and grasping. The

The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, specifically tailored to meet precision demands for the Higgs boson and other research areas while maintaining an adaptable sensitivity to diverse potential discoveries. The SiD's robust silicon vertex and tracking system, complemented by its high central magnetic field, ensures precise momentum measurement. The detector's finely granulated calorimeter system, designed for particle flow analysis, delivers accurate energy resolution across a wide energy range. Given the approaching construction timeline for the ILC, the time has come to reassess the design choices made during the design phase and incorporate the significant progress made in detector research and development over the past decade. This paper outlines R&D-driven design refinements aimed at optimizing the detector's performance, incorporating cutting-edge technologies such as 65 nm ASICs, high-brightness ILC beams, and the latest understanding of physics requirements. These upgrades are expected to yield improved performance, including a 10% enhancement in vertex resolution, a 10% gain in track segmentation, and an 10% enhancement in calorimeter energy resolution. Furthermore, the paper discusses implementation challenges, R&D strategies, and proposed timelines for integrating these advancements into the detector design. The plan outlined in this paper is aligned with the design phase timeline, which is set to conclude in 2023, with a view to proceeding with detailed design and construction preparations in 2024. We analyzed a group of 24 stars within the globular cluster Tononzintla 2, located in the center of the Milky Way, to study the distribution of nitrogen across various temperatures and luminosity levels. This issue isn't solely attributed to the growing scale of these repositories, but also because the Isabelle proof assistant, widely used in this context, was designed to aid automated reasoning rather than produce human-readable proofs. As a result, there's a growing need to develop methods for effectively navigating through large, complex formal proofs, which has already been shown possible through the development of various visualization tools and techniques. However, a more comprehensive approach is required to provide a broader understanding of these proofs and their relationships. In this research, we're exploring ways to leverage natural language processing to generate concise, clear summaries of large, complex formal proofs, which can then be used in conjunction with visualizations and other navigation tools to create an integrated understanding and navigation framework for large formal proof repositories. In this paper, we outline the design of such a framework, which we've applied to generate summaries of significant mathematical proofs within the Isabelle library using the BERT-NN model. The results indicate that this approach holds promise for creating accessible pathways to complex formal proofs, which can be shared among a broader audience. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Techniques used for this estimation can be broadly classified into two categories based on whether intermediate intermediate intermediate features are shared or not. Methods that do not share features involve employing two separate networks for encoding both target code and template code features. In contrast, techniques that do share features involve combining the two codes at some intermediate layer, resulting in a single encoded feature that is subsequently used for calculating the object pose. Although the latter approach has shown improved performance and efficiency in comparison to the former approach, there are several potential drawbacks to sharing intermediate features, including decreased model flexibility and accuracy in scenarios with complex backgrounds. To address these limitations, we propose introducing a new type of attention mechanism, referred to as Background-Aware Channel Attention (BACA), that selectively modulates the shared channels based on the degree to which they are related to the background, thereby isolating object-related information. The introduction of BACA results in a significant improvement in accuracy, amounting to around 1.4% mAP, in our experiments conducted using the LINEMOD dataset. Moreover, our approach yields a more efficient solution by reducing the number of shared channels, resulting in a model that requires 12% fewer parameters while achieving a comparable level of performance. The code for our algorithm has been made publicly accessible.

Bond-based Peridynamics, in particular, offers a straightforward numerical framework for modeling material fragmentation through the use of pairwise bonds between material points. However, the introduction of triads in higher-dimensional spaces leads to an issue with bond counting, resulting in an excessive formation of new bonds and thus requiring an ad-hoc solution to prevent unmanageable increases in number of material points during simulations. To address this challenge, this research introduces an innovative approach of counting bonds based on spatial orientation, applicable across various Peridynamic models. As a result, simulations of material fragmentation are no longer hindered by the triad counting issue, enabling a more stable and accurate modeling of material fragmentation, including scenarios involving complex bond configurations and higher-dimensional spaces. This new approach is demonstrated through a variety of benchmark problems, including a 3D plate drop test, in order to verify its effectiveness. challenges. Based on the original idea of Graphical Lasso introduced by Friedman
(2007), Graphical Lasso utilizes L1-L2 regularization to estimate a sparse and
well-organized correlation matrix structure, ultimately reconstructing an underlying
network graph. Despite significant progress in recent years, several key limitations
remain unresolved, such as handling large-scale datasets, diverse data types, and
non-standard graph topologies. To tackle these hard problems, researchers employ
various workarounds, including data transformation, standardization, and node
aggregation. To facilitate further research, the GGLasso library provides users with
a comprehensive set of tools to tackle these challenges directly. It offers a
flexible implementation of multiple state-of-the-art algorithms and a wide range
of customization options, including diverse regularization schemes, general loss
functions, and advanced solver frameworks. Additionally, the library includes a
set of utility functions to facilitate preprocessing, validation, and visualization
of results. With GGLasso, researchers can easily reproduce results from recent studies
and explore new ideas in the General Graphical Lasso framework. It is available at

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been examined, focusing particularly on deterministic integrators applied to biased trajectories, efficient methods using multiple time steps, and the use of a single reference trajectory. We have found that some of these methods provide highly accurate configurational averaging when compared to the full ensemble of biased trajectories, with some even matching the precision of direct simulations of the original SDE. We have evaluated various methods including the Euler-Maruyama scheme, the stochastic version of the Verlet algorithm, the Langevin-Hamiltoniaintegrator, the Legolous method, the multiple time step Brownian integrator, the SHABIE scheme, and the SABIE scheme. We have found that the most accurate methods are the stochastic Verlet algorithm, the Langevin-Hamiltonian integrator, the Legolous method, the SHABIE scheme, and the SABIE scheme, achieving a factor of $N^2$ improvement in computational efficiency with minimal loss of precision. This advancement enables the simulation of large biomolecules with a thousand atoms or more, expanding the scope of molecular dynamics simulations. Moreover, the precision of these methods is sufficiently high to enable accurate free energy calculations using umbrella sampling methods. We have developed an open-source software package called SDE4MD that incorporates the evaluated methods for resolving SDEs and configuring averaging estimators, making it available under the permissive MIT license. The source code can be obtained from the GitHub repository https://github.com/aleksandert/SDE4MD. The software package is compatible with the popular molecular dynamics simulation platform AMBER and can be used in conjunction with the PMEMD code. The software package is compatible with Linux and Windows operating systems. The source code is accompanied by comprehensive documentation, including a tutorial that provides an introduction to molecular dynamics simulations, SDEs, umbrella sampling, and biased configurational averaging. The documentation also includes a comparison of the precision of the evaluated methods, as well as a discussion of the computational efficiency of these methods. The unique orbital characteristics in cubanite can be understood through a molecular orbital analysis, showing that some 3d electrons transition to unoccupied O 2p anti-bonding levels to form molecular orbitals, while others become confined in atomic-like atomic orbitals to minimize on-site Coulomb repulsions. Notably, this exchange enhancement is linked to the unusual orbital configuration rather than charge disproportionation itself. Cubanite's distinct orbital structure may also contribute to its exceptional stability in oxidizing environments. Our findings offer a new framework for understanding the complex physical and chemical properties of cubanite.

This paper presents a computational approach to solve certain types of optimal control problems that have time-varying objectives and constraints. These issues typically involve finding a control strategy to operate a dynamic system in a way that optimizes a performance metric, subject to limitations on its operational parameters. The system is modeled by differential equations whose solutions depend on time and can be calculated using various methods such as numerical integration, direct resolution, or a combination of both. The desired performance is defined by parameters that vary over time and are often derived from statistical analysis of the system's output. Accurately identifying esophageal tumors in CT scans manually is challenging due to the tumors' subtle visual characteristics and the esophagus's complex and variable shape. This difficulty can lead to inconsistent delineation results across different professionals, which can negatively impact the effectiveness of radiation therapy. As a solution, we've developed an approach that uses deep learning to automate the detection and creation of a 3D model for the esophagus and nearby lymph nodes. Our method employs a UNet-like architecture to identify the esophagus and nearby structures in 2D CT images across multiple slices, and a graph convolutional network to create a 3D model for the esophagus and 18 key lymph nodes. We've tested our approach with 109 CT scans from 41 distinct patients, and the results show a high degree of accuracy (Dice coefficient: 0.946 for the esophagus, 0.883 for the lymph nodes) and a low margin call (5.38%) when validated with additional, unseen data (25 CT scans from 11 new patients). Moreover, our approach takes just 500 milliseconds to process each CT scan on a single GPU. This research indicates that a deep learning-based system can efficiently and accurately identify the esophagus and nearby lymph nodes in CT scans, which can enhance the consistency of tumor delineation and ultimately contribute to more reliable radiation therapy. As a bonus, we've developed an intuitive user interface that enables medical professionals to fine-tune the model's performance with just a few clicks. This enhanced model can be applied to various CT scans with a low margin call of 5.38%, which can be further minimized with additional training data. Geosteering, an advanced technology used in offshore drilling operations, enables real-time well plan adjustments to ensure optimal exploration and extraction efficiency. However, the time-consuming and costly process of drilling wells makes it essential to prioritize well locations for geosteering. This task can be optimized by creating a ranked list of wells based on their potential value. In this research, we develop an innovative approach that utilizes multi-objective evolutionary algorithms to solve a complex problem of ranking wells for geosteering. The approach takes into account factors such as drilling costs, hydrocarbon volumes, and the accuracy of real-time formation evaluation data. Our study utilizes actual data from a North Sea drilling project and compares the results of the approach with those obtained from traditional decision-making methods used by drilling companies. The findings indicate that our approach yields more valuable wells with higher hydrocarbon potential and lower drilling costs. Furthermore, the results show that the approach can enhance well value by up to 20% when utilizing real-time data and can prioritize wells for geosteering 2-4 times faster than traditional methods. The study also presents an innovative visualization tool that facilitates the comparison of solutions generated by multi-objective evolutionary algorithms. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively applied to various downstream NLP tasks like relation extraction and machine reading comprehension. Conventional NER models primarily focus on individual entities, sometimes ignoring the nested nature of real-world data. In contrast, our proposed NestedNER model seamlessly integrates the structure of all named entities within a given text, effectively modeling both individual and nested entities simultaneously. By doing so, our model leverages both intra and inter-entity information to enhance entity extraction and classification accuracy. Furthermore, our model employs a holistic representation for each entity, comprising both a start token and a end token, allowing for the efficient modeling of nested entities. Comprehensive experiments on five standard datasets demonstrate our NestedNER model's superiority over conventional NER models, showcasing substantial improvements of up to 6.5% in F1-score on the WNUT-2016 test set. Moreover, our model's effectiveness in exploiting both intra and inter-entity information is explicitly validated through controlled experiments. To facilitate further research, we have released the code, models, and additional analysis at https://github.com/THU-ASRL/NestedNER. Concretely, our code is built upon the PyTorch Transformer repository provided by huggingface, and our models are available for direct download at https://huggingface.co/thu-asrl/NestedNER_wngroup. Moreover, we have published an extended version of our work, including detailed model architecture, experimental settings, and additional analysis, at https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.09451. Consequently, our code, models, and additional analysis at the above-mentioned links offer valuable insights and resources for the NER community. Moreover, we have released an interactive demonstration of our model's performance at https://asrl.thunlp.org/named_entity/named_entity.html. This demonstration enables users to upload their own text data and observe the model's predictions for both individual and nested entities in real-time. In addition, we have also released an annotated dataset based on the WNUT-2019 benchmark, available at https://asrl.thunlp.org/named_entity/wngroup.html, which includes detailed entity annotations and can be utilized for further research. Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. This paper formulates an uncoded distance estimation metric called the Fisher information distance, which is proven to be a consistent estimator for the location of a mobile node within the network. Next, a decoding approach called maximum likelihood estimation is explored to determine the location of the mobile node, which is then shown to be a reliable estimator for locations that are close to the generating distribution parameters. Additionally, numerical computations and theoretical analysis indicate that the variance of the estimated location using both the uncoded and coded approaches is inversely proportional to the square of the number of sensor observations. Finally, an Monte Carlo simulation is used to compare and contrast the accuracy of these location estimation methods. Results show that the variance of the estimated location using both the uncoded and coded approaches is inversely proportional to the number of sensor observations, which meets our theoretical predictions. Furthermore, it was observed that the performance of the maximum likelihood estimator outperforms the Fisher information estimator when the mobile node is closely located to the network, which aligns with our theoretical findings. However, when the mobile node is located at a greater distance from the network, the maximum likelihood estimator performs poorly, which is consistent with our theoretical analysis, while the Fisher information estimator provides a better location estimate with a smaller variance, which is surprising. To validate our theoretical analysis, we conducted additional simulations using different network sizes and distribution models, which yielded similar outcomes. Lastly, a comparison of the variance of the estimated location using a large number of sensor observations and a smaller number of sensor observations revealed that the latter yields a similar level of accuracy, which has significant practical implications. Ultimately, our research contributes to a better understanding of location detection within wireless sensor networks. Moreover, the outcomes of our research have the potential to be applied to other localization problems involving diverse technologies. Lastly, we believe that our results can be improved upon, which motivates further research into this topic.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research focuses on developing automated models to predict code-mixing patterns in written language data. We have investigated various approaches to this task, first analyzing the characteristics of code-mixing data, then exploring models that learn from data and apply neural network architectures to improve performance. We have observed that code-mixing patterns exhibit less regularity and more randomness than language-specific patterns, making it more challenging to build accurate models. We have found that models trained on large datasets and advanced techniques like self-supervised learning yield better results, but may not entirely capture the essence of code-mixing due to over-reliance on data rather than underlying linguistic principles. We have also discovered that models can learn to recognize code-mixing patterns with some degree of accuracy, but often confuse them with language-specific patterns during prediction. As a result, we believe there is a need for more sophisticated models that can better grasp the code-mixing phenomenon from a cognitive perspective and may involve integrating multiple systems that underlie language production and comprehension. In the context of machine learning, such models could be based on approaches like memory-augmented networks that efficiently manage linguistic information to ensure accurate code-mixing predictions. In the future, we anticipate significant advancements in code-mixing research driven by growing multilingual populations, the increasing availability of multilingual data, and the development of more complex neural network architectures that can handle these challenges. Ultimately, this research has the potential to contribute valuable insights to both multilingual communication and natural language processing. Code-mixing models can also be applied to other language contact situations and serve as a foundation for investigating other complex language phenomena. In the long term, we envision a future where machine learning models can effectively communicate across languages, mirroring the abilities of multilingual humans. In this future, research in code-mixing will play a pivotal role in advancing the field of multilingual communication and contributing to a more inclusive and equitable NLP ecosystem. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could facilitate more accurate evaluation but might not be necessary for a basic assessment. I propose a straightforward method to gauge image descriptions' quality based on their comprehensiveness, accuracy, and organization, which can be applied using only human descriptions and machine descriptions. Experimental results indicate that this framework effectively differentiates good and poor human descriptions with moderate precision. Furthermore, researchers are interested in the Ta-based materials' ability to become NMR-sensitive by replacing oxygen with nitrogen. Additionally, these materials possess unique magnetic and electric properties, making them suitable for the spallation sources needed for hadrontherapy cancer treatment. In this study, researchers used NQR to investigate the local structure of Ta-based perovskites, specifically Ta/V/O/N with varying vanadium content, and also explored the effect of replacing oxygen with nitrogen in Ta/O/N. The replacement of oxygen with nitrogen was found to increase the NQR frequencies and the Ta-N bond lengths, and also led to the appearance of NQR signals from the nitrogen nuclei in the Ta/O/N system. In this work, we investigated the distribution of online misinformation across different states in the US, revealing that there is a significant correlation between misinformation dissemination and certain personality traits, such as conscientiousness, and also found distinct dissemination patterns for misinformation and regular news across various states. Furthermore, we utilized these findings to inform the development of two effective counter-factual detection models, one utilizing a dual-environment setup and the other utilizing a state-aware setup, both significantly outperforming the baseline model with a 13.2% and 5.4% improvement in F1-score respectively, verifying the significance of considering the influence of personality traits and geographical divisions in the development of counter-factual detection models. Moreover, our analysis of the characteristics of misinformation circulation at the state level can provide valuable policy recommendations for mitigating the spread of misinformation in different regions. In addition, our research highlights the significance of incorporating multiple data sources to counter misinformation, as well as the benefits of employing a more advanced language model, such as T5, for counter-factual detection. Recent advances in learning from few labeled samples have sparked interest in semi-supervised detection techniques. Conventional semi-supervised detection methods primarily focus on improving performance with limited labeled data and negligible or no utilization of vast amounts of unlabeled data. In high-stakes applications like financial fraud detection, vast amounts of data are readily available but expensive to label. To address this challenge, we developed a novel semi-supervised detection algorithm, SS-DT, which effectively leverages both limited labeled data and abundant unlabeled data for robust detection. Specifically, SS-DT utilizes decision trees to effectively handle data streams, incorporate labeled data for initial model training, and utilizes gradient boosting on unlabeled data for iterative model enhancements through robust feature extraction. Experimental evaluations on real-world financial transaction datasets showed that our proposed method, SS-DT, outperformed conventional semi-supervised and fully supervised detection methods, achieving up to 23% improvement in F1-score and 27% improvement in AUC-ROC compared to the baseline methods. Moreover, our approach demonstrated superior scalability and robustness to varying labeled data ratios. The code for our research is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/SS-DT. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a more direct method of learning, the audio provided by humans during these demonstrations is often overlooked. In reality, audio can be very helpful in learning tasks. This study analyzes audio features associated with human instructors who are demonstrating tasks to robots. It identifies and assesses three key featuresâ€”speech-related features, task-relevant language features, and social interaction featuresâ€”that provide valuable information about the instructor's intentions and can influence how the learner interprets the demonstration. Three experiments were conducted to investigate the impact of these features on learning from robotic demonstrations. The findings show that speech-related features have a limited effect on learning due to the visual nature of the task, but features related to the relevance of the task and social interaction do have an impact. It is also evident that the learner is influenced by the audio playback of instructions that are relevant to the task at hand, even if the visual action does not match the auditory instruction. In some cases, the learner is able to learn from demonstrations in which the action does not match the auditory instruction, indicating that the system can learn from audio-visual mismatches. The results of this research can be applied to improve the design of learning interfaces for robotic systems that learn from audio-visual demonstrations. It is also possible that the findings of this study could be applied to other systems that learn from audio-visual demonstrations, such as those found in human-computer interaction. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational systems in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. These issues are critical in the development of an effective automated testing framework for conversational systems. This research is relevant to software engineers, human-computer interaction specialists, and natural language processing researchers who work on the development and evaluation of conversational systems. Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables vast amounts of monolingual data to be incorporated into TM without additional bilingual constraints; secondly, both the memory retriever and the NMT model can be jointly optimized for translation objectives. Experimental results indicate that our monolingual TM-enhanced NMT model achieves superior performance compared to baseline NMT systems and outperforms bilingual TM-augmented NMT models. Furthermore, our model's ability to leverage monolingual data through cross-lingual memory retrieval enables it to excel in low-resource and domain adaptation scenarios. Moreover, we observe that the monolingual TM model's performance rivals that of the bilingual TM model on certain datasets. Lastly, our analysis of the learned representations within our monolingual TM model suggests that the memory retriever's encoding and the cross-lingual memory itself contribute to enhanced representations that facilitate better translation performance. Ultimately, our work validates the potential of monolingual TM for enhancing NMT and paves the way for further exploration of Memory-Augmented Neural Networks in cross-lingual scenarios. The code and data utilized in this research are openly accessible via this link: https://github.com/zhengyunw/monotm.

To recognize new categories from minimal labeled data, few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. However, traditional methods that rely on average operations for calculating prototypes are limited by their assumption of normal distribution for data points. This limitation is addressed by our proposed method, HypoEMA Protocols, which relaxes this assumption and instead models data points as robust units. The HypoEMA Protocols framework is then applied to several prototype calculation methods like Mahalanobis distance, energy-based models, and neural prototypes. By evaluating our approach on miniImageNet, CUB-200-2011, and HICO-60 datasets using matching network learners, we found that HypoEMA Protocols outperformed the baseline method by achieving a 94.57% average accuracy, a 4.17% improvement of 90.40%. This indicates that robust units yield better performance compared to traditional methods. Additionally, our approach is computationally efficient as it only incurs a minimal additional cost of 0.0004 seconds per episode on a GPU. The code for HypoEMA Protocols, including the robust units protocol, is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/HypoEMA-Protocols. The framework can be utilized for various prototype calculation methods by substituting the method in the framework. For example, the implementation of robust units protocol with Mahalanobis distance is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/HypoEMA-Protocols/tree/main/Mahalanobis_Distance. Cross-domain recommendation has made significant progress in recent years, yet most existing methods still rely on a single sparse domain for user and item features. This gap in domain sparsity can lead to suboptimal performance in real-world applications. To address this limitation, we propose a Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) framework that leverages multiple sparse domains containing rich information for enhancing cross-domain recommendations. In contrast to traditional cross-domain recommendation methods relying on a single sparse domain, MSDCR utilizes multiple domains with sparse user and item graphs to provide a more comprehensive and dense co-occurrence representation for both users and items. By integrating an adaptive domain selection strategy and a progressive multi-domain graph learning approach, MSDCR is capable of extracting more reliable and generalizable dense representations from diverse domains, ultimately yielding superior recommendation performance. Experimental evaluations conducted on real-world datasets validate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art baseline methods in terms of recommendation accuracy and efficiency. The code and datasets are publicly accessible at: https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/MSDCR.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It also enables users to define novel convex sets with exotic cones through a compact, user-friendly syntax. Additionally, the framework allows for easy substitution of interior-point methods, making it suitable for both small-scale and large-scale applications with exotic cones, as well as for research into new IPMs. As such, Hypatia provides a comprehensive toolkit for both practical problems and theoretical advancements in the realm of exotic cones. The increasing use of MRI in clinical applications necessitates automated quality control to ensure accurate and consistent data analysis. Given the complex nature of MRI, incorporating multiple analysis components, as well as varying acquisition protocols and scanning devices, a centralized automated quality control system is required to effectively manage these complexities. Our research involves an automated quality control system for MRI-based radiation therapy planning, integrating multiple components, including heterogeneity-based dose-volume analysis, assessment of organ-at-risk and target volume conformity, calculation of planning criteria, and evaluation of treatment delivery feasibility. The system utilizes knowledge graphs to manage the vast amount of information generated by these components, enabling efficient data retrieval through SPARQL queries. A modular design and testing framework were developed to ensure the system's efficacy and accuracy, involving over 200 tests to validate over 100 million executed queries. The system's performance was optimized through caching, query refinement, and removal of redundant components, achieving a significant reduction in execution time and overall efficiency. The streamlined system demonstrated improved performance, with an average query execution time of less than 1 second, and the ability to handle large-scale MRI-based radiation therapy planning cases. The system's design and development serve as a model for creating automated quality control systems in MRI analysis, addressing challenges such as scalability, efficiency, and reliability. As an open-source framework, it is available for download and can be adapted for various MRI analysis applications, enabling the creation of efficient and reliable automated quality control systems. The system's source code can be accessed through the GitHub repository https://github.com/ARIA-Research-Pipeline/aria-qc. The system's design and development are also described in detail in the ARIA Automated Quality Control System Design and Validation Report, available at https://aria-research.org/publications/. The system has been successfully integrated into the ARIA research pipeline and is utilized in multiple research and clinical applications at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center. The system's performance and results have been presented at various conferences and meetings, including the 2020 annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), the 2020 annual meeting of the American Society for Radiation Oncology (ASTRO), and the 2020 annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA). We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. The bilepton model introduces an expanded electroweak gauge group, U(2)/U(1), which could provide answers to several unresolved issues in the standard model, including the origin of the electroweak symmetry breaking and the sum of neutrino masses. Alternatively, this model may arise from a five-dimensional bulk scenario with an extra dimension associated with the weak force, where a U(2) symmetry is preserved to prevent the formation of bulk fermion zero-modes. We investigate the consequences of this model for leptonic dark matter, finding that it necessitates the introduction of bilepton mediators to connect the dark matter to standard model particles while avoiding constraints from flavor-violation and missing energy searches. As a result, we derive more stringent requirements for the dark matter-proton scattering cross-section, which can be avoided by introducing non-perturbative bulk physics or non-standard neutrino cosmology. We also establish the necessary conditions for the bilepton model to accommodate a dark matter component similar to that observed in our universe. Furthermore, we outline the experimental signatures that could identify the bilepton model at future colliders and in dark matter detection experiments. Finally, we highlight the potential for the bilepton model to be probed through precision tests of the weak force at the LHC and in forthcoming experiments. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown great potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defects has so far been limited to studying individual centers, our work presents a comprehensive examination of T-type defect ensembles in silicon, specifically looking at their optical characteristics, spin properties, and optical control of relevant spin channels. Ensemble-based research offers several advantages, including higher probability of finding these defects randomly placed in a microchip, and potentially faster development of practical applications. Notably, our defect ensembles exhibit a 10 nm resolution in distinguishing between different optical transitions under varying magnetic fields, and a 100 Hz frequency precision in optical interferometry. Moreover, our research shows that nuclear spins can be controlled using a sequence of laser pulses, and that the collection of these defects in a small area makes them suitable for use in quantum communication systems based on linear optics. Finally, our work suggests that silicon T-type defects have the potential to serve as reliable photon-spin interfaces in such systems. Additionally, our research is available as an open-source project on GitHub, along with detailed instructions for recreating our experiments using the SiQGate quantum simulator. As a community-based initiative, we invite other researchers to utilize our results, suggest new applications, and contribute their own findings related to T-type defects in silicon. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiagent contextual bandit setting have significant limitations, such as requiring infinite memory or an unrealistically perfect model of the environment. This work overcomes these limitations by providing the first algorithm to rationally discover actions that are not dominated in a general multiagent contextual bandit setting with only finite memory and a general policy class. The algorithm, called Coarse Correlated Equilibria Explorer (CCE-Explorer), achieves this without prior knowledge of the number of agents, the number of actions per agent, or the number of possible states. What's more, CCE-Explorer operates in polynomial time in the parameters that depend on the number of actions, and only logarithmically depends on the number of states, the number of agents, and the memory size. As a byproduct of this work, we also establish the first regret bound for finding Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) in the multiagent contextual bandit setting with only finite memory, and this bound is sublinear and scales polynomially with the number of actions. This result is significant because CCE is a more general concept that includes both Correlated Equilibria (CE) and Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) as special cases. This new lower memory-based regret bound provides the first clear evidence that the general multiagent contextual bandit setting can be addressed with only finite memory. This breakthrough is particularly noteworthy because the same research team had previously proven a lower bound for the special case of single-agent linear bandits with only finite memory-based regret bound, and this new result generalizes that finding to the multiagent context. Reinforcement learning methods utilizing previous experiences, or replay, have shown significant efficiency enhancements. However, the success of these approaches heavily relies on carefully engineered selection criteria for the experiences to be retried. This paper introduces an alternative framework where the value of each individual past experience is determined organically through direct integration with the current policy. A notable benefit of this approach is that it bypasses the need to design a sophisticated replay scheme. Moreover, we demonstrate that this integrated method effectively approximates the advantages of traditional reinforcement learning methods. Nevertheless, calculating the exact value of each past experience becomes computationally expensive due to the requirement for simultaneous consideration of all past experiences and the current policy. To address this challenge, we develop an efficient approximation method based on stratified sampling. This approximation allows us to employ reinforcement learning with a large number of past experiences, even in complex environments such as high-dimensional grid worlds and simple yet demanding CartPole scenarios. The proposed framework is openly available at https://github.com/kuangshenglee/ValueIntegrals. The code has been optimized for efficient computation on a single GPU. As an example, our method was able to successfully train a policy on 10,000 experiences in the CartPole scenario within approximately 10 minutes. Furthermore, we provide an analytical expression for the theoretical time complexity of this method. Additionally, we provide an intuitive explanation for its practical efficiency. To facilitate further research, we introduce the concept of an experience-based policy and provide an analytical expression for its gradient. Finally, we provide an example of an experience-based policy that outperforms a baseline policy through additional training. However, this improvement comes with a significant increase in required experiences. Consequently, efficient replay schemes are still essential for successful reinforcement learning. Nevertheless, our results suggest that the value determinants of past experiences are inherently linked to the current policy. This insight opens up possibilities for the development of new reinforcement learning theories and methods. As such, we invite the broader research community to engage with our findings and contribute to a deeper understanding of experience-based reinforcement learning. Recent theoretical studies suggest that iron-based superconductors possess unique "flat band" characteristics near the center of the Brillouin zone, attributed to mixed orbital composition, specifically SDW-inducing $t_{2g}$ and superconductivity-promoting $s_{\pm}$ orbital contents. This 'flat band' feature is crucial for understanding the material's electronic and possible superconductivity origins. In our work, we utilized high-resolution ARPES to experimentally verify the existence of this "flat band" in (Nd,Gd)FeAsO ($x$=0.4,0.5) by analyzing the measured spectral function and examining the Fermi surface morphology. Our results confirm the presence of this "flat band" in the near-habitual $k$-space regions and the measured binding energies match well with DFT calculations. Moreover, we observed that the "flat band" width decreases with increasing doping level along the (001) direction, which may have implications for understanding the competing orders and superconductivity in these materials. This finding highlights the significance of directly observing the electronic structure using ARPES in order to accurately assess the theoretical models proposed for iron-based superconductors.

Two new strategies have been proposed to apply the supersymmetry method from Gaussian matrices to broader rotation-invariant matrices. Specifically, generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformations and the superbosonization formula have been proposed, and we have demonstrated that they yield equivalent and efficient methods for calculating partition functions and symplectic and orthogonal eigenvalue distributions for non-Gaussian matrices. These novel approaches offer significant advantages in terms of computational simplicity and the ability to handle more general symmetry constraints. Furthermore, we have derived analytical formulas for calculating the superbasic cumulant expansion using both methods, and we have demonstrated that the supersymmetry method can be applied to study interacting matrix models and quadratic matrix models with non-Gaussian potentials. Moreover, we have successfully applied these strategies to calculate the symplectic and orthogonal eigenvalue distributions for non-Gaussian matrices corresponding to Gaussian matrix ensembles, and we have obtained exact expressions for the corresponding density correlations and cumulants. Our findings provide a robust framework for applying the supersymmetry method to rotation-invariant non-Gaussian matrices and enable further explorations of matrix models with orthogonal and symplectic symmetry.

Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. The diverse nature of human conversation remains inadequately captured in existing datasets, which typically focus on a single topic and don't effectively model real-world conversations. These limitations become apparent when they are put to the test in tasks involving semantic manipulation, such as inserting new pieces of information or contradicting original statements. To address this, we have developed the MultiTalk Dataset, which is comprised of pairs of sentences related through a structured graph containing multiple interconnected topics. In order to facilitate accurate model performance on this dataset, we have established evaluation metrics that assess a model's ability to successfully navigate this complex semantic connection network. Models that are trained and evaluated using these metrics and evaluation tools outperform those that are not, as evidenced by our results. Furthermore, we have utilized this dataset to explore the development of models that can conduct conversations centered on multiple topics over the course of many turns. The dataset, evaluation tools, and models are available at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/multitalk. For more detailed information, please see the supplementary materials available at https://drive.google.

Our research investigates how an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) can optimize the performance of a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) M-QAM wireless system. By considering the effects of large-scale propagation and correlated signal paths, we develop an effective spatial and fast-paced optimization approach for activating and adjusting subwavelength reflecting elements. By applying an evolutionary algorithm, we derive a simplified yet effective general formula to achieve maximum system efficiency, both accounting for system dimensions and the characteristics of IRS. Through numerical simulations and theoretical analysis, we show that our approach provides significant performance gains and can lead to substantial improvements in system performance, especially when the number of IRS elements is large. Moreover, our findings indicate that IRS-mediated systems are resistant to phase shifts and phase noise, and that spatial correlation has a minimal impact on system performance when optimized. Ultimately, our results demonstrate the efficacy of our general formula in achieving optimal performance across various system configurations. This work has the potential to serve as a foundation for the development of optimized IRS systems in scenarios involving multiple users and diverse modulation schemes. These clusters are anticipated to persist in certain regions of the phase diagram, even in the absence of an external drive, and could exhibit complex behavior when subjected to a small perturbing force. Our experimental study using a one-dimensional atomic array, where interactions between neighboring atoms are highly resistant, reveals the formation of persistent, motionless clusters at specific sites corresponding to the minima of a potential energy landscape. Furthermore, we observe the cluster's dynamics in response to a periodic perturbation, confirming its intricate behavior as predicted theoretically. By comparing our findings to simulations of the same scenario, we demonstrate that the cluster's dynamics are accurately described by applying a hydrodynamic theory to the robust clusters in a limited region of the system. Our results provide the first direct observational evidence of the cluster phenomenon in gases. Additionally, our study highlights the capabilities of precision experiments on atomic arrays, enabling the investigation of complex, self-organized phenomena resulting from many-body interactions in a robust and cluster-based framework. This could serve as a model for studying other intricate behaviors at the interface of quantum and classical physics. This discovery also underscores the value of combining theoretical and experimental approaches to advance our understanding of complex, interacting systems. Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflicts when multiple modifications are made independently. Existing conflict resolution techniques either fall short in scalability or compromise performance. We introduce the Remove-Win design framework, which leverages analysis of conflict patterns to inform a tailored approach. By design, Remove-Win identifies and prioritizes updates that can be resolved independently, conflicts with which require a more comprehensive recovery process. We demonstrate the framework's efficacy through a case study of a distributed key-value store, which exhibits improved conflict resolution efficiency and system throughput. Furthermore, we evaluate the performance of Remove-Win in relation to system coordination overhead and conflict prevalence. To further contribute to the understanding of conflicts in real-world applications, we introduce a new taxonomy of conflict types and analyze their prevalence in a real-world dataset. Finally, we discuss several directions for future research in this area. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to generate diverse and engaging responses in casual conversations is a significant challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces a novel assessment framework centered on Enhancing the Diversity of Conversational Responses (EDCR). It employs a task called Natural Language Inference (NLI) to evaluate the differences between initial prompts and subsequent, diverse, conversational responses generated by various neural models. To enhance the effectiveness of this assessment, the paper introduces two key advancements. Firstly, NLI is applied to a broader range of tasks to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the relationships between these prompts and diverse responses. Secondly, a novel dataset called NLI Divergence Dataset (NIDD) is created to serve as a labeled benchmark for evaluating the diversity of conversational responses. This benchmark is distinguished by NLI labels that reflect the degree of inferred relationships between prompts and diverse response sets. To further improve the assessment of the diversity of conversational responses, the paper introduces a novel neural model called the Diversity-aware Biased Self-Attention model (DBSAn). This model, which is an adaptation of the biased self-attention model, incorporates an additional attention mechanism that considers the biased NLI labels during the generation process. As a result, the evaluation of the proposed method on the NIDD dataset indicates a significant improvement in the diversity of conversational responses, as measured by the Perplexity Density (PPD) metric. Furthermore, an analysis of the differences between NLI labels and the diversity of conversational responses was conducted to provide valuable insights into the characteristics of high-diversity conversations. To facilitate further advancements in this area, the proposed assessment framework and the NIDD dataset are made publicly available to support research and development of neural models that prioritize the diversity of conversational responses. As an additional contribution, the paper presents an exhaustive survey of the current state-of-the-art models that have evaluated the diversity of conversational responses using various metrics. Automated driving systems depend on predictive modules to assess risks and avoid accidents, however, their current implementation is hindered by expensive and complex technologies. A convolutional neural network known as VGGNet was modified and fine-tuned to analyze acoustic data from the front grille of a vehicle, located in the middle of the windshield, and extract features that predict near-collisions. By incorporating rotational energy into the equation of state, we've developed a method to estimate the rotational influence on hydrogen burning in stars with masses below 0.08 solar masses. Our analysis shows that moderate to high rotational velocities can make 1-D barotropic models enter a stable hydrogen-burning state, meeting the criteria set by Fuller and Garcia-Perez (1989). However, even at very high velocities, these stars won't be able to sustain hydrogen burning for more than a few million years. We've also found that the Schronen-Zharky low-mass star formation scenario can produce a significant number of these stars in stable hydrogen-burning states, especially in the Magellanic Clouds, and we expect about 10,000 such objects in the Milky Way's satellite galaxies based on this model. A new model based on a comprehensive expression for radiation energy has been proposed, and it effectively elucidates the dynamics of afterglows in multiple contexts, including relativistic, non-relativistic phases and fireball radiations with radiative and adiabatic components. The proposed model's general radiation energy equation can be applied to various theoretical scenarios such as jet, spherical expansion and magnetic field-induced emissions. It also enables the extraction of physical parameters including the total initial energy, magnetic field strength, electron density, radius of emission and Lorentz factor for both initial and subsequent stages of radiation. Furthermore, the model can distinguish between two phases of fireballs - the initial, short-lived radiative phase and the prolonged, adiabatic stage. The analysis of observed radiation patterns using the new model reveals that the Galactic New Object, AT2019pea, is best explained by a spherical fireball with a high electron density and moderate total energy, contradicting the jet model. The study of this enigmatic event using the new model also highlights the importance of considering the interstellar medium's electron density for a more accurate analysis of fireball radiation. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. This study delves into optimizing the planarity target, proposing a new algorithm to reduce the minimum number of nodes needed for planarity, and a corresponding hybrid approach combining local search techniques to further improve results. Experiments indicate the method's effectiveness, outperforming existing methods for a range of graph types and sizes. The newly developed approach, along with a related target evaluation algorithm, has been made available as part of an open-source tool. The implementation details, including parameters and coding, are provided for reproducibility and future improvements. The challenge of addressing this problem in 3D dimensions is also explored, introducing initial findings following a basic adaptation of the method. The research is relevant to various visualization domains, including connection maps in biology, network visualization in computer science, and linkage analysis in statistics and genetics. This paper presents a novel walking mechanism, the hybrid gaits thruster biped, which utilizes a unique combination of thrusters and strategically positioned weights to generate momentum for different gait cycles. Unlike traditional bipedal robots that use actuators in their legs, this design uses thrusters placed in the torso and feet to produce momentum during specific phases of the gait cycle. By controlling the direction and magnitude of this momentum through the thrusters, the robot can execute various locomotion tasks. We have mathematically modeled the dynamics of this system and verified its ability to produce multiple gaits, including trot, prance, and bound gait cycles, through numerical simulations. A prototype of the thruster biped has been built and successfully demonstrated its capability to execute a simplified bound gait cycle in a fluidless environment. This innovative design offers a promising approach for achieving multi-gait bipedal locomotion in fluid-filled environments. A precise LHCb method for determining the CKM angle gamma from decays at the tree level is explained. LHCb can generate up to 16 separate measurements, using different decay modes of various beauty and charm mesons, but they do not have the same level of sensitivity to gamma. By combining all available results, a highly accurate value can be obtained. These proceedings provide a detailed overview of several independent determinations used for this combined result and report the most recent outcome available as of Summer 2018. Additionally, the associated uncertainty is explained in terms of the various inputs used in the analysis. As of Summer 2018, the most precise determination yields a value of gamma equal to (68.9 +/- 3.0) degrees. This combined result is compared to indirect and direct determinations derived from Rydberg unitarity and UTfit, respectively, both of which are based on a wide range of experimental data, but have not been updated as extensively as the LHCb results presented here. As such, the most precise determination reported here represents the most accurate available estimate of the CKM angle gamma as of Summer 2018. As more accurate measurements become available in the future, LHCb will continue to refine its analysis using additional decays and more precise results from a total luminosity of 50/fb, with expectations of a value of gamma equal to (68.9 +/- 1.4) degrees by the time the LHC comes to a close. This level of precision will provide a valuable test of the Standard Model and make it possible to perform more reliable searches for beyond-Standard Model physics involving the CKM angle gamma. This study introduces a novel method for distinguishing knots through the use of unknotting sequences. By building upon the concept of quasi-Markov chains introduced by Reinhart and Wynn, we develop an algorithm that explicitly defines a transition matrix. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by applying it to a well-known example from the literature and verify that the resulting matrix accurately reflects the knots' unknotting processes. By conducting an in-depth analysis of avalanches, this paper identifies distinct categories based on the number of nodes they affect and the connectivity of the target node. Specifically, it is found that the likelihood of an avalanche infecting a large number of nodes increases with the network's connectivity, while the likelihood of a small isolated avalanche occurring is unaffected by the degree of the target node. This work also proposes a new metric, called the reduced degree of the avalanche, which is used to compare the effectiveness of node removal in three networks. Finally, this paper explores the potential benefits of targeting specific types of avalanches, particularly those that are highly connected, in the prevention of network attacks. Experimental results based on static networks are presented, and suggestions for future research in this area are provided. Neural language models have significantly influenced the development of NLP systems, which can now efficiently handle a wide range of tasks and possess a comprehensive understanding of language. However, the simplicity of n-gram models makes them an attractive alternative for resource-constrained applications, despite being outperformed by neural models in most cases. This study compares the performance of n-gram models and neural language models using various evaluation metrics including test data size, which reveals that n-gram models excel in small test sets, while neural models dominate in larger test sets. Furthermore, an analysis of system behavior indicates that n-gram models offer a more nuanced understanding of language, which is reflected in the better performance of neural models only when the test set is sufficiently large. This finding is supported by an examination of system performance in relation to the amount of computation required, which suggests that neural models' superiority is largely a result of their heavy reliance on unnecessary calculations in small test sets. In such scenarios, the increased understanding of language captured by n-gram models makes them a more desirable choice in resource-constrained settings. This research is particularly relevant to applications like dialog system evaluation, which often rely on small, artificially constructed test sets to assess system performance. In these scenarios, the results indicate that n-gram models should be considered a more suitable benchmark for system performance. This research is further supported by the inclusion of additional evaluation metrics such as subword evaluation, evaluation of systems with limited training data, and the evaluation of systems with specific performance constraints, which consistently show n-gram models to be a more suitable choice for these scenarios. In conclusion, this study demonstrates that n-gram models offer a more nuanced understanding of language and should be considered a more suitable benchmark for system performance in resource-constrained applications, which is particularly relevant to the evaluation of dialog systems. We define $Q$-Fano threefolds as a special class of $Q$-factorial terminal Fano threefolds, with which we establish the $A$-stability and a proper transformation for an almost complete linear series. This achievement expands upon the earlier results of Shimizu and Takagi regarding Fano threefolds, and our methods incorporate an invariant approach utilizing the birational invariant $Q$-rank. Consequently, our findings provide the first evidence supporting the $A$-stability of Fano threefolds of rank greater than two. Moreover, our techniques yield the first proof of the almost complete intersection threefold $X_{12}$ having an 11-dimensional family. Furthermore, we demonstrate that 4-dimensional $Q$-Fano threefolds are either unirational or have an infinite rational family. This research is an initial step in our investigation of rational families among 4-dimensional Fano manifolds. It is our intention to build upon these results in future publications. 

This paper is part of our broader investigation into the rationality of Fano threefolds, and it presents an expansion of our earlier findings in [Shimizu-Takagi-Preprint]. Three-dimensional face reconstruction and alignment present difficulties when dealing with images featuring head poses that deviate from frontal and areas obstructed from view. Current methods that succeed in these situations often rely on additional information such as 3D models or markers attached to the subject's face. In our research, we introduce an end-to-end technique that generates 3D face models and aligns them with 2D landmark points without the need for labeling the images. This method utilizes a self-supervision regime in which 2D and 3D information are compared directly to minimize the gap between them. We enhance this comparison by integrating Riemannian surface analysis to account for the non-linear nature of 3D face geometry. Our approach is simple yet effective and achieves high accuracy levels without relying on labeling, making it suitable for applications involving diverse populations. We demonstrate the efficacy of our technique by achieving top rankings in the widely contested LFW dataset face reconstruction and alignment challenge. The code for our research is available for replication at our website.

We investigate the novel phenomenon of fractonic modes within a class of models characterized by a higher-critical-dimension Lie group symmetry. This analysis applies to the Ginzburg-Landau-Hertz framework, which represents a generic approach to chaotic quantum systems that can be disconnected from their equilibrium descriptions. We perform a detailed examination of the fractonic mode's properties, including its wave function, propagation constraints, and associated charges. Moreover, we demonstrate how the model can be modified to eliminate the fractonic mode's anomaly. Additionally, we discuss the implications of our findings for models exhibiting higher-critical-dimension Lie group symmetry and suggest that these models may be used to study the fractonic mode in the 2+1d Thouless scenario. Furthermore, we propose that the sound mode's constraint in the 3+1d Thouless scenario may be explained by a higher-critical-dimension U(1) symmetry within the Ginzburg-Landau-Hertz framework. Finally, we discuss the possibility that this explanation may be tested through the measurement of the sound mode's velocity in superconducting devices.

Research has been conducted to evaluate linear models with numerous parameters in high-dimensional environments characterized by non-sparse data. These studies typically assume the independence of data samples, which is not addressed by our research. We developed an evaluation framework for linear regression models in dense environments involving dependent data samples. Our framework comprises an infinite-parameter model and a four-dimensional family of linear autoregressive processes that can mimic various dependencies, including long-memory, short-memory, and simultaneous independence at multiple scales. Our primary finding shows that under dependent data conditions, the performance of the linear autoregressive process can be precisely evaluated using its spectral density, particularly how its shape at different frequencies influences the convergence rate of risk estimates. This discovery extends the traditional theory of dependent data, featuring distinct frequency-domain effects on the convergence rate of risk estimates. Our research also provides an empirical framework for evaluating the predictive performance of linear models in dense environments characterized by dependent data. This framework is demonstrated using two examples of dependent data sets: financial returns and internet traffic records. Our results indicate that conventional cross-validation techniques can lead to biased estimates of out-of-sample prediction accuracy in certain situations of dependent data. Furthermore, our research reveals that the performance of the infinite-parameter model can be comparable to that of the standard big-data model when data samples exhibit short-memory and are sufficiently large. This paper delves into various speech enhancement methods, focusing on deep learning-based techniques and their underlying architectures. We provide an in-depth analysis of prominent models, including Convolutional Neural Networks, Recurrent Neural Networks, and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory networks, highlighting both their individual strengths and the comparative benefits of combining masking, permutation, and alternative architectures in overcoming key challenges such as suppressing background noise and managing non-linear spectral transformations. Through theoretical insights and empirical evidence, we demonstrate the potential for these complex speech signals to be effectively modeled using simplified approaches that account for linearity and non-linearity in the speech production process. We also explore potential research paths, suggest evaluating models using objective measures that align with human perception, and emphasize the necessity for more comprehensive benchmark datasets to advance the field of speech enhancement. This comprehensive review aims to stimulate further innovation in speech enhancement technology. A negative pressure room (NPR) in biolabs and BSL-3 labs is crucial for containing pathogens that pose significant threats to national security. These facilities require a specific negative air pressure level to prevent the escape of microorganisms into the surrounding environment. Maintaining the desired negative pressure relies heavily on the proper function of the air pressure system, which in turn depends on the sealing of doors. Door sealing plays a vital role in achieving the required negative pressure needed to contain hazardous pathogens. The goal of this research is to develop an automated system capable of ensuring the doors in NPRs are properly sealed, which is essential for maintaining the necessary negative air pressure. The proposed system utilizes pressure sensors, along with a data collection and analysis software, to monitor and assess door sealing in real-time. The system was successfully implemented and tested for accuracy in two different NPRs located at the USAMRIID facility in Fort Gordon, Georgia. The results showed that the system is effective in detecting leaks in doors within a few seconds of closing, which is a critical timeframe for the containment of deadly pathogens. The system also demonstrated the ability to provide immediate visual alerts to facility staff through color-coded lights indicating proper sealing, minor adjustments needed, or significant leaks requiring immediate attention. The system has the potential to enhance the safety and efficiency of NPRs in biolabs and BSL-3 facilities. The software used in this research is also compatible with the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) guidelines for verifying the functional performance of NPRs. The system can be modified to accommodate various types and sizes of NPRs, as well as different types of doors and pressure systems. The system's findings have also contributed to the revision of the USAMRIID's NPR verification protocol.
