Deep neural networks (DNNs) have reached new heights in various computer vision tasks, thanks to the significant progress made in self-supervised pretraining. Despite achieving impressive results, these models still rely heavily on large, labeled datasets. Active learning (AL) offers an attractive solution by selectively asking human annotators to label model uncertainties and hard cases, thus efficiently utilizing limited human resources and extending data access to a broader range of sources, including potentially noisy or weakly labeled data. In this work, we investigate the combination of AL with self-supervised pretraining, introducing a novel framework known as pseudo-alternating optimization, where we alternate between generating diverse data using self-supposed models and selecting nearly diverse samples from potentially noisy or weakly labeled data using AL models. To achieve this, we employ both an entropy-based model uncertainty estimation and a graph-based diverse data sampling method. Experimental results on CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and Places365N under extreme data constraints show that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, indicating that our framework efficiently combines self-supervised pretraining and AL. Moreover, we demonstrate that our proposed method not only enhances model performance under limited labeled data but also improves robustness to noisy or weakly labeled data. The code and data used in this study are available online at https://github.com/zhengyangsun/AL-SSE.

Wireless communication technology has made rapid progress in recent years and is now an integral part of daily life. As the world becomes increasingly dependent on these technologies, ensuring secure data transfer between vehicles at intersections has become a pressing concern. Current methods used to simulate and evaluate intersection communication protocols are often inadequate, failing to capture essential aspects of these systems in action. In our research, we develop a comprehensive co-simulator for the VEPCAS framework, enabling a holistic evaluation of protocol security properties in relation to system design parameters. This simulator allows us to define and apply safety criteria to evaluate the risk of accidents based on vehicular movements and signal control. By utilizing the ATSC tool, we perform a formal verification of the simulated system to assess its security properties and identify potential risks. The benefits of our approach are illustrated through a case study of the WAVE system and a simulation of the VEPCAS framework, demonstrating the advantages of using our simulator, particularly the WAVE protocol with 802.11p at intersections. Our results indicate a significant enhancement in safety, achieving a low risk of accidents (<10^-6) within a reasonable latency period (<0.25s), when compared to an ideal scenario. This research provides a foundation for in-depth evaluations of various communication protocols and signal control algorithms, enabling the development of secure and efficient vehicular networks. However, our research reveals that this anomaly can be detected under certain conditions in the vortex lattice of a type-II superconductor. The origin of this observable feature is linked to the movement of vacancies within the vortex lattice rather than the movement of electrons near the vortex cores. Theoretical models have previously suggested the possibility of observing the Hall anomaly in this manner, although they were considered unrealistic at the time. Our findings indicate that the local disorder of the vortex state has a more substantial impact on the Hall anomaly than previously thought, necessitating the inclusion of vacancy disorder for an accurate understanding of the transport properties of type-II superconductors. Furthermore, our research implies that the vacancy disorder may also contribute to the onset of the normal-state Hall conductivity at non-zero magnetic fields. Consequently, this may provide a means of identifying the presence of vacancy disorder within the vortex state. Our numerical results are verified by comparisons with existing experimental data. Additionally, our study suggests that the vacancy disorder may be a crucial factor in determining the transport properties of type-II superconductors, including the movement of quasiparticles within the vortex state. This may have significant implications for the development of high-magnetic-field superconductors, where the vacancy disorder is likely a dominant factor. Our research is also relevant to other disordered systems displaying coexistence of order and disorder, such as the coexistence of ferromagnetism and spin glass disorder. In such cases, our study may provide a framework for understanding the interplay between these competing phenomena. In the case of high-magnetic-field superconductors, research into vacancy disorder is crucial for a deeper understanding of the vortex state and the development of materials capable of sustaining superconductivity in high magnetic fields. This is an important consideration for applications of superconductivity in high magnetic fields, such as magnetic resonance imaging and magnetic constrained applications. In such cases, fields of up to 20-30 Tesla are typically required, which may necessitate the development of superconducting materials capable of functioning in fields exceeding 30 Tesla. In order to achieve this goal, it is essential to develop a comprehensive understanding of the vacancy disorder within the vortex state of these materials. In this research, we develop a framework for incorporating vacancy disorder within the Ginzburg-Landau models, which enables the simulation of transport properties in the presence of magnetic fields. Our simulations demonstrate that vacancy disorder has a significant impact on the Hall conductivity

To ensure that machine learning models used in critical situations are highly reliable, various techniques such as verification methods and auditing processes can be employed to enhance their trustworthiness. A notable approach to achieve this involves creating proofs that the model's predictions align with its underlying design parameters and operational guidelines. However, implementing this method poses significant challenges, including verifying the validity of the proof and the auditing process itself. In this research, we propose an automated framework that utilizes algorithms to verify the correctness of the proof and the auditing process. This framework leverages tools from the SMT solver community and utilizes a standardized format for the machine learning model, audit data, and verification proofs. This research was applied to a real-world scenario involving the analysis of medical diagnosis models. The results showed that the proposed framework can efficiently verify the correctness of proofs and the auditing process in real-time, outperforming human experts in evaluating the validity of the proof by a significant margin. Furthermore, this research demonstrated the capability to automate the verification of proofs and the auditing process across multiple machine learning models, highlighting the potential for this framework to be applied to various other safety-critical applications. However, the research also identified potential scalability issues with the current approach, particularly when dealing with large-scale machine learning models. In such cases, the method may become computationally intensive and may require the use of distributed computing to achieve optimal results. In conclusion, the proposed framework offers a promising solution for enhancing the trustworthiness of machine learning models in critical situations, but further research is needed to address the scalability concerns. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, in agreement with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, the measurement of the transverse momentum of the top quark and the charge asymmetry of the two quarks revealed values of 20 GeV and 0.083, respectively, with uncertainties of 11 GeV and 0.033 for the former quantity, in line with predictions from various theoretical models. The task of generating SQL queries from text data pertains to converting unstructured text into structured database updates or queries. This complex task involves two vital components: identifying relationships between entities and formulating SQL commands. While numerous studies have explored this challenge in isolation, real-world scenarios demand models that can handle multiple, unrelated topics. In this research, we address cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing by developing a neural model and fine-tuning it on multiple topics with only limited paired data available. Our approach leverages pre-trained language models for both encoding text and SQL code, followed by the application of attention and graph linear units to model entity relationships and generate accurate SQL syntax. Machine learning models can be highly effective when trained using large, high-quality datasets. Nevertheless, building such models is notoriously difficult when working with limited, low-quality data, especially in sensitive domains where only sparse and unlabelled datasets are available. Theoretical frameworks like differential privacy can safeguard privacy, yet they significantly reduce the available data, rendering them impractical for such scenarios. The problem of private learning on sparse, unconnected graphs is particularly challenging due to its inherent complexity, which is compounded by the scarcity of nearby data points, lack of labels, and graph structure that is only partially understood. In our work, we introduce a novel private learning framework called DP-GraphNearestNeighbours (DP-GNN), which leverages the unique structure of each dataset's graph by employing a two-pronged approach. Firstly, DP-GNN is utilized for neighbour discovery and data reduction based on the estimated interconnectivity. Secondly, an adaptive mechanism is applied to ensure differential privacy for remaining data points. Our framework is evaluated on six datasets, which indicate that DP-GNN achieves superior accuracy at a lower cost compared to traditional private learning methods. Furthermore, our results show that DP-GNN is robust in scenarios where the graph structure is partially misunderstood. In this research, a novel approach is introduced to automatically generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define an optimization problem that ensures the generated roads are physically plausible and resemble real roads. As control points are adjusted, the corresponding road geometry changes significantly, necessitating a localized approximation to predict short-term effects on the system. To address this, we introduce a dual-time horizon approach, splitting control generation into two optimization stages: a long-term design based on simplified dynamics and a real-time adjustment using detailed vehicle models to minimize errors. This strategy was evaluated on multiple scenarios, demonstrating improved accuracy and safety compared to a single-time-horizon approach and a baseline method. Notably, our method achieved a 30% reduction in errors at higher time horizons (10 seconds) without significant increases in computational costs. Successful applications of this research include enhancing the testing of autonomous lane-keeping systems and simulating real-world driving scenarios for training and validation. Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. Recent advancements in deep learning, particularly the use of Recurrent models, have led to significant improvements in this area, however these improvements come with a cost of increased computational requirements and model complexity. This paper challenges these approaches by presenting a novel architecture that leverages external memory cells inspired by Neural Turing Machines, allowing for efficient and flexible temporal attention to be learned during inference. This model achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods on the ActivityNet dataset while requiring substantially less training time and model parameters. Notably, it exhibits an impressive 10 times reduction in parameters and 2-3 times decrease in training time when compared to existing methods. Furthermore, this paper introduces an innovative strategy for learning memory cell weights during inference, enabling the incorporation of additional memory cells in the proposed architecture. Experimental results and thorough analysis of the model's performance, computational efficiency, and memory usage are also provided. This work is made available as the Temporal Action Detection model, a publicly accessible repository. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhenglei1010/TAD-NMT. The long-lived, high-frequency coherent structures known as "holes" or "cavities" that form in plasma turbulence are of great interest to researchers. These structures, found in the Earth's poloidal hole region and the solar corona, consist of regions with reduced plasma density surrounded by enhanced magnetic field strength. Within these areas, localized electron motion creates a significant contribution to the cross-field current. The current's direction, however, poses a challenge to existing theories of plasma turbulence. In order to further understand the relationship between cavities and the turbulence that sustains them, we utilize high-resolution simulations of weakly stable turbulence in sloping magnetic landscapes. Our findings show that cavities form in regions of maximum turbulence amplitude and move directionally in response to changes in the background landscape. When encountering an obstacle, cavities become compressed and maintain their coherence, ultimately breaking down into smaller cavities that continue moving independently. The results of our research support the notion that cavities serve as localized regions of reduced plasma density linked to the enhancement of magnetic field strength. The motion of these structures is influenced by the direction of the background shear and the local direction of the turbulence, while their formation is driven by the turbulence itself. The discovery of cavities in our simulations, coupled with their characteristics and behavior, provides a deeper understanding of the complex phenomena observed in the solar corona. The findings of our study also raise further questions regarding the relationship between cavities and the energy released through solar flares and coronal mass ejections. Given an independent and identically distributed sequence of letters embedded in a long random text, the annealed large deviation principle (LDP) is characterized by a rate function that equals the specific relative entropy of the observed letter distribution among all possible distributions. This result can be extended to LDPs for the empirical process of a dependent sequence under an annealed topology, where the rate function is expressed as a sum of two components: the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution among all stationary distributions, and a term that accounts for dependence, characterized as the relative entropy of the observed distribution among all shift-invariant measures with given mean empirical frequency. These findings are particularly demonstrated for independent sequences satisfying a LDP with a rate function with multiple minima, resulting in an observed distribution that is a mixture of the minimum-point function and the equilibrium distribution. Additionally, the dependence of the rate function on the rate at which the sequence's dependence diminishes as its length increases is explored, leading to new results on the asymptotic properties of the rate function and its components as this rate tends to zero. All results are obtained without assuming the sequence's stationarity or the validity of a LDP. Instead, the annealed perspective is utilized, enabling the application of the annealed LDP to non-stationary sequences and sequences lacking an equilibrium distribution. Moreover, the specific relative entropy's role in LDPs is clarified through a general variational formula, applicable even to sequences lacking an equilibrium distribution. This formula is derived by combining the annealed LDP for the empirical process and its stationary counterparts, thereby extending the specific relative entropy's defining characteristic to sequences without an equilibrium distribution or stationary distribution. Continual learning models, trained on multiple batches without access to the entire dataset, encounter challenges when faced with new data. Our research focuses on an efficient approach known as "frozen pretraining," where a pre-trained model is used for initial performance and only specific learnable components are fine-tuned for each new dataset. Moreover, the model's ability to adapt to new classes with limited labeled data demonstrates its potential for real-world applications. We also analyzed the performance of various loss functions and optimization techniques to optimize continual learning. Our findings suggest that the "frozen pretraining" approach has a robust capacity to generalize well to new classes with a relatively small number of labeled samples. We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space that contains a specified set of Jordan curves, and investigate its properties. This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of the surfaces with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class in certain types of metric spaces. Furthermore, we establish that when the ambient space has a certain topological characteristic, maps that are relatively 1-homotopic are also relatively homotopic. Additionally, we demonstrate that strong local H"older regularity, characterized by a specific exponent depending on the dimension and the properties of the ambient space, is a feature of area-minimizing surfaces under certain conditions. This result extends previous work by Simon and Schoen, and provides a proof for the conjecture made by Simon. Finally, we show that strong local H"older regularity is a characteristic of area-minimizing surfaces that are also relatively 1-homotopic, and demonstrate its connection to the properties of harmonic maps and the minimal surface theorem. 

Keywords: Relative 1-homotopy type, surface with minimal area, strong local H"older regularity, harmonic maps, area-minimizing surfaces.

However, the development of more efficient solutions, particularly those with linear scalability in relation to the number of players, has been a long-standing goal in algorithmic economics. The algorithm's performance is evaluated in a comprehensive theoretical framework, which provides a precise analysis of its computational efficiency in relation to both the number of players and the problem's structural parameters. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment using k-fold cross-validation to account for limited training data. However, doing so forces the model to learn from different subsets of data for each parameter setting, hindering its ability to optimize these settings. This problem becomes even more pronounced when data is scarce, as is common in scientific studies involving expensive or difficult-to-obtain experiments. In such cases, models are typically refined using Monte Carlo cross-validation (MCXV), a method that involves multiple independent evaluations of the model on different random subsets of the available data and uses their average performance to adjust the parameters. In this work, we introduce a novel MCXV framework that leverages the benefits of both Monte Carlo cross-validation and gradient-based optimization to find the best model parameters. This framework is based on the Nose-Hoover thermostat dynamics, a well-established thermodynamic molecular dynamics method, and is mathematically proven to converge to the optimal parameters that minimize the cross-validation loss. Moreover, we provide a detailed implementation of the algorithm, discuss its key features, and demonstrate its effectiveness by applying it to three distinct machine learning models, including linear regression, support vector machines, and neural networks, using both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results of these experiments show that the algorithm outperforms traditional MCXV in all cases, requiring significantly fewer evaluations while achieving comparable or better performance. The source code for the algorithm is openly available for other researchers to utilize and adapt for their own machine learning applications. Furthermore, we also introduce an online visualization platform that enables researchers to compare the performance of different algorithms and provide the research community with open access to our results, encouraging the exchange of ideas and the comparison of new methods. This way, researchers can compare the performance of different algorithms and share their findings with the community. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) with Teacher-Student architectures have successfully incorporated external knowledge for task enhancement, primarily leveraging online databases or pre-trained models as teachers. Despite their success, these approaches are limited by resources and knowledge gaps when targets or training data are scarce. In such situations, exploiting off-policy experiences or distant knowledge can be beneficial. To address this challenge, we introduce a flexible knowledge distillation method called Reversing Knowledge Distillation (RKD), allowing the relaxation of traditional constraints such as shared parameters and separate teachers. RKD is formulated as an optimization problem that can be resolved using an efficient gradient-based update mechanism. Experimentally, our results show that RKD achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art knowledge distillation methods while effectively utilizing off-policy experiences or distant knowledge, leading to significant improvements in models applied to few-shot learning, targets unknown, and knowledge transfer scenarios. The code is available at https://github.com/zhengyang421/Reversing-Knowledge-Distillation.

We investigate how photon recoil influences the absorption of light in ultracold gases consisting of two hyperfine states of the $^{87}$Rb D$_2$ transition. Our research reveals that photon recoil has a notable effect on the absorption profile, causing it to broaden and shift in relation to the laser frequency. Furthermore, under conditions typical to lattice experiments, both effects become substantial, leading to an intricate interconnection between absorption and scattering properties. Our findings also imply that photon recoil results in an asymmetrical distribution of atoms between the two hyperfine states, a phenomenon that can be mitigated through the use of a laser with a narrower frequency profile or by employing a different hyperfine transition. Moreover, our research provides a framework for relating absorption and scattering properties in ultracold gases, making it relevant to the context of lattice clocks and other applications requiring precise control of photon-atom interactions.

A transition from force to friction-driven behavior occurs during thickening, with implications for the flow properties and microstructure developed under high stresses. The model also accurately predicts the effects of increasing shear modulus on the flow properties and structure of the network, including the development of shear bands and a significant increase in normal forces between neighboring particles. The developed model allows for the comparison of flow properties and network structure to those found in entangled polymers and granular materials. A notable distinction is found in the force distribution between these systems, with a bimodal distribution observed in the network of hard disks, in contrast to a unimodal distribution seen in entangled polymers and granular materials, all of which exhibit long-range forces. The distinct characteristics of the network of hard disks, specifically the bimodal force distribution and a distinct pair of forces corresponding to the shear and confining stresses, may provide a means for distinguishing the effects of friction and force on the structure of soft matter networks. The model demonstrates that increasing the strength of long-range forces leads to a decrease in normal forces between particles, a shift in the force distribution to shorter distances, and an increase in shear stresses necessary to produce the same level of disorder in the network. The model is validated against experiments involving a dense suspension of hard disks subject to long-range forces, with a notable agreement in flow curves and microstructure. This research paper proposes a novel framework for safety-guaranteed control of complex nonlinear systems subject to input limitations. Specifically, it develops an Input Constrained Control Barrier Function (ICCBF) that ensures the system stays within a predetermined safe boundary while minimizing energy expenditure. The main contribution involves showing ICCBF's equivalence to Control Lyapunov Functions (CLFs) and demonstrating its local uniqueness. Moreover, the framework is applied to a practical example involving a quadcopter's orientation control. Computational efficiency is achieved through the use of smooth, differentiable formulations of both ICCBF and its derivative, enabling the development of an optimal control solution using direct transcription methods. The effectiveness of the proposed framework and algorithms is demonstrated through simulations and actual quadcopter experiments. The findings highlight the potential of input-constrained control techniques to achieve both safety and optimality in complex robotic systems. The COVID-19 pandemic's disruptions to global trade, coupled with pre-existing overcapacity and inefficient shipping networks, have created a critical congestion crisis in container shipping. To gain deeper insight into this complex issue, a computational model incorporating key factors such as shipping schedules, vessel capacity, cargo demand, and carrier behavior was developed and solved using an algorithm that reflects the strategic decision-making of carriers. Empirical analysis using historical data from the Asia-Europe trade route helped validate the model, and computational experiments were conducted to examine the effects of different variables on the crisis, particularly the impact of capacity utilization, demand variability, and network structure. Notably, the results indicate that increased demand beyond 95% of capacity may significantly raise the risk of congestion, and more direct shipping routes can reduce congestion by as much as 30%. Furthermore, the model suggests that carriers' ability to adjust their schedules in response to changing demand conditions plays a critical role in mitigating the crisis. To address these challenges, the study recommends a range of policy interventions, including the adoption of dynamic freight contracts, changes to slot allocation practices, and investments in shipping infrastructure. The research also highlights the benefits of using computational models to analyze complex shipping network dynamics and identify opportunities for improvement. The model and data employed in this study are publicly available to facilitate further research and testing by other scholars. The study's findings are set to be validated with actual data from carriers once access is granted. The proposed research framework is seen as a starting point for exploring other critical issues in container shipping, such as the effects of climate change on shipping networks and the implications of new trade agreements. The study's results are relevant to policymakers, carriers, and shipping associations seeking to mitigate the effects of the congestion crisis and promote sustainable and efficient shipping practices. The research is part of a broader project that aims to develop a comprehensive theoretical model of shipping networks, building on existing research in this area. The project's outcomes are intended to contribute to the advancement of computational transportation science and inform policy decisions that affect the global shipping industry. Furthermore, this correspondence enables the extension of Thurston's point-counting theorem to veering triangulations. Additionally, the volume of the corresponding terrain is expressed in terms of the dynamics of the rational map. This result is then utilized to derive an alternative expression for the volume of terrain volumes previously described by Lecuire and Levenbaum. Moreover, an inequality is established to measure the volume of terrain volumes relative to the volume of terrain volumes associated with irreducible rational maps. This inequality is shown to be an equality in situations where the terrain volumes are topologically equivalent to each other. As a consequence, it is demonstrated that the volume of terrain volumes is distinct for veering triangulations corresponding to non-isomorphic rational maps. Finally, this distinction leads to a method of distinguishing between many veering triangulations. Moreover, this approach enables the solution of the non-unique veering triangulation problem for rational maps of degree at least 2. Furthermore, this new description of the boundary of loom spaces is shown to be equivalent to a product space that includes the boundary of veering triangulations as a component. This deformation preserves features like Ahlfors regularity, Poincare inequality validity, and tangent cones with positive scalar curvature. In Part II, we employ surgery-style arguments to successfully remove the singular sets present in these geometries. Beginning with a compact, minimal subset defined within a manifold satisfying certain conditions, we can perform a sequence of surgeries to eliminate all singular areas, ultimately arriving at a smoothly compact, minimal subset within a conformally deformed manifold possessing positive scalar curvature. Notably, the overall sequence of surgeries is both controlled and predictable, guaranteeing that the resulting compact, smooth minimal subset exhibits strong similarities to its original singular counterpart. Moreover, this process is also applicable to areas that are not necessarily compact, allowing us to obtain non-compact, smooth minimal subsets defined within a manifold of positive scalar curvature. These results can be further generalized to apply to various types of volumes and growth rates. Ultimately, our findings provide a significant framework for understanding the topology of compact, singular areas within a manifold of positive scalar curvature. This peak amplitude is directly proportional to the viscosity of the vortex liquid multiplied by the square of the thermal gradient and inversely proportional to the magnetic field. Penalized predictive control (PPC) is a model-free optimization method derived from model predictive control (MPC), which reduces PPC to an efficient computation by minimizing a quadratic function subject to linear constraints. Our contribution involves showing that employing PPC with a properly designed cost function and penalty matrix essentially mimics the behavior of its MPC counterpart. Furthermore, we have developed an explicit expression for calculating PPC parameters that yield a desired cost function behavior. These findings enable us to relax assumptions on state and control vector linearity, providing a practical solution for robust performance in scenarios where the future input and state trajectories can be anticipated with certainty. Moreover, we have established that online computation of PPC is no more demanding than its offline counterpart, requiring only $O(n^3)$ operations compared to $O(n^2)$ for its static counterpart, where $n$ represents the number of variables. We have also demonstrated the superiority of PPC over MPC in terms of scalability for large systems by applying it to a linear quadratic regulator problem of unprecedented size. We have approximated the performance of PPC under uncertainty conditions by utilizing nominal system trajectories and validated our approach with two case studies. The results obtained with PPC outperformed those achieved through MPC for systems of sizes $10^3$, $10^4$, and $10^5$ dimensions. The code used for this research is openly accessible at https://github.com/ivanfoster/penalized_control. We have also included within the code a Python application that generates the plots presented in this research, utilizing the matplotlib library. Moreover, the implementation of PPC is comparable in efficiency to the established optimization software SNOPT, as verified through a system of $10^3$ dimensions, necessitating the rejection of our contribution for publication on one specific journal due to its editorial policies. Nonetheless, we have successfully disseminated our research in its present form. 

Keywords: model-free control, model predictive control, nonlinear control systems, optimal control, state space models.

One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers of the two stars, or their separation, with one star potentially becoming a compact remnant if conditions are right. To study these events, researchers rely on computational simulations of the CE phase. However, these simulations are hindered by the requirement for a realistic representation of the interaction between stars and their surroundings, which necessitates a well-behasted approach using robust solvers. Despite the availability of robust solvers for individual stars, the use of smoothed mesh methods like finite volume and finite difference schemes has significant limitations when modeling the CE phase due to their inability to handle non-overlapping domains efficiently. In contrast, smoothed-particle hydrodynamics (SPH) offers a more suitable framework for modeling the CE phase, which involves significant non-overlapping domains. However, SPH has faced criticism for its poor performance in resolving sharp interfaces, which is exacerbated in the CE phase. In an effort to address these limitations, researchers have explored alternative methods, such as combining SPH with other hydrodynamics codes, which often result in hybrid approaches that are difficult to maintain over the course of a CE phase simulation. In an attempt to overcome these challenges, a new approach has been developed that utilizes a robust solver for individual stars and the Lagrangian smoothed-particle approach for representing the envelope. In this new approach, particles are assigned to either the stellar component or the envelope component based on their association with either the potential energy of the stars or the potential energy of the envelope. This separation enables the efficient use of robust solvers for individual stars and the Lagrangian smoothed-particle approach for representing the envelope. As a result, this new approach allows for the accurate modeling of the CE phase, which involves significant non-overlapping domains, and facilitates the use of robust solvers for individual stars. In an effort to validate this new approach, it has been applied to a well-studied CE scenario involving a massive star and a companion with a highly eccentric orbit. We investigated the drag experienced by a long, thin cylinder moved through a granular medium by performing experiments with cylinders of varying length-to-diameter ratios. Our findings show that the drag anisotropy in these situations isn't greatly affected by the direction from which the force is measured, except when the force is applied perpendicular to the cylinder's long axis. Our data indicate that the drag anisotropy of a cylindrical intruder changes its behavior based on the cylinder's length-to-diameter ratio, shifting from isotropic behavior for ratios less than 3 to anisotropic behavior for ratios greater than 3. Our results also reveal that the drag force can be broken down into two components: one that is directly proportional to the force exerted normally to the cylinder's surface, and another that is influenced by the cylinder's length and diameter but not the direction from which it is applied. We developed a theoretical framework that takes into account the angular displacement of grains at the point of contact with the cylinder and the possibility of grain rearrangement, and we used this framework to create a model that explains our experimental data. We found that our model is able to accurately predict the drag force's dependence on the cylinder's length-to-diameter ratio, and that it may be applied to a broader range of intruder geometries. However, we also acknowledge that our model assumes a fixed and uniform confining pressure, and that further research is needed to validate its application to more complex and dynamically changing situations. Futhermore, we observed that the drag force experienced by a cylindrical intruder exhibits a critical force below which the force becomes highly nonlinear and direction-dependent, and that this critical force is directly proportional to the confining pressure of the granular medium. We believe that this critical force represents a threshold for grain rearrangement and intruder movement, and that it may be an important factor in understanding the dynamics of intruders in granular materials. Overall, our research provides new insights into the complex and nonlinear behavior of granular materials when subjected to forces applied through an intruder, and highlights the need for further research into the microscale phenomena governing these situations. Additionally, we suggest that our findings may be relevant to the study of intruders in other non-Newtonian fluids, such as polymers and suspensions. Finally, we propose that our results may be used to improve existing models for intruder forces, and that they offer a new perspective on the issue of force directionality in granular materials.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings also suggest outflows play a crucial role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, with implications for the development of massive galaxies. Furthermore, we observed outflows moving at high velocities, likely powered by the merger that triggered the galaxy's starburst, as well as slower-moving outflows caused by the galaxy's ongoing star formation. Our research highlights the significance of outflows in managing the conversion of gas into stars, a key process that shapes the evolution of galaxies. It also underscores the importance of studying the interactions between outflows, gas, and star formation in galaxies, particularly during periods of intense starbursts. By examining these interactions, we can gain a deeper understanding of how outflows influence the formation of galaxies and the central black holes within them. In contrast, we've developed a Structured Bayesian Optimization framework that leverages the computer system's underlying structure to focus limited experimental resources on promising configuration paths. By applying this approach to a real-world cloud workload, we've achieved a 4x reduction in required experiments while finding a 30% better optimal configuration. Our method's performance gain results from efficiently exploiting structural knowledge that informs where to look for optimal solutions, thereby outperforming traditional methods which must experiment their way to this understanding. Although our technique yields significant performance gains, it's essential to note that these gains are achieved without any prior expertise on the system's optimal configuration. As a result, our approach still discovers a system's optimal structure and corresponding configuration in the desired performance tier in the orders of tens to hundreds of seconds, a duration that's substantially shorter than the time it takes to run the system under normal operating conditions. Furthermore, our method's efficiency can be further enhanced by an order of magnitude with minimal performance degradation when employing a coarser search space. Ultimately, our research offers a Structured Bayesian Optimization framework that represents a foundational framework for efficiently tuning complex computer systems. The classic use of Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) to analyze statistical data, based on independent observations, is a well-established technique. However, when working with data from stochastic processes, where multiple observations are closely linked, a combination of asymptotic independence and a known distribution can lead to inferior results. This paper introduces a new general method to improve MLE, called Deep Neural Network Maximum Likelihood Estimation (DNN-MLE), allowing for the efficient estimation of parameters from data, even in cases of significant dependence and unknown theoretical distribution properties. Theoretical and practical evidence demonstrate DNN-MLE's effectiveness in process data settings, outperforming traditional MLE with only a small increase in computational cost. This is further illustrated by two successful applications of DNN-MLE: one in signal processing and another in machine learning. The source code for these examples is freely available online. By leveraging the flexibility of DNNs and the simplicity of MLE, DNN-MLE offers a powerful and accessible solution for parameter estimation in data-driven settings. On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to its normal subgroups of index 2. These subgroups divide the tree into two equivalent parts. We also explore the relationship between periodic measures and these subgroups' conjugacy classes. This relationship is described by a compact right uniform transitive graph whose vertices represent the conjugacy classes of index 2 subgroups and whose edges represent the conjugation between them. This graph is constructed from the Cayley graph of the group acting on the tree. Furthermore, we show that the positive measures on this graph, which are invariant under group actions, can be lifted to periodic measures on the Ising model. These measures are unique up to scalar multiplication and there is a one-to-one correspondence between them and the invariant measures on the graph. If the graph has no loops and its edges are distinct, we prove that there is a one-to-one correspondence between its invariant measures and those of the Ising model. If the graph has isolated vertices, we demonstrate that there are measure correspondences that preserve periodic measures with positive probabilities on those vertices. Additionally, we establish the uniqueness of the quenched free energy of the Ising model when the graph has no loops and distinct edges. If the graph includes loops or has overlapping edges, the uniqueness of the quenched free energy may not hold. We provide an example where the Ising model's quenched free energy is non-unique. We also derive an explicit formula for the quenched free energy when the graph is a tree without loops or overlapping edges. This formula is analogous to the Bethe free energy equation, a self-consistency equation for the variables that characterize the periodic measures. We conclude by discussing the relationship between the periodic measures obtained and those proposed by Katsura within the context of quantum systems. Quantum systems' periodic measures correspond to index 2 subgroups within the dynamical group's centralizer, whereas the classical Ising model's periodic measures correspond to index 2 subgroups within the group that acts transitively on the tree's Cayley graph. We also discuss the potential for generalizing these results to other discrete interacting systems on trees. We end by highlighting the potential for applying these results to study the dynamics of quantum systems in their interrelation with classical statistical systems. Despite its versatility, implementing high-order methods on non-uniform grids poses a significant challenge. To overcome this obstacle, a new approach has been devised, enabling the construction of second-order methods for Hamiltonian PDEs. This innovative approach ensures that the underlying Hamiltonian remains preserved, a crucial property inherent in most numerical techniques. By leveraging this new framework, several explicit and implicit time-stepping schemes have been created, each with a proven second-order accuracy. To enhance convergence, a technique known as "immersed boundary method" can be employed, allowing for the numerical solution to utilize high-order methods on non-uniform grids within each time-step. Through the use of high-order methods on non-uniform grids, significant improvements in computational efficiency and precision can be achieved. However, this approach necessitates the solution of a large, approximate Hamiltonian system. To address this challenge, several iterative methods have been developed, each offering a viable solution strategy. To validate the performance of these new time-stepping schemes, numerical experiments have been conducted. Furthermore, the new schemes have been applied to an ideal MHD model, a notoriously challenging problem, and the results indicate that they can produce high-resolution, smooth solutions. This innovative approach has far-reaching implications, enabling the development of more efficient and accurate numerical methods for complex problems. As such, it has significant potential to drive significant advancements in numerical research. We developed three-dimensional hydrodynamic models of superbubble formation to
study the early stages of dust production, specifically in low-metallicity
environments, for a time frame of approximately 0.5 million years. Our models
account for dust creation through supernovae and the growth of dust grains in
the interstellar medium. Assuming a fixed dust-to-metal ratio, we tracked the
amount of dust produced in the superbubble and its surrounding area. Analyzing
our results, we estimated the rate of dust grain growth to be around 0.1 to 1
times the rate of supernovae in the inner regions of the superbubble, and this
rate decreased with distance from the central stars. Based on our models, dust
grains grew primarily in the cooler outer regions of the superbubble, while the
inner hotter regions were dominated by the dissipation of supernova mechanical
energy. However, our models also indicated that the dissipation of this energy
occurs more efficiently when dust grains are present. Consequently, the efficient
cooling of the gas in the outer regions of the superbubble is facilitated by
dust grains, and we estimated that the cooling rate is enhanced by a factor of 1
to 10 due to dust grain growth. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the
supernovae's impact on dust production is significantly more important than the
effect of gas self-abundance in the inner regions of the superbubble. Nevertheless, the overall mass of dust formed in these regions remains relatively small, on the order of a few thousand times less than the total dust content observed in the Milky Way. This discrepancy arises because our models only account for the early stages of dust production within a single superbubble, and a more comprehensive study encompassing multiple generations of superbubbles is required to fully address this issue. Moreover, such a comprehensive study would also need to consider the effects of gas inflows and outflows, as well as the merging of superbubbles, to accurately capture the full dust production process. Consequently, our research provides a fundamental understanding of dust production within a single superbubble but also highlights the necessity for a more intricate analysis of the complex dust formation processes that occur in the universe. Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances using lidar sensors is a critical task for autonomous vehicles, but it is also a challenging one to master. The difficulty lies in identifying rare and distant targets by training models on balanced datasets. To address this imbalance, we propose a novel approach that combines data augmentation techniques tailored to point cloud data. These techniques enable the creation of artificial targets with specific characteristics, allowing for the generation of a more balanced dataset. By applying this approach to a single dataset, we were able to effectively mimic targets with characteristics that required collection in the wild, such as those found on highways. Notably, our method does not involve the use of pseudo targets, which are constructed from existing targets through manipulation, in contrast to other approaches. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through experiments conducted on the Baidu ApolloWaymo dataset, a publicly available dataset, in the form of metric learning and target detection tasks. Our results show significant improvements over baseline models trained on unbalanced datasets, indicating that our data augmentation techniques are robust and transferable to other datasets. The code and models developed as part of this research have been made available for public use. Further research into the field is encouraged by our findings.

The temperature-dependent speed of sound in spin-polarized strange quark matter was identified, and we established the minimum temperature for the stability of spin-polarized strange quark stars at various magnetic field strengths. Additionally, we established the critical temperature for the stability of spin-polarized strange quark stars in the absence of a magnetic field, confirming that it aligns with previously reported values. Computer simulations of spinning strange quark stars in a vacuum were utilized to determine the relationship between the star's spin frequency and the rate of elliptical oscillations, and we calculated the emission spectra of thermal spin-polarized strange quark stars across various temperatures and magnetic fields, and in the presence of a strong magnetic field, we observed the emergence of spectral emission in the X-ray, gamma-ray, and infrared bands. The thermal emission spectra of spinning strange quarks exhibit a broad spectral range that encompasses X-ray, gamma-ray, and infrared bands, and we anticipate that future space missions will detect the infrared emission spectrum of spinning strange quark stars. The detection of infrared emission from spinning strange quark stars would provide conclusive evidence for the existence of these exotic celestial objects. Moreover, we found that a strong magnetic field significantly enhances the emission of infrared radiation from spinning strange quarks, and we propose that the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope be utilized to investigate the infrared emission from spinning strange quarks in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Finally, we established that the density of spin-polarized strange quark matter is lowered in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and we predict that the density of neutron stars will exhibit a similar decrease in the presence of strong magnetic fields, and that this effect will be observable in low-density neutron star candidates. The findings of this research will be verifiable through the detection of infrared emission from spinning strange quarks, and the density of neutron stars in low-density neutron star candidates. The detection of these celestial objects will confirm the existence of exotic matter in the universe. Furthermore, the properties of spin-polarized strange quark matter will provide a deeper understanding of the universe's most fundamental constituents

A graph G is classified as Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian (PMH) if it lacks a perfect matching in G and every minimal cut in G contains a hamiltonian cycle. This concept was initially introduced by Lovasz and Plummer in their book titled "Matching Theory". A graph is considered PMH-critical if it is PMH and the removal of any edge from the graph results in a non-PMH graph. Our research focuses on determining the number of 2-edge-connected simple graphs with at most 11 vertices that are PMH-critical. Specifically, we will present the results of our analysis in the form of a table and also provide examples of PMH-critical graphs to support our findings. Moreover, we will offer examples of 2-edge-connected simple graphs with at most 11 vertices that are PMH-critical in our research dataset. Notably, these examples will supplement existing knowledge of PMH-critical graphs, as identified by Yoro and Zhang, by adding five new graphs to the existing list of 16 graphs. Among these newly added graphs, four will be featured in a special issue of this journal, whereas the fifth graph will be presented in a forthcoming article by Yoro. Yoro's contributions to this research are the result of his doctoral studies under the supervision of Zhang. Recent research on block designs by Amarra, Devillers, and Praeger, involving specific quadratic polynomials, shows potential connections to a significant conjecture known as the Bunyakovsky Conjecture. This conjecture posits a relationship between certain algebraic functions and number-theoretic concepts, specifically concerning the densities of numbers generated by these functions, as well as densities of congruence classes. Building upon their work, we extend their findings to a broader range of parameters, establishing a connection between their designs and the Bunyakovsky Conjecture. Additionally, our research reveals new instances of numbers with specific quadratic factors, providing a connection between these factors and the densities of numbers generated by the algebraic functions mentioned earlier. Furthermore, we present a new example of a design with a higher number of blocks, as well as a new lower bound on the size of certain sets containing numbers with specific quadratic factors. This achievement is made possible by an innovative application of a recent result on the distribution of square-free numbers due to Pomerance. We also outline a potential approach to generalize our results to a broader range of parameters. Moreover, we explore connections to ongoing research in number theory. 

Keywords: Bunyakovsky Conjecture, Quadratic Polynomials, Block Designs, Number Theory.

This approach requires the presence of heavy, right-handed neutrinos with large Majorana masses to make the small neutrino mass possible. In this context, we examine the effect of left-handed neutrinos having a Majorana nature rather than being purely left-handed as typically assumed. Instead, we introduce a global $U(1)_{L_
u}$ symmetry to explain the near-degeneracy of the lightest Majorana neutrino mass within the Standard Model. Utilizing this symmetry, we can derive the relationship between the lightest neutrino mass and the scale associated with the $U(1)_{L_
u}$ symmetry, which we find to be in the range of $0.05\,\mathrm{eV}$ to $0.35\,\mathrm{eV}$ for the mass of the lightest neutrino. Furthermore, we investigate the connection between this scale and the parameters of the heavy right-handed neutrinos, which are found to be in the range of $10^{11}\,\mathrm{eV}$ to $10^{14}\,\mathrm{eV}$ for the lightest two of these neutrinos. In addition, we explore the implications of our model for the generation of the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe. Ultimately, we find that our scenario is compatible with the available observational data, which includes the results from neutrinoless double beta decay experiments, the effective number of neutrino species, the cosmic microwave background, and the abundance of primordial elements. Consequently, our model predicts a non-zero electron neutrino mass, which will be confirmed or refuted in the near future with the completion of the KATRIN experiment. Moreover, we find that our scenario is consistent with the observed pattern of neutrino mixing, which arises as a consequence of the symmetry $U(1)_{L_
u}$ acting on the three generations of neutrinos. Finally, we find that our model includes a right-handed parity symmetry, which is broken at the level of the right-handed neutrino interactions, resulting in a Majorana mass term for these particles. Consequently, we predict that the lightest right-handed neutrino has a mass in the range of $10^{11}\,\mathrm{eV}$ to $10^{14}\,\mathrm{eV}$. This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are organized on a grid. A streamlined variation of the Rao-Blackwellized point mass filter predicts the density of unobserved targets, arranging them in an orderly grid-based structure. Contrary to conventional Gaussian mixture models, which suffer from'spurious and diffuse components', this approach maintains a tidy and coherent representation of unobserved targets. As a result, the grid-based density can effectively prune false positives resulting from false alarms, thereby improving the accuracy of target detection. The effectiveness of this grid-based density is demonstrated through simulations of target detection and tracking scenarios. Compared to conventional algorithms, it is shown that the grid-based density exhibits superior performance in terms of precision, recall, and the mean squared error of target location. In particular, it is found that the algorithm's ability to represent unobserved targets as a coherent grid-based density leads to a significant reduction in the mean number of components in the filter. In scenarios with limited target density or slow target movement, an analytical variation of the filter is also developed and found to perform similarly to the numerical version. In such cases, the algorithm's memory usage and computation time are significantly reduced. In conclusion, the grid-based representation of target appearance probabilities is shown to lead to a more accurate and efficient implementation of the filter. In scenarios with high target density or rapid target movement, a stratified variation of the filter is developed, which divides the grid into smaller sections to improve tracking performance. The challenges and potential solutions to extending this approach to three-dimensional scenarios are also discussed. In such cases, potential solutions could involve the use of cloud-like representations of targets and the application of cloud-then-samples filtering. The associated code for this research is publicly available on GitHub. This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior degenerate diffusion component. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, and subsequently deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame. Notably, the new Carleman estimate incorporates an interior point and is derived utilizing a horizontal weighted energy approach, along with appropriate time-weighted inequalities. Moreover, our results yield a significantly improved observability inequality, providing explicit constants and a precise structure for the cost functional required for control. Ultimately, this enables the identification of an optimal control location and duration, thereby contributing to the resolution of a nonlinear convex optimization problem. Computational examples are provided to illustrate the effectiveness of this approach in determining optimal control solutions in both theoretical and practical scenarios. Moreover, our innovative use of Carleman estimates paves the way for addressing more intricate population models involving multiple populations and nonlinear diffusion components. Lastly, the associated numerical challenges are discussed and potential strategies for resolution are outlined.

Our method involves creating a simulation environment that can estimate the expected utility of each possible action, taking into account the probability of achieving goals such as scoring or preventing the opposing team from scoring. The model is refined through reinforcement learning to make more accurate predictions. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging remains a complex challenge, particularly when interpreting data with small amplitudes. Conventional full-waveform inversion is limited by the mapping issue and tends to stick to artificial models. A new approach called wavefield reconstruction inversion aims to address this problem by reconstructing the wavefield that matches observed seismic data, rather than inverting for subsurface properties directly. This approach is mathematically formulated as a least-squares optimization problem using the adjoint method, and we introduce a new time-domain implementation of WRI based on this formulation. By comparing it to the frequency-domain implementation, we find that the time-domain method produces more accurate results and is more robust in terms of convergence, likely due to the reduced impact of temporal aliasing. A further comparison of time-domain WRI to time-domain FWI using the Marmousi model demonstrates that WRI can generate more detailed and realistic reconstructions of the subsurface, especially in areas with complex geometries and small impedance contrasts. Notably, WRI is able to recover detailed information about small-scale structures, such as faults, without the artifacts that FWI tends to introduce under strong wavefield conditions. This improvement is attributed to the reduced nonlinearity of WRI when compared to FWI. Overall, the results of this study support the use of time-domain WRI for accurate and robust reconstruction of subsurface wavefields. However, further research is needed to extend this method to seismic imaging using multiple sources and receivers, and to investigate its application to different types of seismic data, such as data acquired in the presence of noise. Additionally, a comparison of time-domain WRI to other imaging methods, such as time-domain FWI and semi-blance-based imaging, is also required to better understand its performance under different conditions. This study provides a foundation for these extensions and comparisons in future research. We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between photons within the resonators, allowing us to build optical diodes and isolators. Notably, we've demonstrated the functionality of an optical diode using two degenerate modes in a Michelson interferometer setup, and the functionality of an optical isolator using a coupled resonator system with nondegenerate modes. Both systems operated at high speeds, with data transfer rates reaching 1 Gbit/s and optical isolation levels exceeding 30 dB. This approach offers a compact, efficient, and coherent method for controlling light without the need for thermal tuning or the integration of electronic components. We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the spin period to be 12.424 seconds with a significant error margin, confirming previous measurements from 2010 and 2016. Our spectral analysis revealed a 0.67 keV thermal neutron temperature originating from the accretor's surface and a high 0.87 keV temperature from the companion's infrared emission, consistent with 1.57 keV observed in 2016. The iron abundance was found to be marginally elevated at 1.4 times the solar rate, in contrast to the significantly higher iron content observed in 2016. The 3.79 x 10^18 Hz cutoff frequency, a product of the neutron star's magnetic field, showed a notable decrease of about 30% compared to 2016, resulting in a magnetic field strength of approximately 6.04 x 10^{12} Gauss. The radial distance between the pulsar and the molecular cloud, as inferred from the soft state spectrum in 2016, was estimated to be around 300 parsecs with a significant margin of error. However, this analysis was excluded from the main study as it did not meet the necessary criteria for Type-I spectrum classification. Furthermore, we detected significant positive and negative orbital sidebands in the Fourier spectrum with amplitudes of 0.35 and 0.27 electrons respectively, corresponding to an orbital period of 19.78 hours and an eccentricity of approximately 0.20. These findings are consistent with previously reported values for the system's parameters. Our analysis of the hardness intensity diagram revealed a quasiperiodic behavior with a 1.58 day cycle, potentially linked to the orbital period, as well as two distinct branches, indicating the presence of a hard thermal cutoff that varies with orbital phase. The lower branch in the hardness-intensity diagram, observed during the decline phase, is characterized by a 0.53 keV thermal cutoff, in contrast to the 0.67 keV cutoff seen during the rise phase. These results provide further insight into the behavior of IGR J19294+1816, particularly its complex HIDs and the variation of the cutoff energy with orbital phase. To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetric ecological model is developed for two competing species, one of which has unidirectional dispersal capabilities. By applying the method of invariant manifolds, the model is reduced to a pairwise interaction model that accurately reflects the dynamics of an original four-dimensional system. Numerical computations and visualizations of the reduced model reveal a complex, dynamically dynamic landscape affected by the immigrant species' ability to settle in new habitats. As immigration increases, the species with dispersal capabilities gains ground, while the stationary species' ability to occupy space diminishes. The model's findings are confirmed through a comparison with an established model featuring symmetric species competition. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of the invariant manifold method in analyzing complex ecological systems and highlights the importance of considering the effects of dispersal and immigration on species competition. The developed model can serve as a foundation for future studies on the dynamics of ecological systems characterized by asymmetric species interactions. The approach to reducing complex models through the identification of invariant manifolds may also be applied to other ecological and biological models. Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, and their use continued through the Middle Ages. Sundials played a crucial role in classical Islamic civilization, where the Sun's daily movement was closely observed and utilized for prayer and daily life purposes. As the civilization progressed, sundials evolved to accommodate local time zones and geographical specifications, revealing the advanced understanding of astronomy and mathematics among Islamic scholars. This study aims to examine sundials used in the Islamic world during the Middle Ages, focusing on examples from the Nasser District in Cairo, Egypt. Recent archaeological excavations uncovered several undisturbed tombs containing sundials, which were used to determine their local time and connection to the Islamic calendar. By utilizing non-invasive techniques such as 3D scanning and archaeological data, this study successfully reconstructed the sundials and calculated their local time. The findings indicate that the sundials were aligned with the rising and setting of the Sun during specific dates, which coincided with Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha celebrations. The discovery of the sundials' alignment with the solar year and the Islamic calendar provides new insights into the mathematical understanding of the Islamic world during the Middle Ages. The study also raises questions about the possibility of the sundials being linked to the measurement of the solar year, which is equivalent to 365.24 days, and how this understanding might have influenced the Islamic calendar's calculation. The findings from the Cairo-based sundials may serve as a starting point for further research into the use of sundials in other regions within the Islamic world during the Middle Ages. The study's results also highlight the significance of combining archaeological and astronomical data to gain a deeper understanding of the historical context and the mathematical and astronomical knowledge of past civilizations. The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is being explored for the purpose of spherical aberration correction in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Researchers investigated the potential of these phase plates to achieve high-resolution imaging by simulating and analyzing the performance of various designs. The study indicates that custom-made phase plates can attain a level of spatial resolution down to 0.4 Angstroms, which is comparable to the resolution provided by the spherical correction system in TEMs. Moreover, the study reveals that the optimal design of the phase plates is highly dependent on the TEM's spherical correction system and can be optimized through the use of multi-objective genetic algorithm simulations. The findings also show that the performance of the custom-made phase plates is comparable to that of the spherical correction system in TEMs, with an information capacity of down to 0.4 Angstroms. The study's results provide valuable insights into the design of effective programmable electrostatic phase plates for the improvement of imaging in TEMs. The potential of these phase plates to improve imaging resolution makes them a promising alternative to spherical correction systems. The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its quality and completeness, the underlying representation of this text is often overlooked, despite its significant impact on model performance. This paper argues that merely assessing text-generated results is insufficient and proposes a more comprehensive approach to enhance representation understanding. We introduce a novel prediction task called the Next Token Prediction Score (NTPS), which gauges the representation's ability to forecast the next word in a sentence. To validate this approach, NTPS is applied to a thorough analysis of representation influences on multiple factors, including fluency, semantically-driven tasks, and dialogue tasks. Experimental results show that NTPS can effectively evaluate the effectiveness of various models and evaluation methods in these scenarios. Moreover, by utilizing NTPS, we demonstrate its utility in guiding the design of better evaluation strategies and advancing the state-of-the-art in dialogue models. The proposed NTPS is made available to the research community through an accompanying toolkit that is easy to utilize and adaptable to diverse evaluation scenarios. By adopting this approach, we hope to promote a shift towards a more holistic understanding of representation quality in data-driven dialogue models. This shift emphasizes not just text-generated quality but also the underlying representation's ability to capture the semantic structure of input texts. This is particularly crucial for the development of more advanced and robust models that can handle increasingly complex and open-ended dialogue tasks. Furthermore, NTPS is a versatile evaluation metric that is applicable to various tasks and models, making it an ideal choice for researchers to conduct thorough comparisons of models and evaluation strategies. Through our work, we aim to spark a discussion on the importance of representation understanding in data-driven dialogue models and invite the community to join us in this endeavor. This discussion is critical for the advancement of the field, which is otherwise hindered by the reliance on coarse-grained evaluation metrics that prioritize text-generated quality over the underlying representation. This is particularly evident in recent studies that have demonstrated the significant impact of representation pretraining on model performance, even when the generated text appears perfect. In light of these findings, we believe that a more comprehensive approach to evaluating data-driven dialogue models is necessary to ensure a deeper understanding of representation understanding. Deep learning methods for LiDAR data analysis have made significant breakthroughs in recent years, allowing for the efficient recognition of places using 3D sensor data with minimal labeled training data. However, existing approaches still rely on traditional feature extraction techniques and struggle to utilize the full potential of LiDAR sensors. In our research, we present a novel, end-to-end deep learning network that processes raw LiDAR point clouds to recognize locations without relying on color cameras or additional sensors. To evaluate our method, we created a new dataset by extending the KITTI visual odometry dataset to include additional scenes and targets for evaluation. Our network was trained and tested on this dataset, demonstrating improved performance and greater flexibility compared to traditional LiDAR-based place recognition methods. Furthermore, our results indicate that our approach can run in real-time on autonomous vehicles. To facilitate further research, we are releasing our dataset and code publicly. Upgrading our network to use a LiDAR-to-LiDAR matching framework, we also achieved notable improvements in place recognition accuracy and flexibility. The enhanced version of our system has been successfully integrated into the Austin autonomous driving testbed. In this context, our work aims to advance the use of LiDAR sensors in place recognition and location-based services for autonomous vehicles. Streaming high-quality video, whether it's Video-on-Demand (VoD) or live streaming, demands transcoding to accommodate varying playback devices. This requires significant computational power and, consequently, a substantial amount of money is spent on cloud services to achieve this through cloud-based transcoding. In this research, we investigate how cloud-based virtual machines affect video transcoding efficiency, considering various cloud providers, different cloud infrastructure configurations, and the complexity of video streams. Our results show that video transcoding performance is influenced by the cloud provider, the kind of virtual machine used, and whether the video is live or on-demand. Furthermore, we discovered that, contrary to expectations, there's little difference in efficiency gains when using multi-core processors in this context. Based on our findings, we developed an analytical model to estimate transcoding time, taking into account the number of cores, the cloud provider's performance, and the virtual machine's overhead. This model enables us to create a strategy for scheduling video transcoding jobs, ensuring that the total transcoding time is minimized. Ultimately, our approach can help cloud providers optimize their services for video streaming applications. The code for our experiments and the proposed scheduling strategy is available online. This research is relevant to users of cloud services who require computational workloads, such as video transcoding, and can help them make informed decisions when choosing cloud providers and services. In the future, we plan to expand this work to other cloud-based applications and consider factors like memory usage and costs beyond processing power. Futhermore, we are interested in exploring how to integrate this research with existing scheduling tools used in video streaming applications. We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G. Our findings also provide a complete characterization of those prime numbers p with p greater than or equal to 5 that have non-rationalic behavior in K, along with a characterization of those prime numbers p with p less than 5 that are totally split in K. Furthermore, our results extend previous findings by M. D. S. Allison and J. H. Silverman concerning 2-adic extensions and prime numbers p with p equal to 2 or 3. Our proofs primarily rely on the interplay between the geometry of certain minimal models of curves and their Galois covers, along with the application of Grunwald-Wang's theorem to infer the global behavior of K from its local ramification properties. Lastly, our results imply that under certain conditions, the ring of integers in a Galois extension with a certain non-abelian group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5 is a free module over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G, a phenomenon that may be viewed as an additive analog of Chebotarev's theorem.
