A fundamental aspect of neural development, interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM), involves the rhythmic movement of nucleated neurons between the ventricular and luminal surfaces of the neuroepithelial tissue as the brain expands. Although this process has been observed for decades, the driving forces behind IKNM remain unclear due to a lack of direct measurements of the spatial coordinates of migrating nuclei. Using a novel, high-resolution, light-sectioning microscopy technique, we have taken sequential images of individual nuclei within mouse cerebral cortices as they migrate and completed their full journeys. Our data demonstrates that the spatial distribution of nuclei is random at the start of their migration but becomes confined to specific layers as they progress, ultimately incorporating themselves into the established neural tissue layers with remarkable precision, often with a 90% success rate or higher. Our research indicates that the primary mechanism governing IKNM is a branching process driven by surface tension and cell-cell adhesion forces, which pull the luminal layer towards the ventricular surface due to the accumulation of nucleated neurons. Consequently, a stress gradient forms that propels the nuclei towards their ultimate destination. Our findings provide a new understanding of the interkinetic nuclear migration process and its implications for neural tissue expansion. Researchers within the same institution often rely on their institutional email as their primary means of communication. Unintended email exchanges can occur when auto-generate email tools are used, compromising confidentiality and potentially allowing attackers to bypass spam filters. In collaboration with multiple research institutions, we investigated the reachability of their email communication networks. We also highlight the value of email communication network analysis in identifying vulnerabilities and propose several avenues for further exploration in this area. Although our study focused on email communication networks within research institutions, our methods are versatile and applicable to other closed systems comprising trusted entities that utilize email. Inspired by the pseudogap phenomenon in cuprates, a novel feature known as an "exceptional van Hove singularity" was hypothesized to arise at the Fermi surface's center in strongly interacting electron systems. This singularity is associated with a unique, four-fold symmetric van Hove ridge that emerges as a result of interacting electrons deforming the system's Brillouin zone. However, whether this exceptional van Hove singularity actually exists has remained a topic of debate. In our study, we employed superconducting Sr$_2$RuO$_4$ as the primary research subject. By integrating a precise model of the Fermi surface, derived from experimental specific heat data and detailed structural information, we accurately captured the exceptional van Hove singularity's effects. Furthermore, we utilized renormalization group theory to analyze the interactions within this system, accurately modeling the electron-electron scattering off the Fermi surface. Our results demonstrate that the exceptional van Hove singularity serves as a critical bottleneck for charge flow, leading to the formation of a pseudogap in charge, while also giving rise to a $\mathbf{d}_{x^2-y^2}$-wave pairing gap. This finding provides a conclusive explanation for Sr$_2$RuO$_4$'s unique electronic properties. Moreover, our study offers an accessible framework for investigating other electron systems featuring singular Fermi surfaces. By integrating experimental data and theoretical modeling, we can gain a deeper understanding of the interplay between interactions and the Fermi surface, ultimately revealing the underlying causes of a wide range of phenomena, from pseudogaps to superconductivity. Consequently, this research may provide new insights into the complex behaviors observed in other strongly interacting electron systems.

The undergound facility, ASEN, which utilizes cosmic-ray muons to measure spallation neutrons at a depth of 10 meters, is discussed. ASEN's detector system consisting of nine layers of horizontal and vertical plastic scintillators sensitive to muons passing through its center is described. These detectors allow for the calculation of neutron yields by observing the delayed detection of neutrons following muon passage. Data collected over 100 days in March and April 2019 at ASEN's site in Noto, Japan is used to determine the dependence of neutron yields on muon direction and energy. As a consequence, this effect leads to a gradual change in the rate of rotation. Notably, this impact is most pronounced for asteroids that have highly irregular shapes, as these shape irregularities generate a considerable difference in the cross-sectional areas between the sides facing the sun and those in the shadow. Among the notable examples of asteroids affected by this effect are (16) Psyche, a metal-rich asteroid that is a primary target for the NASA's Archimedes mission, and (21) Lutetia, which was studied by the European Space Agency's Rosetta mission. To better understand the composition and properties of these asteroids, it is essential to make accurate measurements of their spin states and the torques that affect their rotations. This paper reviews the current understanding of the YORP effect, its detection methods, and the techniques used to model its mechanisms. It also highlights the challenges associated with these models, particularly when dealing with the complexities of irregularly shaped asteroids. Furthermore, it discusses the limitations of existing observational data and the potential of future missions to make more precise measurements of the YORP effect. Ultimately, this paper emphasizes the significance of accurately modeling the YORP effect to achieve reliable results in future missions aimed at studying the composition and properties of asteroids. It also outlines the computational approach to modeling the YORP effect, including the use of numerical integrations, shape models, and thermal models. Additionally, it presents a new method for evaluating the YORP integral that considers the surface temperature of the asteroid and its reflection/emission properties. The rise of social media has transformed online interactions and turned users into active participants of digital communities. Twitter, in particular, has become a platform where users engage in diverse conversations, including discussions on politics, sports, entertainment, and more. In this study, categorizing users into core groups based on their shared interests poses an interesting problem. By applying density-based clustering to Twitter users' co-following patterns, we can identify distinct communities of users that share similar interpersonal connections. We then compare user engagement within these communities, revealing notable variations in interaction intensity across different topics. For instance, discussions about politics provoke more reactions, whereas sports and entertainment spark more retweets and likes. Furthermore, our approach enables us to analyze user behavior within each community by clustering tweets based on their content and identifying key indicators that characterize online conversations. We applied our methodology to a dataset of over 150 million tweets spanning a year and covering a wide range of topics, including news events, celebrity news, sports, and more. Our research provides valuable insights for developers of online community detection systems, social network analysts, and marketers seeking to optimize their targeting strategies. We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure. This group-theoretic incompatibility occurs due to the surface's topological characteristics, specifically its fundamental group being non-trivial. A corresponding result is derived for homeomorphisms of a compact surface with boundary, whose action is highly transitive within a specific Roelcke precompact framework, cannot limit the surface's cut system to a single component. These findings are extended to homeomorphisms of a compact surface without boundaries, whose action is highly transitive within a specific Roelcke precompact framework, cannot prevent the surface from having infinitely many non-trivial loops. These non-compactness results for homeomorphisms of compact surfaces are contrasted with compactness results for homeomorphisms of compact boundaryless surfaces, specifically those without non-trivial loops and with highly transitive actions within a specific Roelcke precompact framework. Additionally, this research is connected to graph theory via homeomorphisms of graph embeddings, particularly compact surfaces of trees whose embeddings' homeomorphism groups cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure. Lastly, this work is related to ongoing research in topological dynamics and the study of homeomorphism groups through the compact-open topology's inherited structure. Several open questions in this area are also posed. 

This article extends earlier findings presented at the 71st Permanent Seminar of the Topological Dynamics Group, held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, during the period from August 23 to 27, 2021. 

Keywords: Homeomorphism groups, compact surfaces, boundary-fixing homeomorphisms, Roelcke precompactness, topological dynamics.

Precise stellar characteristics are crucial for both astrophysics and exoplanetary science, especially when studying M-dwarfs as they are common in the galaxy and often host terrestrial planets. Yet, M-dwarf radii remain poorly understood due to limited observational data and inconsistent theoretical modeling. This study leverages the extensive radii distribution map created using the TESS mission's data to identify anomalies in M-dwarf radii. By analyzing nearly 300,000 stellar radii observed in 26 days for each of the 18 most frequently targeted M-dwarf stars in the SDR4 catalog, we identified outliers with unusual radii values. Among these, we discovered 26 anomalous objects with radii significantly deviating from their expected values, indicating possible stellar or planetary over-inflation. We estimate the probability of each anomaly being a genuine astrophysical event, accounting for potential biases introduced by the TESS observing strategy. For the remaining 11 cases without obvious explanations, we suggest potential causes, including stellar or planetary mergers, mergers involving two M-dwarfs with a massive white dwarf, and scenarios involving a planetary system disruption, such as planetary system instability or a stellar flyby. These unusual objects may provide opportunities to study rare astrophysical events at their onset stage. Moreover, this study highlights the significance of using time-series spectroscopy to monitor M-dwarf stars with potentially inflated radii, which could indicate the presence of a planet similar to Theia in our solar system. Ultimately, this work underscores the value of the SDR4 catalog in identifying unusual objects and the importance of using these stars as a proxy for studying the Earth's solar system. Finally, this study paves the way for a more in-depth statistical analysis of the M-dwarf sample set to better understand the radii distribution in this stellar class. Confining modes known as line waves form at the edge of a unique interface composed of two specially designed electromagnetic surfaces, and their behavior is distinct from both surface plasmon polaritons and leaky-wave guidance modes. By creating a continuous, self-supported line of charge and current, line waves offer a novel platform for wave manipulation, enabling the realization of non-dispersive line waves through carefully designed metamaterials. This study explores a new type of line wave that operates in the microwave frequency range and is generated by a metasurface consisting of electric dipole resonances arranged in a honeycomb pattern. Numerical simulations and theoretical modeling reveal that this line wave exhibits a high-contrast effective permittivity and possesses a unique characteristic that allows it to maintain a constant phase velocity while propagating. A theoretical expression for the line wave's phase velocity is derived and verified by numerical simulations. Furthermore, the loss in line wave power is investigated and found to be governed by an exponential decay based on the distance from its source, and an analytical expression for this decay is provided. A theoretical limit for the line wave's phase velocity is identified and the conditions necessary for achieving it are discussed. Experimental verification of the line wave is demonstrated through microwave measurements on a 10 GHz frequency metasurface, and numerical simulations on an optical frequency metasurface. A theoretical model for line wave mode converters is proposed, and successfully validated through full-wave simulations and microwave experiments. A line wave-based antenna that efficiently converts the line wave into a radiated wave, and provides a high gain and directivity, is designed and tested. The results show that the line wave antenna achieves a gain of 10.3 dBi and a directivity of 8.3 dBi at 10 GHz, and the line wave-based antenna outperforms existing antennas in the microwave frequency range. Additionally, numerical simulations indicate that the line wave antenna can maintain high gain and directivity in the terahertz frequency range. A line wave-based phase array antenna is also proposed, and full-wave simulations demonstrate its capability to efficiently convert the line wave into a radiated wave, providing a high gain and a narrow beam with low side lobes. The line wave-based phase array antenna is capable of scanning a wide angle, and outperforms existing terahertz antennas in gain and directivity. The proposed line wave-based antenna and phase array antenna offer promising applications in the efficient conversion of line waves into radiated waves, and may lead to breakthroughs in the development of high-performance antennas.

Although the integration of database systems has been successfully achieved through data interlinking, the high complexity of certain queries remains a significant challenge. Our research focuses on understanding how the incorporation of self-joins affects the complexity of these queries when using linked data sources. By incorporating the concept of treewidth, we developed an in-depth analysis of the impact of self-joins on the efficiency of query processing. Our results demonstrate that the complexity of queries with self-joins can be mitigated through the selection of optimal join orders, resulting in an associated reduction in treewidth. Furthermore, we developed an iterative algorithm to determine whether a given database satisfies a given query condition, and this algorithm exhibits enumerative complexity that is directly proportional to the product of the database's treewidth and its number of entities. Additionally, we investigated the application of this approach to various types of data, including both simple and complex entities, and conducted performance evaluations using actual datasets from the linked data repository. Our research has the potential to contribute to the development of more efficient database query processing systems in the future. However, it is essential to acknowledge that the approach is primarily theoretical in nature and may not be suitable for large-scale, high-performance database applications due to its enumerative complexity. Nevertheless, it remains an important research area that is relevant to the current state of database technology. Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to infinite strings, and this equivalence holds regardless of whether the input strings are viewed as a whole or in parts. Under one such model, the computability of a function is equivalent to its continuity when restricted to regular recognizers, a finding that stems from the unambiguous generability of cross-sections for recurrent points. In contrast, if we allow non-deterministic recognizers, the relationship between computability and continuity is no longer equivalent, as demonstrated by a controllable, computable function whose continuity requires non-deterministic recognizers. In addition, the necessary control to separate determinate and indeterminate computations for cross-sections is shown to be effectively decidable over infinite strings, a decision that becomes undecidable when considering finite strings. Furthermore, the complexity of decision problems related to the indeterminate vs. determinate separation for cross-sections, as well as first-order logic over infinite strings, is examined in the presence of additional symbols that do not affect the outcome of first-order queries. Lastly, an infinite separation between the complexity of determinate vs. indeterminate computations for cross-sections is established over finite strings, a distinction that does not hold over infinite strings. This line of inquiry is rooted in prior research that explored the relationship between computability and continuity using different formal models and additional evidence requiring the consideration of additional, non-critical components. As such, the primary focus of this work is on the relationship between those models that can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to infinite strings. In this context, different formal models are examined to better understand which of their equivalencies provide new insight and which do not. As an example, the consideration of additional, non-critical components led to an examination of the complexity of decision problems related to the indeterminate vs. determinate separation for cross-sections, as well as first-order logic over infinite strings, with additional symbols that do not affect the outcome of first-order queries. In this context, the term 'non-critical' is used to describe components that do not affect the outcome of such queries. In contrast, the additional components being considered in other contexts do affect the outcome, as seen in the case of cross-sections, but are still considered 'input' for the formal model in question. In such cases, those components are viewed as critical in their own right and are therefore considered essential to the formal model. In this context, the term 'critical' is used to describe such components that are viewed as fundamental

Researchers have analyzed collision data with an integrated luminosity of 3 inverse femtobarns, and through amplitude analysis of specific two-body decay events, they have obtained information about the polarization states of these decays. Specifically, they have observed the $B^0$ decay to a pair of $K^*$ mesons, as well as the $B^0_s$ decay to a pair of $\phi$ mesons or a pair of $K^*$ mesons. A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of selecting relevant covariates.  This bias-corrected estimator is developed using a influence function that matches the original estimator and is an integral part of a general framework for bias reduction in extreme value theory.  The influence function of the original estimator is characterized by a single component that is independent of the model parameters and depends on the specific distribution of errors.  The properties of the bias-corrected estimator are established, including consistency and asymptotic normality, making it possible to perform inference using conventional methods.  The performance of the bias-corrected estimator is evaluated through simulation studies, and it is also applied to real-world datasets.  Source code for the estimator and related functions is available online.  A related paper has been published in the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B. To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable control-effective state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the boundary of the reachable control-effective state space and estimate the time to reach a target state. Unlike first-order methods, the new algorithm reduces the computational burden by a order of magnitude while maintaining similar accuracy, as demonstrated in theoretical and numerical comparisons. We've also shown that the success of this method depends on a non-degenerate condition of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation and provides a method for verifying if this condition is met. To further enhance performance, we've developed a technique to utilize coarse grids during the calculation of the reachable control-effective state space. The resulting algorithm can be utilized in control design applications, such as trajectory planning and life-expectancy estimation, as shown in theoretical and numerical examples. The implementation of this algorithm is available as part of the HJTools open-source software. The current version of this software can be found at https://github.com/bernd-pock/HJTools. Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) have gained popularity recently, particularly in the context of few-shot learning, for efficiently extracting rich representations from images and videos. However, the success of MLPs is heavily reliant on their depth and width, which can result in overfitting and make them difficult to apply to more complex and longer sequences like videos. To address these limitations, we introduce Dual-MLP (DMLP), an innovative architecture that utilizes two separate and nested MLPs. DMLP leverages the end-to-end learning capability of the first MLP to produce a compact, low-dimensional signal that is easily processed by the nested second MLP. The output of the second MLP then serves as the final representation for the input sequence. DMLP's two-component structure allows for the application of self-attention and other positional encoding methods, which can be incorporated to enhance performance. We experimentally validate DMLP's effectiveness by applying it to the tasks of supervised learning, few-shot learning, unsupervised learning, and sequence-level tasks, such as action recognition in videos and sound classification in audio. DMLP consistently outperforms standard MLPs and other prominent architectures, including Transformer and Graph-based models, with notable improvements of up to +16.4% in accuracy on the EPIC-KITCHENS dataset. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/DMLP. DMLP's success is attributed to its ability to produce high-quality, compact signals that facilitate efficient and accurate processing by the nested MLP. This is further supported by an in-depth analysis of DMLP's performance with various activation functions, layer compositions, and input sequences of different lengths and complexities. To facilitate the application of DMLP to new domains and tasks, we provide a comprehensive set of guidelines that can be adapted to tailor the architecture to specific requirements. DMLP's innovative dual-architecture design paves the way for the development of more efficient and accurate signal representations in images and videos. Moreover, its generalizability and flexibility make it an attractive choice for the broader signal processing community. The complex and dynamic nature of animal perception within the human ventral temporal cortex (VTC) remains an area of significant research interest. A recent study suggests that animal recognition patterns across various VTC regions follow an orderly sequence of animacy, rather than a strict categorization of distinct animal types. This finding is supported by either of two theoretical frameworks: the feature drift hypothesis, which proposes that the VTC's organization is structured around a gradual shift from general animacy detection to specific feature extraction; or the map expansion hypothesis, which suggests that more advanced regions within the VTC are capable of recognizing increasingly complex animals by building onto earlier, basic recognition abilities. To test these ideas, the study utilized a novel statistical approach to identify and remove any patterns resulting from the hierarchical organization of the VTC itself. By doing so, researchers were able to assess whether the animacy continuum present in the data can be accounted for by a lower-dimensional representation that ignores the VTC's structural organization. In doing so, the animacy continuum persisted, indicating that the VTC's organization plays a significant role in the observed pattern of animacy. Furthermore, the study demonstrated that both the feature drift and map expansion hypotheses can effectively model the data, with a combination of the two offering the most plausible explanation. Additionally, the study found that the most viable models were capable of accurately predicting patterns of activity within the posterior inferior temporal lobe even when tested with new animal data. The research also explored alternative models, including one based on the taxonomy of animals, and found that a combined approach that takes into consideration both the structure of the VTC and the taxonomy of animals provides the best fit to the data. The study's findings have significant implications for our understanding of the VTC's organization and the recognition of animals. It also highlights the importance of accounting for the hierarchical organization of the brain when analyzing complex patterns of activity and when developing models of these systems. Finally, the study's results suggest that the recognition of animals within the VTC is a highly distributed process, with distinct regions playing a crucial role in the recognition of different animals. The study's approach and findings can serve as a valuable framework for investigating other complex perception and memory phenomena, such as the recognition of non-biological entities (e.g., foods, man-made objects) and the organization of semantic memory more broadly. The study's statistical approach and novel analysis of the VTC's organization also provide a new perspective on the long-standing debate over whether the brain's organization is best characterized as a hierarchical or distributed system. We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs. Furthermore, our extension enables the expression of performance-related properties such as programs' execution times and the number of oracle calls made during operation. We have established multiple rules for the application of the Hoare logic's basic reasoning steps, including sequencing, conditional branching, loop iteration, and the use of mutable memory stores. Additionally, our extension enables the derivation of quantum relational hoare logic theorems when comparing programs that employ different types of data storage, including mutable arrays and linked lists. We have also developed a quantum program that serves as an illustration for demonstrating the capabilities of our relational hoare logic when considering multiple storage formats. Notably, this program's correctness proof requires the use of performance-related expectations when comparing its components. We have successfully verified the correctness of several actual quantum programs utilizing our relational hoare logic, in addition to providing the underlying theoretical framework for this verification. The relational hoare logic that we have developed represents a fundamental advancement in the field of quantum program verification, as it enables the expression of performance-related properties and efficient comparison of programs with differing data storage formats. As such, it has significant implications for the development of efficient and reliable quantum programs in the future. Furthermore, our approach can be adapted to support additional programming languages, in addition to quantum relational hoare logic's potential applications in the verification of classical-programs that incorporate multiple data storage formats. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases can be significantly fueled by small groups of highly infectious individuals who interact with many others. To understand the impact of such super-spreader events, which occur frequently, on the basic reproduction number $R_0$, it's essential to consider their effect in combination with other transmission sources. In classic epidemiological models, $R_0$ is a steady-state indicator, reflecting the long-term average of reproductive values in a well-mixed population. However, during an epidemic, especially when there are significant deviations from perfect mixing, as seen in global connectivity and online connections, it's more accurate to use multi-scale $R_0$ values to assess transmission. By taking these factors into account, our research introduces a new approach to estimating $R_0$ in a more realistic way. It also provides a framework for identifying super-spreader events and their impact on the epidemic, using data from recent outbreaks caused by highly contagious individuals, such as carriers of the N501Y mutation in the UK and Brazil, and an American with the Kappa mutation who infected nearly 50 people on a flight. Based on empirical data, we simulate various scenarios to illustrate the significance of super-spreader events and their effect on the epidemic, especially when the underlying transmission network remains relatively stable. Furthermore, our research offers strategies for mitigating the impact of future super-spreader events, such as targeting travel restrictions at high-risk populations and locations. By factoring in the psychological effects of widespread fear on transmission, our research also presents a scenario in which fear-based changes in behavior could lead to a second wave of infection after the initial outbreak. In conclusion, our research highlights the critical role of super-spreader events in driving the spread of contagious diseases and stresses the importance of targeted public health policies in preventing further outbreaks. These findings are particularly relevant to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, but the research methods presented can be applied to the study of other infectious diseases. Futhermore, our research is available as an open-source project, allowing users to access the code and contribute to the project through the GitHub repository. Additionally, our research includes a visualization tool that enables users to explore the spread of disease through interactive simulations. A comprehensive analysis of the physical characteristics of young star clusters in the LMC, conducted by comparing observed radii to predicted values based on mass, age, and a cluster's specific location within the galaxy, has yielded significant insights. For 4449 clusters aged 100-500 million years, a notable correlation between the observed and predicted radii was found, taking into account the effects of gas dispersion and cluster motions. Notably, a distinct mass-radius relationship was identified for small clusters, consistent with similar findings in the Milky Way and SMC, while larger clusters in the LMC deviated from this pattern. A separate analysis revealed that younger clusters in the LMC, with radii above 2 pc, exhibit a larger size distribution than younger clusters in the SMC and the Milky Way. These results suggest that younger clusters in the LMC tend to constrict their envelope more efficiently as mass increases, up to a certain point, after which they deviate from expected behavior. It is proposed that the onset of non-standard behavior for larger clusters in the LMC may be linked to a critical mass related to the cluster's tidal disruption during its evolution. Additionally, by comparing the velocity dispersions of bound and dissolved clusters in the LMC, a velocity-radius relationship was established, showing that more massive clusters, regardless of their binding status, exhibit similar velocity distributions. This finding supports the idea that velocity dispersion is primarily influenced by a cluster's mass rather than its binding status. It is also observed that the mass-radius and velocity-radius relationships in the LMC are consistent with similar relationships found in the SMC and the Milky Way. These mass, radius, and velocity relationships are expected to hold constant across different galaxy environments and are seen in both young and intermediate-age clusters in the LMC, providing a foundation for predicting the physical characteristics of star clusters based solely on their mass and velocity. This capability will be instrumental in identifying and analyzing distant and unresolved star clusters in various galaxies and across the cosmos. By leveraging these predictions, researchers can better understand the formation and evolution of star clusters in different galaxies and under varying conditions. This paper examines the relationship between integers that are y-friable (or y-smooth) and the Dickman function. Specifically, we derive an explicit estimate for the count of y-friable integers up to a given x in terms of the Dickman function. This estimate is accurate to a high degree of precision (i.e., within $x^{\rho(1)}$). We also provide an alternative formulation for estimating the count of y-friable integers, which is more manageable from a computational perspectives. Building upon prior work, we establish a connection between the Dickman function and the distribution of y-friable integers. We demonstrate that the proportion of y-friable integers to all integers that are at most x in size converges to a value that is determined by the Dickman function. This value is expressed as an integral of the Dickman function raised to a specific power. We also investigate how this proportion is affected when we consider a broader class of integers that are considered "almost" y-friable. We establish an upper bound for the impact of using a broader definition of y-friability, which is proportional to the square of the difference in the parameters that define these two classes. We derive this upper bound by analyzing the local distribution of y-friable integers within a relatively narrow range. Given any non-erasing free monoid morphism σ and subshift X, its image subshift Y under σ and the associated complexity functions p_X and p_Y exhibit the following relationship: there exist constants c, d, and C, where p_X scales by a factor of at least c times d, while scaling at most C, in the half-open interval [cd, C). This relationship provides an upper bound of the form p_Y(t) ≤ C*p_X(C*t) for sufficiently large t values, indicating that the average complexity of Y over time is dominated by the average complexity of X multiplied by a constant factor C, which can be determined in advance despite the possible infinite complexity of both Y and X. Moreover, if σ is recognizable and injective, it maintains the same language structure, resulting in an isomorphism between the syntactic monoids of Y and X, indicating identical factor complexities for both Y and X, thereby yielding the upper bound of p_Y(t) ≤ C*p_X(t) for any t value, where C is the product of the cardinalities of the images of σ and its inverse. This research extends prior knowledge on the relationship between subshifts and free monoid morphisms. Additionally, it offers a general upper bound for the average factor complexity of an iterated subshift, as well as specific upper and lower bounds for the average factor complexity of its image under a non-erasing free monoid morphism. Furthermore, it presents an example of a subshift with an unbounded factor complexity function that exhibits a quadratic growth rate when applied to its image under a particular free monoid morphism. Moreover, it establishes a connection between the average factor complexity of an iterated subshift and the cardinality of the image of the underlying free monoid morphism. Lastly, it poses open questions on the relationship between the average factor complexity of an iterated subshift and its topological entropy, as well as on the properties of subshifts with unbounded factor complexity functions.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled data to selectively draw from prior experiences and incorporate relevant past training data into the model.
Through the use of a customized contrastive learning approach, ReCross is able to selectively draw from relevant past experiences, and by utilizing a batch normalization technique, it is able to prevent over-reliance on freshly acquired information.
Our results show that by adopting this approach, we are able to significantly enhance the cross-task generalization ability of these large language models when compared to baseline methods, resulting in performance improvements of up to 11.5% in zero-shot settings and 3.5% in few-shot settings. Moreover, an analysis of our data suggests that there may be an unbounded potential for further improvement as the size of the dataset continues to expand. Additionally, an examination of the learned representations through t-SNE and PCA reveals distinct patterns in both the methods, with ReCross exhibiting a more organized and diverse distribution of representations. Finally, an assessment of the learned weights through a simple linear model indicates that the weights learned through ReCross possess valuable predictive power in forecasting performance on new tasks. This work offers the initial framework for exploring unsupervised cross-task generalization in massive language models, and future research is encouraged to build upon this foundation. The code and data utilized in this research are available for public access at https://github.com/THU-GLA/ReCross. The results presented in this paper have been successfully replicated and are available for review.

To address this challenge, we developed the m-ar-K-FastICA approach, utilizing mathematical derivations to explicitly derive the inverse of the kernel function used, thereby enhancing the method's performance, particularly when dealing with large-scale or noisy data. Our results show that the m-ar-K-FastICA approach outperforms the conventional ICA and ICA-based kernel methods in terms of extraction accuracy and computational efficiency. Moreover, the m-ar-K-FastICA approach exhibits robustness in feature extraction for large and noisy datasets. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. If W is finite, our calculation aligns with the number of orbits under its action on the set of edges within its graph representation. If W is not finite, we establish that the number of spheres in its boolean complex converges to a finite number. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula to compute this limiting number. Furthermore, we establish that the graph parameter $\beta_2$ introduced by Tomari and Kawaguchi, which measures the number of edges in the graph representation of W's quotient group, is equivalent to the number of spheres in |S| dimensions, thereby confirming a previously stated conjecture. Lastly, we extend this confirmation to a broader set of circumstances, also providing a new geometric interpretation of $\beta_2$. 

Keywords: Coxeter groups, discrete Morse theory, boolean complexes, homotopy types, graph theory. 
MR Abstract: Let (W,S) be a Coxeter system. We construct the boolean complex Δ_W whose vertices are the involutions in W. Using discrete Morse theory, we find that for a large enough dimension d, Δ_W has the homotopy type of (d+1)(|S|-1) spheres. We derive a recursive formula to compute the number of spheres in this dimension, and if W is finite, this equals the number of orbits under its action on the edges of its graph representation Γ(W). If W is not finite, this number converges to a finite limit and we compute it explicitly. Moreover, we show that this equals the graph parameter β_2 introduced by Tomari and Kawaguchi, and confirm their conjecture. We also extend this result to a broader set of circumstances, and provide a new geometric interpretation of β_2.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption and spread of false information, mainly online, which has led to public health confusion and misdirection. To combat this spread, it's essential to understand the underlying causes, analyze the characteristics that contribute to its dissemination, and identify key targets for intervention in modeling rumor propagation. In this research, online discussions and news articles related to COVID-19 were analyzed, and a stochastic model for rumor propagation was developed, incorporating factors like the source's credibility, severity, and the number of initial spreaders. By applying the model to real-world data, its components were quantified and verified through statistical testing. Furthermore, the model was utilized to estimate the impact of interventions aimed at slowing down false information's spread. Results from multiple datasets showed that the model effectively replicated the observed behavior of rumor propagation, and varying the parameters that influence it allowed for valuable insights to be gained. For instance, it was observed that, as the severity of the rumor increased, the model exhibited a sudden shift from slow to rapid dissemination, and that, in some cases, a small group of influential individuals could single-handedly spark widespread propagation. Additionally, the model revealed that, in certain instances, the most effective strategy for mitigating the spread of the rumor was to target the source of the misinformation, and that, in other cases, the number of initial spreaders became the critical factor. The developed model can be applied to various scenarios and may be used to inform data collection procedures, and its components have practical applications in evaluating the credibility of sources and estimating the severity of a health crisis. The model's findings can also be employed to design more effective interventions aimed at slowing down the dissemination of false information. The model is available online for public use. A stabilizable boundary feedback controller is designed for the Navier-Stokes equations using a linear control scheme with an oblique boundary orientation. Specifically, controls are applied to an inclined boundary located along the top of a two-dimensional, horizontally extended channel. It is demonstrated that this control strategy generates a damping effect in the upper fluid layer, leading to asymptotic decay of long-wave disturbances in the lower fluid layer. The effectiveness of this control is shown through numerical simulations and analytical stability estimates. Notably, the design exploits the distinct behavior of waves in the Navier-Stokes equations, with different characteristics emerging based on the ratio of their horizontal and vertical components. A helical layer model is utilized to illustrate how the direction of wave propagation influences this ratio and, consequently, the location of boundary layers and ribbons formed under rolling-up vortices. The design takes advantage of the distinct behavior of waves in different directions and targets the most unstable upper fluid layer for control. The design's limitations and potential extensions to other fluid dynamics problems are also discussed. Strain-induced crystallization occurs when mechanical forces cause crystalline regions to form from a disordered polymer structure, resulting in enhanced mechanical strength and improved thermal stability. This research aims to expand the technological potential of unfilled polymers by exploring their mechanical and thermal properties during strain-induced crystallization. Initially, mechanical property changes and thermal behavior were analyzed in various polymers with different crystallization activation energies. Notably, it was discovered that mechanical property enhancements are limited to a specific range that is unaffected by thermal stability improvements. Furthermore, a mathematical model was developed to explain this phenomenon and predicted the existence of an optimal activation energy for mechanical property enhancement, which aligns with experimental observations. This activation energy is relatively low, indicating that mechanical property enhancement can be achieved with minimal strain and temperature conditions. Consequently, selecting a polymer with an activation energy close to its thermal activation energy is crucial for optimizing strain-induced crystallization. Ultimately, this research provides valuable insights into tailoring the mechanical and thermal properties of unfilled polymers through strain-induced crystallization, enabling the development of high-performance materials with exceptional mechanical strength and thermal stability achieved with minimal strain and temperature conditions. This could lead to innovative applications, such as the creation of self-reinforcing materials with exceptional durability in harsh environments. Moreover, this research may also contribute to the understanding of crystallization in semicrystalline polymers, which is critical for predicting their long-term performance and developing computational models that accurately simulate their mechanical behavior over time. To explore the impact of doping on the topological superconductivity of Bi$_2$Se$_3$,  we model this material using a tight-binding Hamiltonian derived from angular momentum conservation. By examining the topological characteristics of the full doped Hamiltonian, we investigate the requirements for creating a topological superconducting phase and the associated gap formation. Furthermore, by analyzing the pairing correlations among the electrons, we identify the emergence of unusual pair-hopping terms that contribute to the interaction and may facilitate the topological superconducting phase. These pair-hopping interactions are found to be robust against perturbations caused by lattice distortions. Additionally, we investigate the effects of strain on the system and find that it can be used to manipulate the topological superconducting phase. Our study provides theoretical insights and predictions for the topological superconductivity of Bi$_2$Se$_3$ that can be experimentally verified. One of the primary difficulties in Imitation Learning is obtaining high-quality feedback from instructors, which is further compounded when the instruction is imperfect. This problem becomes even more challenging when the instruction is provided through pre-labeled data, which is typical in supervised learning tasks. In such scenarios, learning from incomplete and inaccurate labels can be particularly detrimental. This paper introduces a novel framework known as Selective Learning from Demonstrations (SLED), which enables the selection of valuable information from combined sources, including feedback from instructors and pre-labeled data. By leveraging an efficient method for learning two dimensional sub-spaces, SLED effectively retrieves the valuable information by learning a low-dimensional sub-space with minimal error, thereby producing improved outcomes when compared to conventional approaches. The benefits of SLED are demonstrated through a series of experiments conducted on real-world datasets, which show significant enhancements in performance when compared to standard supervised learning methods. The source code for SLED is openly available for public use.

Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have achieved significant success in processing artificially created rainy images, but they struggle with real rainy images due to the large discrepancies between the two. This difficulty prompts researchers to seek an alternative approach, one that focuses solely on extracting clear components from mixed images of objects against clear backgrounds. This study redefines the task as a single-image super-resolution problem and proposes a new network architecture called the Non-Local Attentive Recursive Residual Convolutional Neural Network (NLR3-NNU) that utilizes both local and non-local attention mechanisms to achieve better results. Evaluations using a dataset of real rainy images compiled from Flickr, in comparison to traditional image processing methods and contemporary deep learning techniques, demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method. Furthermore, experiments conducted on artificially created rainy images and comparisons to state-of-the-art models reveal the NLR3-NNU's ability to generalize well across various scales and settings. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. Moreover, our approach proves resilient to various labeling schemes and different types of human errors. A thorough comparison of our method with the standard technique of individual comparative evaluations confirms a substantial reduction in costs, achieved without requiring advanced algorithms. The findings also revealed distinct patterns of brain activity associated with an increased risk of drug abuse and varying results based on the specific drug type. The study's results contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between brain function, drug consumption, and the machine learning-based prediction models. Portfolio optimization is a critical application of modern finance, yet its computational intricacies make it challenging to implement large-scale projects. Despite the efficacy of the Monte Carlo method in valuing complex financial derivatives, its slow convergence rate and requirement for extensive simulations make it impractical for complex scenarios. In contrast, the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) has shown promise for solving linear and non-linear programming problems, but its implementation is hindered by the need for expensive variational executions on noisy quantum devices. In this research, we utilize the HHL quantum algorithm to develop an efficient solution for portfolio optimization problems, leveraging its $\mathcal{O}(Ulog^3(n))$ runtime complexity to achieve significant computational savings. By running a series of HHL-based simulations on a classical qubit simulator and IBM Quantum devices, we demonstrate the advantages of this approach, particularly when dealing with large portfolios or low-risk assets. Notably, our results indicate that HHL-based solutions can provide actionable portfolio recommendations, even with the limitations imposed by current noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. This research provides a foundation for further exploration of the HHL algorithm in finance and highlights the potential for hybrid classical-quantum approaches to tackle complex computational problems. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a wide range of spoken languages, our research leverages the connection between the models' linguistic representations and the underlying text data. This approach is challenging due to two main issues: the significant gap between labeled data and the vast amounts of unlabelled web text that the models are expected to generalize to in the testing phase, and the difficulty of effectively transferring the models' knowledge about the structure of language during multimodal training. To address these challenges, we propose the use of a contrastive loss function that encourages the models to pay closer attention to the differences in the linguistic characteristics of labeled and unlabelled sentences during multimodal training. We have tested our approach on two tasks: low-resource ASR and cross-lingual pre-training of ASR models. The results show that our method leads to a notable improvement in the models' performance when they are trained on limited amounts of labeled data and also facilitates the efficient transfer of knowledge from models trained on one language to another. The model's ability to generalize to unlabelled web data during training is further highlighted by its ability to fine-tune the models to a high level of accuracy on the labeled data after they have been trained on vast amounts of unlabelled data. The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 provided the first direct evidence for the existence of brown dwarfs. Initially, estimated to have a mass around 40-60 times that of Jupiter, with a surface temperature around 600-650 Kelvin, these new retrievals using modern spectroscopic methods have revised those estimates to a mass of approximately 41 times that of Jupiter, along with a surface temperature of around 580-600 Kelvin, making GJ 229B one of the coolest solid-body radiating objects detected to date. Located approximately 6.5 parsecs from our solar system, GJ 229B offers valuable insights into the formation and evolution of the coolest objects in our universe. The concept of unclonable encryption, a feature that bars an adversary from producing various encrypted iterations of the same unencrypted data, is what this study aims to introduce to the realm of information theoretic privacy. Building upon previous work by Aggarwal and Bussink, who proposed single-copy encryption with an adversary's clonability metric 'q', this research extends that concept to multiple copies of data by introducing an additional metric 'p'. An information-theoretic framework for analyzing 'p' is also developed within this study. Furthermore, this research creates two new protocols that achieve both 'q' and 'p' security, ensuring an adversary cannot create multiple copies of the same data, nor can they produce different copies of the same data. These protocols are proven secure in the sequential and parallel adversary models, respectively. This research is applicable to various scenarios, such as identity-based and key-policy attribute-based encryption systems. For example, convection in the Sun is responsible for surfacing its hidden radiative energy, which in turn drives mass loss through solar flares and coronal mass ejections. In contrast, stars like the Sun experience weak winds due to their interaction with the radiative zone that prevents gas bubbles from escaping. 

However, in stars like the Sun that lack strong convection, these weak winds are likely dominated by magnetic fields that restrict gas movement, as seen in the case of the Sun itself. Therefore, understanding the fundamental drivers of mass loss in the Sun requires a deeper examination of the convective zone and its potential influence on the solar wind's behavior.

Furthermore, the Sun's mass loss through its convective and coronal components, such as solar flares and coronal mass ejections, is significantly more substantial than its radiatively driven wind. Consequently, the volume of mass lost from the Sun through these processes far exceeds the amount lost through its wind alone.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in heterostructures. In this study, we investigate the Proximity Effect in Sr$_2$MgO$_4$-graphene and Sr$_2$RnO$_4$-graphene heterostructures using a combination of experimental and theoretical methods. Sr$_2$MgO$_4$ and Sr$_2$RnO$_4$ are representative materials with strong spin-orbit coupling and contrasting electronic properties, offering a chance to study the unique influence of each on graphene's Proximity Effect. Our findings indicate that the Proximity Effect in these systems primarily results from the interaction with Sr$_2$RnO$_4$, and we identify the underlying mechanism as the transfer of lattice distortion and correlated electrons from Sr$_2$RnO$_4$ to graphene. This leads to the modification of graphene's electronic states and the emergence of hybridized orbitals with Sr$_2$RnO$_4$. A theoretical model incorporating the 4d electrons of Sr$_2$RnO$_4$ and the 2p electrons of graphene successfully reproduces our experimental observations. Notably, this model highlights the significance of considering the intricate interplay between the electronic and lattice structures of complex transition metal oxides when analyzing the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect. This research offers a deeper understanding of the unique properties emerging at interfaces between strong spin-orbit materials and 2D systems. These findings may also contribute to the development of novel spin-orbit coupled systems with unique electronic properties. We investigate the training of neural networks with Lipschitz continuous weights, where the coefficient is optimized in an entropy-regularized framework. We demonstrate that this method yields networks with Lipschitz constraints that are equivalent to those produced by projection methods, yet enjoys the benefit of avoiding abrupt function changes. We also establish connections to both adversarial training and robust optimization techniques. Empirical results indicate that our approach leads to substantial improvements in model generalizability and accuracy across multiple datasets and network architectures. We found our method to be particularly effective when data is scarce, achieving notable reductions in error rates of up to $18\%$ in certain scenarios. We have made our source code publicly accessible.

HD 80606 is a notable exoplanet due to its extremely long and eccentric orbital path around the G5V star HD 80606. Every 111 days, the exoplanit passes close to its star, resulting in a significant increase in the heat it receives, causing its surface temperature to rise dramatically to as high as 1,500 K. This extreme heating is similar to what occurs with the exoplanet HD 189733b, but it has a much shorter and less eccentric orbit. As a result of its highly eccentric orbit, HD 80606b experiences extreme variations in its insolation levels, leading to distinct spectral characteristics during its close approach and distant phases. To better understand the atmospheric properties of this planet, a team of astronomers conducted a comprehensive analysis of HD 80606b's spectral energy distributions during both its close approach and distant phases. The data were collected using the MIRI instrument on the JWST during two observations, one covering the close approach and the other the distant phase. The analysis revealed that the energy distribution during the close approach is consistent with a thermal radiation model originating from a circular region with a temperature of 1,400 K and a radius of approximately 1.5 times the radius of the planet. In contrast, the data from the distant phase were best fit with a two-temperature model, featuring a hot temperature of 450 K in the upper atmosphere and 300 K in the lower regions. The analysis also estimated the mass loss rate in HD 80606b's upper atmosphere to be about 10^9 kg/s, a rate that is significantly lower than expected for a planet in this close-in, highly eccentric orbit. The findings suggest that HD 80606b's atmosphere may be less dense than initially thought, possibly due to the presence of a slow and gentle mass loss process, such as a stochastic exfoliation of atmospheric atoms and molecules occurring over a broad range of orbital phases. The data also provided an opportunity to study the JWST's MIRI instrument, specifically its ability to detect the planet's thermal emission during the close approach, and to compare these results with previous observations. We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. Moreover, our research reveals that the graph's embeddability in an upward planar layout is linked to a parameterized problem known as Recognize-TRIANGULAR, used for recognizing directed trees within a graph. Our study provides the first known solutions for the recognition problems of general directed graphs within the realm of upward planar layouts, providing a theoretical basis for several previously unresolved parameterized problems. Notably, this leads to 3APX-hardness being reduced to 2APX-hardness for the general case of directed graphs. Additionally, our research introduces an efficient brute-force method for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout, specifically when the graph contains few source vertices. This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our research employs a novel metric known as the entanglement Fisher information, which serves as an indicator to detect critical phenomena in quantum systems. Notably, we discover that the entanglement Fisher information exhibits peak behavior at specific thresholds of chemical potential within the SU(1,1) symmetric system, which is indicative of non-Landau Fermi liquids' behavior. Lastly, our findings suggest that information capacity can be utilized as an order parameter to characterize the phase transition in non-Landau Fermi liquids' systems. Ultimately, our work provides quantitative evidence supporting the universal operator growth hypothesis and highlights the utility of information capacity as an effective indicator for phase transitions in quantum systems. Moreover, our research paves the way for further exploration of operator growth within non-Lie-symmetric systems.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward framing of tasks. Current imitation learning frameworks, however, are largely confined to simple tasks involving point or vector trajectories. This limitation is addressed by a new algorithm that extends kernelized movement primitives to more complex targets, allowing for the imitation of diverse curved trajectories. The new framework retains the computational efficiency of the original KMP method by utilizing a linear representation of task space. We demonstrate the efficacy of this new algorithm through the imitation of complex curved trajectories in both joint and end-effector space for a 7-DoF robotic arm. Results show that it is possible to accurately replicate a wide range of target trajectories with minimal learning data, achieving an average error of less than 3 cm. This new algorithm is made available as an open-source Python module compatible with the PyDP movement primitive library. It can be easily integrated with popular robot control frameworks such as PyRobot and Taskman, enabling seamless integration with imitation learning algorithms. This represents an important step towards the development of more advanced, flexible, and scalable imitation learning solutions for complex robotic tasks. Furthermore, the method's underlying theory provides valuable insights into the fundamental nature of movement primitives and learning from demonstrations. Lastly, the success of this approach has significant implications for the development of future robot learning frameworks that can efficiently handle complex tasks while minimizing computational requirements. A novel class of superconductors featuring odd parity has been discovered, exemplified by Sr$_2$MnReO$_6$, where Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman magnetic field may induce competing phases of superconductivity and magnetism. Employing the Gutzwiller method for heavy fermion materials, our calculations demonstrate that Rashba coupling and Zeeman field can generate triple-point-like crossings in the electron and hole pockets of the tetragonal Brillouin zone, leading to superconductivity mediated by inter-orbital pairing. Triple-point-like crossings are critical for this mechanism as they produce $d$-wave like superconductivity and magnetism competition, characterized by magnetic field delayed onset in the presence of superconductivity. Notably, this phenomenon is distinct from the heavy fermion superconductors, where magnetic field typically coexists with superconductivity. Rashba coupling and Zeeman field can be manipulated experimentally via electrical current and magnetic field applications, respectively. As a result, our findings suggest that Sr$_2$MnReO$_6$ may be an ideal candidate for studying Rashba-driven competition between superconductivity and magnetism. By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The discovered phase shift occurs at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point for the onset of superconductivity, specifically in the doping range of $x=0.17$ to $x=0.19$. The transition temperature of this transition varies with the doping amount and the specific direction measured and is in the range of 0.6 K to 1.5 K for $x=0.18$. The structure of the interlocked vortex lattice is influenced by the magnetic field's direction and the material's doping level, and we propose that the observed transition is linked to the unique arrangement of the vortex lattice's 6-fold symmetry. Moreover, our findings suggest that the material's response to the magnetic field's pressure is insufficient to account for the transition, and instead, the transition is more likely the outcome of competing interactions between the vortex lattice's asymmetry and the applied magnetic field. The discovered transition may also provide a means to directly study the material's normal state by magnetic field, a state that is difficult to study using other methods due to the material's superconducting properties. Furthermore, we propose that the transition may be linked to unusual features observed in the material's thermal conductivity at higher temperatures but under very strong magnetic fields. Additionally, we have determined the material's sound wave velocity and absorption properties, and we have established a method for distinguishing between the material's vortex lattice structure and its normal state by measuring sound wave velocity and absorption in very strong magnetic fields. The developed technique may be applied to other materials with interlocked vortex lattices to distinguish between their different states of matter. The research was conducted using the TMT-CBN tunnel diode oscillator-based sound wave velocity and absorption measurement system at the University of British Columbia and the FHDA-based thermal conductivity measurement system at the University of Tokyo. The magnetic field measurements were conducted at the University of Geneva using a pulsed magnetic field system with a 45 T capacity and a 1.3 T capacity resistive magnet at the University of British Columbia. Theories describing highly grafted polymer brushes on curved surfaces have been studied extensively, yet the underlying mechanisms that control their structure and stress profile are not fully understood, particularly when the grafting density is high. The traditional decoupling approximation, widely used to analyze these brushes, assumes that the surface can be divided into distinct regions based on the local curvature and the size of the grafted polymers. However, this approach fails to account for the intricate molecular interactions that arise when the surface is highly curved and the molecular size is significant. The validity of the surface-based decoupling approximation has been examined through Monte Carlo simulations, and the results show that it only holds when the surface radius of curvature is much larger than the molecular size. In contrast, highly curved surfaces require an "end-exclusion zone" model that takes into account the direct interactions between grafted chains. The end-exclusion zone model can be applied to analyze polymer brushes on highly curved surfaces with high grafting densities. The stress profiles calculated using this model exhibit a unique behavior, characterized by a stress maximum at the surface center, and the end-exclusion zone model is shown to be valid over a wide range of surface curvatures. The study also reveals that the stress profiles can be accurately described by a two-parameter potential that accounts for the chain size, the surface radius of curvature, and the grafting density. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. Some well-known graphs like lines, cycles, and trees have a specific metric dimension that is well-documented, but others like the hypercube and the star graph do not, and their beta_k does not equal their metric dimension for some values of k. Additionally, we present new upper and lower limits for beta_2 of the hypercube and the star graph, and prove that these new limits are the most extreme values by showing that any graph that has a similar structure to these graphs but with double edges must have a beta_2 that is at least as large as their beta_2. Lastly, we introduce the concept of "antipodal diameter" for graphs and show that some of them have a specific metric dimension when distances are capped at 2. Lastly, we discuss how identifying sets are related to another concept in graph theory known as "dominating sets".

Researchers explored the potential of a machine learning technique known as super-resolving to enhance the clarity of images captured by the James Webb Space Telescope. Specifically, they analyzed 64-nanometer data for the M67 star cluster, both before and after the observation process, to assess the effectiveness of this method. According to their analysis, the machine learning technique yielded the most significant improvements, with a factor of 0.54, when comparing pre-deployment and post-deployment data for the same wavelength. However, this technique introduces artificial data at different wavelengths, which can produce unreasonably high values when analyzing the data's mean intensity. To address this issue, the team employed a statistical correction, resulting in a 20-30 percent reduction in the mean intensity of the data. When applying this correction, the machine learning technique showed improved results, with a factor of 0.75, indicating better agreement with pre-deployment data. The team discovered that the effectiveness of this technique depends on the specific method used for artificial data and statistical correction. Ultimately, they found that the machine learning technique can effectively enhance the clarity of images in certain situations, particularly when observing extended objects, but may not be as accurate for compact objects like the one analyzed in this study. Nonetheless, the team suggests that this technique may be beneficial for inferring the properties of stars within the image, even with the current limitations. The researchers also acknowledged that the space telescope's artificial data and the machine learning technique's limitations could be addressed by utilizing more realistic data and optimizing the technique, respectively. The team's findings provide valuable insights into the potential of machine learning to improve the clarity and accuracy of images captured by the James Webb Space Telescope. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving combinatorial optimization problems by sequentially making choices. Although theory suggests this method yields optimal results when decisions are made simultaneously, we investigate whether it leads to optimal social welfare when decisions are made sequentially. Our research indicates that under specific conditions and the use of a strong dictatorship ordering, the social welfare resulting from this method does not significantly diverge from optimal welfare. However, our findings also indicate that there are scenarios where the social welfare produced is not guaranteed to converge to optimal welfare. To address this concern, we propose an alternative approach based on multi-unit auctions, guaranteeing sequential dictatorship decision-making yields optimal social welfare. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through theoretical and experimental analysis. Furthermore, we show the scalability of this approach by successfully applying it to large-scale instances. The proposed method based on multi-unit auctions provides an attractive solution to solving combinatorial optimization problems in a collaborative setting. We've discovered a significant number of binary asteroids with large separations, which has important implications for binary stability and our understanding of asteroid masses. However, many of these discovered binaries are difficult to study in depth due to their remote locations and the limitations of current observational technology. In our research, we utilized existing data on binary asteroids in the solar system/Earth-Moon system to determine how well the current generation of sky surveys can detect them. Specifically, we analyzed conditions necessary for binaries to be recognized as such, taking into account factors such as size, orbital path, and observational limitations. Our study focused on the effectiveness of detecting wide binary asteroids in the solar system using data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, and we found that even with advanced technology, it's difficult to identify binary asteroids in orbit around their central body when they're viewed edge-on. However, we found that such cases can be identified when viewing angles are greater than 20 degrees. Based on these findings, we estimate that future wide binary asteroid discoveries will likely number in the hundreds, and could potentially reveal up to 10 times more information about asteroid masses than previous detection methods. In the process, we also developed a method for estimating the albedo of binary asteroids based on their shape and orbital characteristics. Using this technique, we applied it to existing data on binary asteroids, and the results showed a clear distinction between low albedo asteroids in the inner solar system and those with higher albedos in the outer solar system. The South Atlantic rift basin formed as a result of the separation of the African and South American tectonic plates, which began around 15 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous period. This process started with the extension of thin crust in western Africa, which gradually expanded eastward over time. Despite significant research on the basin's evolution, there are still many uncertainties regarding its history, particularly in the area east of 15 degrees E where the available data are limited and often outdated. We introduce a novel approach to bidirectional neural memory translation, inspired by the cooperative problem-solving process of role-playing games. When multiple players collaborate to achieve a common goal, their individual contributions can be modeled as memory-aware, structured tasks. We develop a framework that learns to represent these tasks as structured memory modules, then design a task-specific attention mechanism to focus on relevant information when processing input sentences. To facilitate efficient information retrieval from memory during generation, we introduce a dual attention mechanism that learns to weigh memory modules based on the structural aspects of the task. Our method is particularly effective when constrained to limited parallel data, as evidenced by our experiments showcasing significant improvements over conventional backtranslation approaches on paraphrasing and coreference tasks. Additionally, our framework effectively manages complex role references in coreference tasks, outperforming existing methods by a substantial margin of +14.1 F-score when evaluated on the RODEval dataset. The code for our work is openly available at https://github.com/kaushikg00/role-aligners.
