Despite significant research on Lexical Semantic Change Detection, most approaches remain limited to standard model assessments. This study deviates from this focus, shifting towards change discovery - identifying previously unknown word meanings emerging over time within a comprehensive corpus vocabulary. By extensively fine-tuning both a type-based and a token-based methodology on German datasets, our work showcases their applicability in discovering new words with evolving meanings. Additionally, our proposed framework is designed for nearly full automation of evaluations, enabling rigorous testing and validation of both existing and newly identified words. Furthermore, our work highlights several case studies on discovered words, showcasing both the methodologies' effectiveness in capturing lexical semantic change. Moreover, our results on previously established evaluation benchmarks are comparable to those obtained through human assessment. Moreover, our work is made available to the community through a publicly accessible repository.

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Using a Boer-Mulders function-like density, we define a corresponding function for the deuterium case, denoted as $g_1$, and investigate its relationship with quark spin alignment. Furthermore, we differentiate between intrinsic and extrinsic contributions to $g_1$. In an attempt to make it amenable to LHCb measurement, we transform $g_1$ to a variable mass scale, $M^2$, and discuss the associated scale uncertainty. Additionally, we consider the case where quark spin alignment is independent of the choice of frame, and we investigate the possibility of observing $g_1$ through transverse momentum distributions in Drell-Yan processes. Finally, we outline strategies for extracting $g_1$ at the LHC using a combination of inclusive and semi-inclusive measurements. These strategies are expected to yield unambiguous evidence for quark spin alignment properties.

Building upon the concept of knotoids, this study develops an analytical framework to systematically identify and assess knots within proteins of any topology. This framework is utilized to create a comprehensive database of knotted proteins, which is then employed to quantify the prevalence of knotted structures in proteins. Furthermore, a dataset of highly stable protein structures is used to establish probability distributions for knot type and size, location of knots along the protein sequence, and the relationship between knots and protein topology. These findings provide a foundation for developing statistical methods to identify unusual proteins based on their knotted characteristics. As demonstrated with three examples, this approach enables the identification of rare knotoids and prediction of knotted regions in proteins. This framework is particularly relevant for post-genomic studies, as it facilitates the comparison of protein structures encoded within genomes. By integrating this framework into the CAPRI- Knots database, researchers can leverage existing statistical analysis tools via a web-based interface. To resolve the discrepancy known as the Hubble tension, early dark energy (EDE) has been proposed. Although research on EDE is progressing, its impact on primordial black hole (PBH) formation remains an unexplored area. We examine the effect of various EDE models on the abundance of PBHs, considering both power spectrum modifications and nonlinear processes. Our analysis indicates that EDE significantly influences the PBH formation rate in specific contexts, potentially linking PBHs to explanations for dark matter or the cosmological black hole population, even if the EDE density is relatively small. Additionally, we find that the commonly used transfer function approximation is no longer accurate when modeling the effects of EDE on PBH formation. Furthermore, we highlight the significance of taking into account the non-linear effects of EDE in relation to the transfer function approximation. Finally, we suggest that future N-body simulations should be designed to account for the influence of EDE on the matter distribution at small scales. These simulations will be crucial in accurately modeling the effects of EDE on PBH formation and better understanding the potential relationship between PBHs and EDE. Ultimately, a more comprehensive exploration of the EDE-PBH connection will provide valuable insights into our understanding of the early universe and its components. We investigate the implications of an anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem on the Heisenberg uncertainty principle in systems that exhibit symmetry breaking. Initially, our findings confirm that the anomalous NG theorem results in an altered uncertainty principle, which takes on a specific form derived from the Heisenberg principle. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the anomalous theorem effectively captures the non-linear interactions present in a system, and these captured interactions then manifest as deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle. Moreover, our analysis indicates that the anomalous theorem can be viewed as an extension of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle to systems characterized by symmetry breaking, and this relationship between the two theorems holds true regardless of the system's complexity, including both relativistic and non-relativistic systems, as well as those with a finite number of degrees of freedom or an infinite number of degrees of freedom. Additionally, we provide explicit mathematical examples to verify our theoretical conclusions obtained from the anomalous NG theorem, and these examples include both exact and perturbative scenarios. Lastly, we discuss the fundamental significance of our findings within the context of quantum field theory. Recent studies suggest that generating counterfactual data can aid in improving machine learning models by making them more robust and accurate. Nevertheless, the process of large-scale counterfactual data generation is still a complex task due to the need for extensive human input and costly model retraining. We present DISCO, a cutting-edge framework that automates large-scale counterfactual data generation with minimal human involvement and without the need for retraining the original model. By leveraging a combination of advanced techniques such as iterative targeted sampling, progressive counterfactual modification, and efficient model utilization, DISCO is capable of producing high-quality counterfactual data at a significantly lower computational cost. Experimental results using real-world datasets and models demonstrate that the counterfactual data generated by DISCO can lead to notable improvements in model performance, with an average boost of up to 12.5% in F1 score. Moreover, an open-source implementation of the DISCO framework is available for public use, along with accompanying code and pre-trained models that can be adapted for various counterfactual applications. Moreover, we introduce a user-friendly web interface for the DISCO framework, providing an intuitive visualization of the counterfactual data generated and enabling seamless collaboration among human annotators. By providing an open-source framework that is both efficient and effective, we aim to facilitate advancements in the development of counterfactual machine learning methods. Moreover, we introduce a user-friendly web interface for the DISCO framework, providing an intuitive visualization of the counterfactual data generated and enabling seamless collaboration among human annotators. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds promise for creating ultra-thin heterostructures. To investigate this, our team selected the Heusler compound Fe$_3$GeTe$_2$ for a comprehensive study. We employed a combination of in-situ techniques during low-energy electron diffraction and reflectivity measurements to remotely deposit Fe$_3$GeTe$_2$ onto graphene at various substrate temperatures. Our results show that the crystal structure of the Heusler compound matches the underlying graphene lattice when cooled to 300 K, indicating remote epitaxy. However, at elevated temperatures, a transition occurs, revealing a √3×√3 R30° oriented structure that aligns with microripples observed in atomic force microscopy images, likely resulting from the formation of a Moiré pattern caused by lattice mismatch. We also discovered that this structure can persist up to 500 K before transforming back to the 1×1 epitaxy observed at higher temperatures. Notably, this temperature-dependent behavior is consistent with the thermal energy required to form a Moiré pattern. To further understand this phenomenon, we performed density functional theory calculations to analyze the interaction between Fe$_3$GeTe$_2$ and graphene at different temperatures. Our results demonstrate that the remote epitaxy transition can be induced by a thermal energy of 0.24 eV, which is in line with our experimental findings. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes. However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical and expensive. This paper introduces a novel framework that allows for the generation of complex high-dimensional data with multiple predefined conditions using only low-dimensional labels. We formulate an approach to learn a continuous latent space representation that preserves the data's structural characteristics and enables flexible manipulation of the GAN model for multi-condition generation. By projecting labels onto a intermediate space and combining them with noise, we ensure the generation of realistic samples while maintaining the diversity of the desired conditions. Notably, our method enables the generation of multiple conditions from a single latent code without needing to train separate GAN models. Experimental results validate our approach's effectiveness in multi-condition generation tasks, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled data. We achieve impressive performance on both the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, a more challenging scenario with the Fashion-NIST dataset, and an additional experiment in medical image analysis. The proposed technique provides a new direction for research on flexible GANs with multiple conditions and may be applied to various real-world data scenarios. The code is available at https://github.com/zhengyangfeng/ MultiConditionGAN.

The origin of high-energy gamma-ray emissions from galaxies located at immense distances from the Milky Way remains an unresolved puzzle. Many of these distant galaxies, which include quasars and radio galaxies, emit significant amounts of gamma-rays in the energy range of 1-10 GeV when observed using the Fermi satellite. By analyzing 24 years of data from the MAGIC ground telescope and the Fermi satellite on 69 distant gamma-ray emitters, our research discovered a strong correlation between gamma-ray emissions and radio emissions from these sources. Furthermore, by analyzing 12 years of data from the MAGIC ground telescope and the Fermi satellite on 7 nearby blazars, which are extremely powerful and oriented almost directly at us, our research found a strong correlation between gamma-ray emissions and the rate of matter falling into these sources, which is consistent with expectations based on quantum theory. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose. However, the subjective nature of cardiac auscultation by healthcare professionals can lead to inaccuracies. This study focuses on creating an objective, automated system for cardiac abnormality diagnosis through improved cardiac auscultation analysis. Initially, an automatic noise reduction technique was developed to minimize background sounds in cardiac auscultation recordings. Subsequently, a set of distinctive features was extracted from the cleaned recordings to characterize cardiac abnormalities. These features were used in conjunction with machine learning algorithms to classify cardiac conditions. Our research utilized a diverse dataset containing recordings of normal and abnormal cardiac sounds from multiple sources. Experimental results from multiple experiments indicated that a combination of the recordings themselves and the extracted features in conjunction with a support vector machine classifier yielded the highest accuracy levels of 99.79%. Moreover, our research demonstrated that the extracted features hold significant diagnostic value in cardiac condition diagnosis. This study's findings have the potential to contribute to the development of low-cost, point-of-care systems for cardiac diagnosis through automated analysis of cardiac auscultation recordings. This could be particularly beneficial in resource-constrained settings where cardiac auscultation is commonly employed due to limited access to imaging technology. Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of categories. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that weren't encountered during training. This is particularly evident when evaluating models trained on a limited set of classes when tested on all instruments in the taxonomy. Experimental results indicate a significant boost in performance with only a minor increase in computational costs. Academic researchers heavily rely on search engines like Google Scholar and online bibliographic databases like PubMed for their research, but they predominantly consume information by browsing through lists of search results, sorting them based on relevance. In contrast, these search platforms underutilize the wealth of information contained in the abstracts of research articles and fail to account for the significance of specific information like title, authors, affiliations, abstract text, citation counts, and related publications. In the context of Question Answering, this knowledge base serves as the foundation for answering questions related to the literature. Current approaches to Question Answering focus solely on utilizing the text of abstracts to answer questions, neglecting the potential value of other bibliographic attributes. In our research, we introduce a new Question Answering dataset that incorporates the full range of attributes present in Google Scholar, specifically designed to evaluate models that can leverage these attributes to answer questions about the literature. We also present a novel approach, a framework called Attribute-Aware Fusion, that enables the effective utilization of these attributes in Question Answering by employing a combination of attribute-specific models and a unified fusion module. Our results show that our approach yields superior performance when compared to the current state-of-the-art approaches, emphasizing the significance of attributes in Question Answering. Furthermore, our analysis of model performance in relation to attribute type and corpus knowledge demonstrates that the Attribute-Aware Fusion framework is capable of harnessing the benefits of attributes effectively. Ultimately, our work signifies a significant step forward in the development of Question Answering systems capable of interpreting academic papers and has far-reaching implications for applications that rely on the literature, such as scientific discovery and hypothesis evaluation. In the process, we also introduce a novel set of evaluation metrics for Question Answering models that consider the quality of answers in light of the underlying evidence presented in the literature. This study presents novel non-dimensionalized Kermack-McKendrick models that maintain their original spatial and temporal dynamics while eliminating superfluous parameters. The original model is transformed into a form that all model variables converge to a range between 0 and 1, reducing the need for ad-hoc boundary conditions and enabling simulation across an infinite boundary. The new models are then applied to an infinite population under periodic boundary conditions, using Fourier series to represent spatial and temporal dynamics. The resulting non-dimensionalized models provide a flexible framework for analyzing epidemic models using asymptotic methods, enabling the exploration of complex dynamics at any level of complexity. The proposed method is specifically demonstrated with an SIR model featuring a nonlinear incidence function, showing the emergence of asymmetric oscillatory behavior and localized epidemic waves following a large increase in travel speed. The asymptotic solution is validated through a comparison with simulations, highlighting the approach's potential for further investigating epidemic models using numerical techniques. The method can be applied to other Kermack-McKendrick models, such as those featuring multiple strains or non-local transmission dynamics. The approach enables an in-depth analysis of epidemic models, facilitating a deeper understanding of the underlying dynamics and making it suitable for application to real-world problems. This study focuses on a scenario where an $O(10)$ TeV Majorana fermion is produced through a diquark operator and interacts with a standard model meson through an $SU(3)$ flavor symmetry broken by the CKM matrix. Furthermore, we utilize flavor constraints from low-energy experiments, specifically the neutron electric dipole moment and $K^+$ decay, to establish an upper limit for the Majorana fermion's coupling constant of $10^{-3.5}$, based on a $2$ standard deviation confidence level. This limit can significantly impact the parameter space available to multilepton signal searches at the LHC, and we estimate that with the full $13$ TeV LHC dataset, this new physics could be detectable for a significantly broader range of flavor invariant effective field theory's diquark couplings than previously considered. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter forms for lengthy phrases, commonly found across various written materials. While they are beneficial for brevity, they can be challenging to recognize, especially for individuals with limited domain knowledge. This difficulty is compounded by the fact that the same acronym can have multiple interpretations depending on the context, posing an obstacle for natural language processing systems. Presently, existing models primarily focus on identifying acronym definitions within a specific domain, but they struggle to adapt to new contexts and domains. This research introduces a novel approach that leverages contextual and domain knowledge to identify acronym definitions, extending the capability to cross-sentence and cross-domain understanding. Furthermore, our proposed method surpasses existing models utilizing domain-specific knowledge through the incorporation of contextual knowledge, ultimately achieving superior performance in benchmark evaluations. The integration of contextual knowledge allows our model to excel in comparison to models that rely solely on domain-specific knowledge. Moreover, our approach successfully applies to out-of-domain context predictions, showcasing the ability to effectively utilize domain-specific knowledge for cross-domain acronym definition identification. This research is supported by the availability of large-scale knowledge graphs containing domain-specific information, which is also utilized to enhance the performance of the model in cross-domain evaluations. This is further illustrated by our results in the TACRFSUM dataset, which demonstrates a notable enhancement in performance when using contextual knowledge, ultimately achieving a 12.5% increase in F1-score in comparison to domain-only models. This research is also accompanied by the introduction of a novel dataset, ACRIQUE, which is a context-aware and domain-agnostic acronym definition dataset comprising 10 diverse domains and featuring over 36,000 annotated instances. This dataset is an expansion of the previously mentioned TACRFSUM dataset, which is now available in its entirety with the addition of context information. This research is open to further exploration and is made accessible to facilitate advancements in the field of acronym understanding. We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on spin-zero atoms, we examined the significance of collisions that transfer spin and the photoassociation process in creating atom-molecule pairs from a condensate using a two-component description. By applying this approach, we were able to derive an effective model that includes phase-locking interactions and collisional processes. We found that collisional fields can either enhance or diminish the conversion efficiency, depending on the magnitude of a spin-unit density compared to an atom's density within the molecule. We also simulated the effects of these collisional processes through a quantum nonlinear circuit model and the atom-molecule dynamics in an optical lattices. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of dark-state filtering on coherent conversion in two hyperfine states. Notably, we found that collisional unitarity can lead to complete phase-locking in systems with low molecule density. However, this occurs at a significantly slower rate than phase-locking in systems without spin-exchange collisions. We also found that coherent conversion can be significantly improved by a factor of up to $10^4$ through the application of dark-state filtering. Finally, we applied this technique to a Bose-Einstein condensate consisting of multiple spin units and demonstrated that it can result in the phase-locking of $N$-body molecules within the molecule. Brain tumors pose a significant threat to public health, often diagnosed at advanced stages due to limited awareness symptoms.  Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) serves as the primary diagnostic tool for brain tumors, accurately pinpointing tumors in hard-to-reach areas with minimal invasiveness.  Advanced techniques like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) have revolutionized MRI-based tumor detection and grading through efficient pattern recognition, leveraging vast amounts of pathological data with concise annotations.  Yet, collecting such extensive datasets proves challenging, especially for rare tumor types like Chordoma, which necessitates specialized diagnostic centers and pathology labs to collect data.  To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach to create artificial chordoma tumors by manipulating real MRI scans of the same patient, thus creating diverse datasets with detailed annotations at little extra cost, enabling training and testing of deep learning models on artificial-data without affecting actual patient diagnosis.  We employed a sophisticated technique called CycleGAN to generate high-quality artificial tumor scans, which were validated through experiments using a unique dataset comprising 211 MRI scans of Chordoma tumors, alongside assessments of the generated models' performance using metrics like ROC-AUC and F1-score, ultimately yielding a baseline accuracy of 0.88 when testing against real-world data. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods with physical insights from forward models. However, existing rendering techniques fail to meet the demands of complex scenes and high-resolution images, largely because they don't account for occlusions and surface disconnections. To address these limitations in scene reconstruction tasks, we introduce a new approach based on differentiable spline rendering, which leverages the capabilities of B-splines to represent coherent and detailed scenes. By formulating a shape regularization term derived from the B-spline basis, we develop an efficient optimization strategy that directly minimizes disconnections and other issues caused by missing data. This results in a method that accurately handles occlusions and efficiently reconstructs scenes from images, especially in cases where the scene is complex or the image resolution is high. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach with several experiments, including both synthetic and real-world data, showing it can outperform current state-of-the-art methods. The code for our approach is available online at https://github.com/ChenZh-SJTU/DS-Scene-Reconstruction.

A popular technique used in video recording, interlacing, generates double the frames per second for a given bandwidth, however this technique generates visually unappealing images unless properly processed. Interlacing is particularly common in sports videos, which often contain complex backgrounds and foreground objects in motion, making them particularly difficult to handle. Current methods based on super-resolution, such as the MSRES and the one proposed by Wang et al., fail when applied to interlacing factors greater than 2, leading to a significant gap in video interlacing technology. This gap can be bridged by re-examining the interlacing process and recognizing it as a resolution enhancement problem from half to full resolution, rather than a classification issue. A new framework based on progressive learning, known as the Progressive Interlacing Network (PIN), is introduced, which enhances resolution in a step-by-step manner from the original image to twice the resolution, and finally to full resolution. The evaluation of the proposed PIN model on the Real-UVG and the enhanced Real-UVG datasets, which contain real-world data with interlacing factors greater than 2, shows that it outperforms the state-of-the-art methods based on super-resolution and the one proposed by Wang et al. in terms of PSNR and SSIM. The results of the PIN model on real-world videos, including a tennis video with complex background and foreground objects in motion, demonstrate its ability to handle challenging scenes while maintaining visual clarity. The source code and the dataset used in this research are available online at https://github.com/zhengzhengfeng/PI-NET. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications including flood risk management. Traditional numerical methods, although reliable, are often slow due to their river flow velocity predictions being based on complex and slow-to-calculate solvers. Machine learning algorithms, capable of making rapid and accurate predictions, present an attractive alternative. In this research, a novel hybrid approach was developed, combining the strengths of both numerical methods and machine learning algorithms. A central solver was first used to create high-resolution, flow velocity data for various river conditions in a virtual laboratory setting. A machine learning algorithm was then trained on this data to predict river flow velocities at specific points along with other properties such as water elevation and flow direction. The results showed that the machine learning model's predictions were highly accurate, matching the accuracy of the original solver, and was particularly effective at predicting velocities in areas with complex topography. Furthermore, the model's ability to efficiently handle large numbers of simultaneous predictions was demonstrated. The research demonstrated the potential of this hybrid approach to enhance the performance of numerical solvers in real-world flood risk management scenarios. The model developed as part of this research is openly accessible on GitHub, along with the associated code, and can be found under the project name RiverFlowML. The project's website includes a comprehensive user guide to facilitate its use and customization. Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate predictions and inferences, and we provide an overview of the field's key aspects, highlighting potential applications and future research directions. Specifically, we discuss the use of causal deep learning in enhancing interpretability, developing robust models, and handling imbalanced data, and also touch on related topics such as causal deep learning's connection to generative models and the utilization of external knowledge. Furthermore, we outline available methods for causal inference and provide an assessment of the field's future trajectory and the challenges it must overcome. This comprehensive survey and ongoing research in the field are made available to the community through this survey, and we hope it will contribute to further advancements in causal deep learning. This survey has been made available to the community through an accompanying repository, along with the authors' ongoing research in the field.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains challenging. Our research utilizes a multi-laser 1D extension of the scanning technique to obtain highly resolved temperature and optical property data in a fixed bed reactor.  By using three lasers to scan a single line in a transverse direction, we can obtain temperature readings in approximately 1 second with 1°C accuracy in areas as small as 0.125 cubic centimeters.  This was demonstrated in a packed bed of spheres at temperatures of 500°C and 700°C and also in a bed of catalyst pellets coated with a layer of naphthalene.  Optical property measurements obtained in this way were found to be consistent with previously reported measurements made using a different technique.  This method has the advantage of being faster, more spatially precise, and capable of measuring temperature in areas where dust accumulation would make other methods impractical.  We also successfully demonstrated the ability to use this technique in a reacting fixed bed of catalyst by measuring temperature in a bed converted from naphthalene to phenol over a silver-alumina catalyst.  This method has significant potential to significantly enhance our understanding of mass and heat transfer in fixed bed reactors and could also be adapted for use in other types of packed beds. This note outlines a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions and proves a weakened form of the b-principle for this function class, enabling the extension of certain Madsen-Weiss type theorems to oriented surface bundles. Additionally, it establishes a relationship between the spin structure of a bundle and the number of colors used in an oriented colored submersion, which facilitates the application of the weakened b-principle to a broader range of surface bundles, including those with non-trivial fundamental group. Furthermore, it demonstrates that for any given surface S, the space of maps from S to the Klein bottle is topologically equivalent to a 3-fold covering of the space of maps from S to the real line. This result can be further generalized to a broader class of surface bundles known as the Solv bundle. Moreover, it explores various applications of these findings, including the computation of the space of maps from an oriented surface to the Klein bottle and the extension of classical hyperplane arrangements to a broader class of surface bundles known as the SL(2,C) bundle. Lastly, it suggests potential future research directions related to the b-principle and its applications to a broader class of surface bundles known as the PSL(2,C) bundle. This work is based on the authors' previous research discussed in the paper 'The b-principle for oriented colored submersions' presented at the 2018 conference 'Recent Advances in Compactified Hyperplane Arrangements'. Furthermore, it is currently being expanded into a comprehensive paper titled 'More Maps for Surface Bundles'.

This research compares the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using a fully nonlinear three-dimensional formulation, researchers have encountered significant difficulties in solving resulting systems of linear equations due to their large size, highly irregular coefficient matrices, and stiffness-based non-normalization issues. Several BDDC implementation challenges were overcome, including developing a new coercion step that significantly improved its performance. Although the BDDC method demonstrated comparable or better performance to AMG for most cases studied, further research is needed to establish its robustness and general applicability to similar-scale cardiac mechanics applications. The developed software package, BDCPACK, is now available for download. It includes an implementation of the BDDC solver that uses the Trilinos package, GasGA, for its single-level solver. The code can be accessed through the National Institute of Health's Computational Biology Suite (CBS). The standard Wigner semi-circular distribution's $n$th moment is associated with non-crossing pair-partitions of the index set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$. This connection forms the basis of an inverse formula that allows us to generate a random Hermitian matrix based on a given set of moments, provided those moments satisfy a certain condition. A key aspect of this inverse formula involves non-crossing pair-partitions of the index set. Building on this relationship, we derive an explicit formula for the moment corresponding to each partition of this type. Furthermore, this formula can be applied to random variables other than the standard semi-circular distribution. To accomplish this, we utilize an iterative process that involves an integral equation whose solution is provided by an explicit formula derived from an operator on a Hilbert space. This operator is defined as a product of two others, which are obtained through a change of variable that depends on the partition in question. As a result, we are able to generate novel multi-parameter formulas for calculating moments associated with random variables that follow specific distributions. In addition, we establish an explicit formula for the probability density function of a specific distribution. This distribution is derived from a generalised version of the standard Wigner semi-circular distribution. It is obtained by applying a non-crossing pair-partition transformation to a standard Gaussian distribution on the real line. This new density function has a unique shape that is determined by an explicit parameter, which is a positive value less than one. It is worth noting that this new density function does not correspond to any known distribution in the literature. In addition, we discuss the properties of this new density function, both theoretically and through practical examples. A key aspect of these properties is the location of this new density function's modes. In particular, we show that its mode is located at a specific point on the negative side of a continuous interval that has a clear definition. In order to verify this, we use an alternative approach that is distinct from the methods used to derive this new density function. This alternative approach is based on an explicit formula for the maximum of a function that is obtained by applying a single-step version of the non-crossing pair-partition transformation to a standard Gaussian distribution on the real line. Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. This distinct behavior, observed in certain systems that combine forward walks and self-trapping events, can be accounted for by applying a time-dependent mean-field approach. Our model extracts the essential characteristics of an interacting system by utilizing the full correlation matrix of the diffusion process. We develop a simplified description based on the second moment's time-dependent characteristics and propose an alternative method for calculating these traits from the knowledge of the correlation matrix's time derivatives alone. Our approach is demonstrated using two examples: a one-dimensional ring with interactions between neighboring sites and a two-dimensional square lattice with interactions between nearest and next-to-nearest neighboring sites. Our findings show that the applicability of the time-dependent mean-field approach depends on the system's spatial structure, with tight packing leading to failed predictions and a threshold for successful applications that is highly dependent on the type of disorder present. We also identify the time-dependent mean-field approach's limitations as bound systems that exhibit behavior similar to the infinite-system counterpart over finite periods of time. Our research is further validated by comparing our results to extensive numerical simulations, with some observations highlighting the emergence of bound states in both forward-walk and self-trapping models and the distinct characteristics of free and bound particles in models that combine forward-walk and self-trapping behavior. Additionally, we identify the time-dependent mean-field approach's failure as a sign of bound state formation, and we provide a theoretical framework for bound state energies by applying the approach to models that explicitly exclude trapping events. We also develop an analytical expression for predicting bound state formation in models that combine forward-walk and self-trapping behavior, and we outline the conditions under which time-dependent mean-field calculations can be used to determine bound state energies. Our findings also highlight the equivalence of control Lyapunov functions and abnormal controls, which can be viewed as optimal stabilization trajectories from any initial state to any target state. Moreover, our research involves presenting a method for computing control Lyapunov functions utilizing optimal control techniques. This method is then applied to analyze a specific example involving a polynomial control system. Notably, our results on the connection between global asymptotic controllability and control Lyapunov functions appear novel even within the realm of bounded controls. The latter part of our research explores the computational aspects of these theoretical connections. In practice, this means that if a system has a controllable trajectory from an initial state to a target state, even in the absence of stabilizability, then there exists an optimal control solution along this trajectory, which can be computed using the proposed algorithm. In such cases, this solution can be viewed as a stabilization path from the initial state to the target state, thus demonstrating the concept of sample stabilizability. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue of overconfidence, which can lead to misclassification. Our research focuses on an innovative solution to tackle this problem by introducing ExcConTrast, a contrasting-based extrinsic confidence calibration method. Unlike traditional internal prediction uncertainty estimation methods such as entropy and temperature, our approach leverages classification errors between the model's predicted confidence distribution and an estimated posterior distribution to penalize overconfidence. We utilized ExcConTrast and evaluated its effectiveness on two popular datasets, namely CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, utilizing ResNet-18 and WideResNet-28-10 architectures. Our results indicate that ExcConTrast enhances the calibration of models while maintaining their original classification performance. Moreover, an analysis of our findings includes comparisons with intrinsic calibration methods such as Entropy-based and Temp-based approaches. We also conducted an experiment to visualize the estimated posterior distribution in contrast to the model's predicted confidence distribution, thereby providing insight into the behavior of ExcConTrast. We have made our code and data available for replication at the following link: https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/ExcConTrast. Reinforcement learning has made notable progress in recent years, but numerous difficulties lie ahead for its applications to vast and ever-changing problems. One major hurdle in such scenarios is the significant number of possible actions, which often necessitates the use of neural network-based function approximators to represent policies. Another issue arises when the goal state is undefined, the reward function is unreliable, or both, which poses challenges for existing policy optimization methods. To address these issues, we introduce an end-to-end algorithm that learns to optimize a reliable virtual reward function allowing the efficient solution of vast, dynamic problems with undefined goal states. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by successfully applying it to two complex tasks featuring unreliable real-world rewards and ambiguous goal states. The resulting performance surpasses that of multiple baseline methods, and the learned reward functions exhibit valuable predictive power, highlighting the potential for further analysis and utilization in future research. Our approach and associated test data are available online.

These chaotic MMOs are distinguished by the coexistence of long-duration, nearly periodic episodes of both high and low population states. As the variable prey population's parameters change, the system undergoes a bifurcation from stable coexistence to the occurrence of chaotic MMOs, and subsequently, chaotic MMOs give way to periodic or quasi-periodic solutions in either a transitive or non-transitive manner, depending on the prey population's characteristics. Using data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we analyzed a correlation between the star formation rate in a galaxy's central region and its bulge's morphology. Specifically, we examined the relationship between the H$\alpha$-based star formation rate and the Sersic index $n$, which describes the shape of a galaxy's surface brightness profile. Our study focused on a sample of 4196 galaxies with well-defined Sersic indices and star formation rates. We found that the probability distribution of the Sersic index is not a normal distribution, but rather skewed towards lower values. This skewness is corrected for by using a logarithmic scale for the Sersic index. We found a significant positive correlation between the star formation rate and the Sersic index on a logarithmic scale, specifically $\log R_{\rm H\alpha} \propto 0.21(n-1)$. This result can be explained by the idea that more densely packed, star-forming regions in bulges are associated with higher Sersic indices. We also observed a correlation between the Sersic index and the specific star formation rate, which is consistent with previous findings. Notably, we found that the probability distribution of the Sersic index varies depending on a galaxy's mass, with lower-mass galaxies exhibiting a broader distribution of Sersic indices. This finding is consistent with the idea that lower-mass galaxies have more irregular, less densely packed bulges. We also found evidence that the probability distribution of the Sersic index is influenced by a galaxy's stellar mass, rather than its dark matter mass. This suggests that the shape of a galaxy's bulge is primarily determined by mass supplied by stellar evolution, rather than mass supplied by dark matter. We also found that the probability distribution of the Sersic index is not significantly correlated with a galaxy's star formation rate or specific star formation rate. However, we did find that the mean Sersic index is correlated with these quantities, with higher star formation rates and specific star formation rates associated with higher mean Sersic indices. This finding is consistent with the idea that more actively star-forming galaxies in the late stages of their evolution have more irregular, less densely packed bulges. We also found evidence that the probability distribution of the Sersic index is influenced by a galaxy's orientation, with a preference for certain orientations over others. This preference is likely due to the presence of dust in the galaxy's central region, which can obscure our view of the galaxy's bulge

In the process of understanding public opinions, sentiment analysis plays a vital role. The task typically requires a large amount of labeled data but in some cases, such as in new topic sentiment prediction, there is limited to no labeled information available. We have investigated two approaches to tackle this challenge: one based on the assumption that opinions are connected through a hierarchical structure and the other assuming a more general relationship between opinions, based on their semantic similarities. The first approach involves building a sentiment hierarchy from which a topic's sentiment can be inferred, while the second approach involves learning a sentiment representation from the labeled data and performing semi-supervised learning to extend the representation to the unlabeled data. The second approach is further divided into two sub-methods: one based on the assumption of a linear relationship and the other based on a non-linear relationship. We have evaluated the methods on three datasets, one for finance-related opinions and two for general opinions, and the results show that the hierarchical structure learned from the labeled data can be extended to the unlabeled data with high accuracy. The best performance was achieved by the method assuming a non-linear relationship between opinions, based on their semantic similarities. Notably, it is found that the quantum provocation of classical chaos is observable in regions surrounding classical stable islands, and can be attributed to resonant interactions between the involved quantum states. This phenomenon is illustrated through energy spectra obtained using the diagonalization method. Additionally, we observe that resonant interactions can result in the quenching of quantum chaos caused by semiclassical resonances, an effect that is visible in both the calculations of the semiclassical Lyapunov exponent and in the energy spectra following the adiabatic change of parameters. This study introduces an innovative approach that utilizes a convolutional neural network to extract high-level features from X-ray images and a linear regression model to predict the RT-PCR test results based on these extracted features. The approach was evaluated using a publicly accessible dataset and consisted of multiple trials to determine its effectiveness in accurately identifying severe COVID-19 cases. The results showed that the approach was capable of effectively identifying cases with high CT scores (>14) with an accuracy of 85.7% (+/- 11.9) and cases with low CT scores (<=14) with an accuracy of 92.9% (+/- 4.8). Additionally, the approach was found to be robust in predicting CT scores for both subsets of cases. The findings suggest that the proposed method holds promise for utilizing X-ray images to enhance clinical diagnosis of COVID-19 by providing an objective, data-driven prediction of CT scores. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor image quality or mislabeled main objects. To mitigate this issue, we developed a skewed negative sampling technique that targets challenging relationship proposals. By incorporating this method into a weighted hard negative mining strategy, we achieved significant performance improvements, exceeding existing cutting-edge methods by 3.6% in the Visual Relationship Detection task. Our approach not only reduces the complexity of training but also enables the incorporation of diverse data sources, such as datasets with incorrect or incomplete annotations. For instance, we successfully integrated the Liu et al. dataset, which contains incorrect annotations, into our method, resulting in improved overall performance. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design uniquely captures Caxton C. Foster's pioneering ideas on parallel processing, incorporating the concepts of simultaneous parallel writes and the merging of output values – features commonly omitted in typical CAM applications like network routing. The resulting system allows a host computer to interface with the CAPP over USB/UART using a simple serial communication protocol that we've refined to achieve maximum throughput of 156 KB/s, sufficient to test the parallel processor's core functionality despite being limited by the serial connection. The integration of a 64-bit wide parallel data path and the generation of Q-values (confidence levels) have been demonstrated through successful execution of various test programs, including finding the minimum and maximum values stored across multiple entries, estimating the mean by summing specific bits across multiple entries, and generating Q-values during these operations. The design and performance of the CAPP have been validated using VHDL and verified through successful hardware tests, in addition to utilizing the design to develop a Python-based driver for the CAPP. The design and performance of the CAPP are detailed, and the design is made available under an open-source license for the benefit of researchers and students interested in content-addressable parallel processing. The design and performance of the CAPP have been presented at the 2021 IEEE 14th International Conference on Design/Development and Testing of Computer Aids, and the design and related software are available for download at https://sourceforge.net/projects/capp-fpga/. Current cutting-edge neural code models excel at generating individual code segments but often struggle with complex tasks like entire function code production. To tackle this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages static code analysis for weak supervision. Our method, CodeFUSE, employs type checking and linter data to guide neural code generation using contrastive learning. By testing CodeFUSE on two challenging benchmarks involving Java method code, we show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art transformer-based models and achieves significant enhancements in code quality, accuracy, and diversity. Furthermore, CodeFUSE's learned representations exhibit strong generalization capabilities, enabling the model to excel even in scenarios with minimal supervised code data. Our technique lays the groundwork for future advancements in neural code synthesis through the incorporation of additional weak supervision signals derived from static code analysis. Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing the second terrestrial detection of this phenomenon, known as solar neutron decay protons (sndp). Although the 2004 detection occurred during a full moon, it presents an important opportunity to study sndp in a radioactively crowded environment with a relatively low background. Furthermore, since the 2004 event occurred at a lower altitude compared to previous detections, it allows for a clearer distinction between in-flight decays of incoming cosmic secondary particles and actual sndp events. Consequently, this new data significantly enhances the understanding of sndp properties, particularly their maximum energy, which appears to be around 18.4 MeV with an 89% confidence level, and also provides a clearer picture of the ndp spectral shape. Additionally, the analysis of the 2004 event, combined with the 1982 and 1989 data, reveals a distinct peak in the ndp spectrum at approximately 10.7 MeV with a 97% confidence level, indicating that the ndp spectrum is not solely described by a single power law as previously reported. The discovery of this peak may be indicative of a distinct physical process associated with the generation of sndp. The analysis of the 2004 event also provides a clearer understanding of the spatial distribution of sndp, which appears to originate from a circular area with a diameter of approximately 180,000 km, centered on the solar flare site with a 95% confidence level. Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and frequent updates requiring significant computational resources and memory adjustments. Existing approaches, such as nearest neighbors and deep learning models, struggle with these challenges, leading to our interest in an efficient real-time anomaly detection system for shifting data streams. We introduce a novel method called EfficientStream, based on an updated version of the Mahalanobis distance metric, which standardizes feature data for each individual class, ensuring minimal storage and computation for each new data entry. By maintaining a dynamic in-memory storage that matches the system's hardware, EfficientStream takes advantage of hardware acceleration to perform calculations and adapt to new data entries with minimal adjustments, reducing computational and memory updates. We demonstrate the performance of EfficientStream through a comprehensive evaluation of its efficiency, accuracy, and scalability, comparing it to leading streaming algorithms and hardware-optimized deep learning models, and show its effectiveness on diverse real-world data streams. The optimized version of EfficientStream is available for download at https://github.com/IBM/efficientstream.

The US Supreme Court has ruled that a court can force an individual to disclose a password associated with a device, according to the doctrine of lawful access. This study involves a survey of 703 participants who evaluated the implications of this doctrine on respondents' willingness to disclose passwords and the security measures they employ. The results indicate that, to avoid compromising security information, individuals might refuse to provide passwords, which could have unintended consequences for respondents who are required to disclose access to devices containing vital information. These outcomes are supported by data from previous studies conducted in 2019 and 2020, which showed similar trends in respondents' willingness to disclose passwords. The findings suggest that the doctrine of lawful access has a significant impact on attitudes toward password disclosure. Furthermore, the study reveals that the willingness to disclose passwords is influenced by factors such as device type, security measures employed, and the potential consequences of disclosure. In cases where the potential consequences of non-disclosure are severe, such as loss of life or significant financial losses, individuals are more likely to refuse to provide passwords. In contrast, when the potential consequences are minimal, such as losing access to a device, individuals are more likely to disclose passwords willingly. The study also discovered that the willingness to disclose passwords is higher for devices that contain essential information for daily life, such as calendars and contact lists, compared to devices that do not hold such importance. In cases where the potential consequences of non-disclosure are severe, the willingness to disclose passwords is lower for devices that contain essential information. The study's findings have implications for the doctrine of lawful access and highlight the need for a balanced approach that takes into account the security concerns of individuals while ensuring that law enforcement agencies have the necessary tools to investigate crimes effectively. Ultimately, the study suggests that the doctrine of lawful access should be revised to account for the potential consequences of non-disclosure and the security measures employed by individuals. In cases where the potential consequences of non-disclosure are severe, the doctrine should permit courts to compel password disclosure. In cases where the potential consequences of non-disclosure are minimal, the doctrine should permit courts to compel password disclosure only if the information sought is essential for daily life. In cases where the potential consequences of non-disclosure are moderate, the doctrine should permit courts to compel password disclosure on a case-by-case basis. The study's findings provide valuable insights that can inform the ongoing debate about the doctrine of lawful access and its implications for the balance between national security and individual privacy. It can predict real-world observations and outcomes in scenarios involving linear channel loss, including the associated gain levels, error rates in different measurement bases, and final key rates. Our model, which takes into account the characteristics of source states, entangled states, and measurement instruments, can be applied to various types of MDI-QKD implementations that utilize different source states, such as single-photon Fock states, coherent states with restricted amplitude, and coherent states with no amplitude restrictions. Furthermore, our model incorporates the process of applying baselines and correcting error rates, which is fundamental to the MDI-QKD protocol. By analyzing the simulated data, we derived a simplified formula to estimate the gain in each measurement basis when the source states are highly single-edged, i.e., states with very low probability of having multiple photons or having a high probability of having more than one photons. In contrast, when the source states are highly multi-edged, i.e., states with a high probability of having single photons or having multiple photons with high probability, the gain in each measurement basis is significantly lower than expected for single-photon states. This study presents a novel, high-order numerical method for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under a constant diffusion term. The devised method integrates elements from the Lagrange-Galerkin and semi-Lagrangian techniques, yielding an explicit, conservative, consistent, and robust scheme capable of handling substantial time step sizes. A convergence analysis for the exactly integrated Lagrange-Galerkin approach is provided, along with an implementable alternative that employs approximate integration. The method is particularly useful in modeling time-dependent mean field games equations and similar equations with nonlinear constraints, and it is demonstrated through numerical examples and comparisons. All code used for these examples is included as an appendix to the paper. Although the method is tailored for constant diffusion, it is also applicable to time-dependent diffusion terms that do not change rapidly. However, the scheme may not provide the desired performance or accuracy in such cases. As an aside, the study also presents an analysis of the convergence properties of the Lagrange-Galerkin technique in the absence of diffusion. The study employs a multi-dimensional fit to determine the new physics contributions to each decay mode, taking into account the constraints imposed by experimental and theoretical limits on the new physics parameters. Nonetheless, employing such networks for critical life-altering decisions demands a deeper understanding of their decision-making processes. Unfortunately, most artificial neural networks, including DNNs, function as opaque systems, hindering insight into their internal workings. Although some research has been conducted on enhancing transparency within these networks, much of this work focuses solely on revealing input effects on output, rather than comprehending the network's internal decision-making mechanisms itself. This study proposes an alternative approach to create a fundamentally transparent network that inherently reflects the characteristics of its inputs in its internal workings, making it suitable for life-critical applications. As a numerical indicator, the proposed network's simplicity and efficiency are demonstrated through numerical experiments, followed by its practical effectiveness in real-world scenarios. Moreover, the network's performance is compared to traditional neural networks to evaluate the trade-off between transparency and performance. Finally, the characteristics of this network are further analyzed through computational tools to provide valuable design guidelines and to discuss its potential applications in various scenarios. As the world becomes increasingly reliant on DNNs for life-altering decisions, it is crucial to prioritize the development of fundamentally transparent networks that can be understood and trusted. Typically, lower-mass stars that have expanded retain similar rotation rates across their interior and exterior layers. However, the unique properties of K2-25b challenge this norm. To model this behavior, researchers employed a semi-empirical approach that took into account the star's interaction with the planet, resulting in different rotation speeds for its core and surface layers. The model indicated a 10 km/hr difference in rotation speeds between the outer layers and the star's interior. To validate this finding, several tests were conducted using various models and assumptions. These tests included adjusting assumptions about the star's composition, tidal interactions, and thermal energy distribution. Additionally, a comparison with similar stars showed that K2-25b exhibits rotation patterns that are distinct from its peers. This research provides a first look at the internal dynamics of a low-mass star in its post-main sequence stage and contributes to the broader study of tidal interactions between stars and planets. Furthermore, this discovery may indicate the presence of a partially broken tidal synchronization cycle, a phenomenon that could be characteristic of low-mass stars as they evolve. Fake news has become a significant concern on social media platforms, particularly during emergent events when timely and accurate information is crucial. Although machine learning-based approaches have shown effectiveness in detecting fake news, their reliance on extensive training data and slow adaptability to new topics poses significant challenges. In order to address this issue, a new approach known as few-shot learning was introduced, which enables the detection of fake news with only a limited number of examples. However, existing methods for few-shot learning in fake news detection face several issues, including the need to collect additional data, label costs, and the absence of emergent event datasets. Furthermore, existing approaches typically employ offline methods to select support and query samples, which can lead to inconsistent performance when confronted with new topics or characters in natural language processing tasks. In order to address these limitations, a new approach known as fake news few-shot learning was proposed, which utilizes an active learning method to enrich the base dataset with the most relevant data in each new topic. Experimental results have demonstrated that this approach not only accelerates the adaptation process by an average of at least 2.5 times but also enhances the model's accuracy by an average of at least 3.4% when compared to traditional few-shot learning methods. Moreover, an analysis of the model's performance in relation to the number of additional data it receives has shown that even with as little as 10 extra samples per character per dataset, a significant improvement in accuracy of at least 5.1% can be achieved. Quantum tunneling is highly sensitive to environmental changes and can be controlled through the strategic placement of dopants within a silicon device.  By incorporating phosphorus, a key element, we investigate its anti-bonding states and how they interact with other nearby dopants.  Employing a combination of tight-binding and many-body physics, our simulations reveal the influence of silicon-silicon interactions on these states and how they can be manipulated via a nearby helium atom.  Furthermore, our findings suggest that helium may serve as a catalyst in switching the spin of nearby electrons.  Additionally, we explore the possibility of using helium to facilitate Raman-type transitions between different quantum states and estimate the required duration of a laser pulse for such transitions.  Our study offers a theoretical basis for the development of quantum silicon devices utilizing the unique properties of phosphorus and helium.  We also propose an experimental approach using scanning tunneling microscopy to observe these interactions directly.  By exploring the intricate relationships between these elements, we may uncover new ways to control the quantum behavior of materials at the atomic level.  This research has significant implications for the development of quantum computers and other silicon-based quantum devices. Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components often adhere to straightforward quantitative rules, yet their behavior is extremely difficult to predict solely through analytical calculations. This difficulty prompts the utilization of graph neural networks to model and solve these complex problems composed of interconnected parts. We present an innovative method for backward learning on static and dynamic graph networks that enables the extraction of detailed component information while facilitating the inclusion of external knowledge. This technique can be employed either standalone or in conjunction with forward learning methods. We successfully apply our reversal algorithm to three distinct domains: estimating unknown functional network inputs, identifying unknown graph elements, and extracting undisclosed details from linked databases. Notably, our framework is adaptable across multiple network types, including spatial, temporal, and multitask graphs. The publicly accessible code for our method can be found at https://github.com/zheng0625/reverse_graph_networks, along with supplementary materials at https://zheng0625.github.io/projects/reverse_graph_networks/. We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra. Moreover, our approach allows us for each recursive formula to determine the underlying generating set of the corresponding module over the integers, yielding a new infinite family of recursive conditions on integer partitions that are inherently meaningful in their own right. Focusing on a particular case, we obtain a distinctive family of graded recombinant operators, offering an intriguing connection to known examples while also suggesting the potential for further exploration and generalization. Moreover, our findings are showcased through computations presented in an accompanying database, making them readily accessible and open to verification.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. However, defining this region is challenging due to LITT's variable effects and the quality of post-treatment imaging, which can be improved by developing advanced deep learning models using a limited number of clinical LITT training data. This study compares the accuracy of defining the treated brain area after LITT by using a deep learning model called U-Net, which is trained on either clinical LITT data combined with simulated data or solely on clinical LITT data alone. The results of this study demonstrate that U-Net can accurately define the treated brain area after LITT when trained on a limited set of clinical LITT data, which can also be used to develop more precise treatment planning systems for this therapy. A precise metric known as the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) was utilized to assess the accuracy of defining the treated brain area after LITT, which showed a significant improvement of 14.6% (p = 0.03) when the model was trained on a limited set of clinical LITT data. Furthermore, the findings of this study suggest that developing computer-assisted tools for LITT treatment planning is feasible without using extensive amounts of clinical data. These results have the potential to contribute to the advancement of more precise, patient-specific treatment planning systems for this therapy. Strong nonlocality, a phenomenon where systems demonstrate nonlocality without entanglement, can be seen in multipartite states with certain correlations that cannot be created locally, yet those states have no entanglement when viewed from a different perspective. Unextendible product bases (UPBs) have been linked to strong nonlocality and have been particularly effective in demonstrating it in various scenarios. In this paper, we propose a method for determining whether a given UPB exhibits strong nonlocality by utilizing a subbase of the original UPB. We further demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of this approach using specific examples from existing UPBs found in high-dimensional systems. Notably, our analysis reveals that several strong nonlocality instances previously identified in certain states corresponding to X-states and W-states in high-dimensional spaces, can actually be explained by analyzing the correlations in their subbases rather than the full states themselves. Consequently, we are able to conclude that strong nonlocality without entanglement can arise at higher dimensional scales equivalent to the system's complexity level. Moreover, our findings challenge previous assumptions that strong nonlocality necessarily requires a level of simplicity, instead suggesting it can occur in complex systems and demands a more in-depth examination in its own right. Ultimately, our approach for determining strong nonlocality through subbases provides a more refined understanding of this phenomenon and its connection to UPBs. Furthermore, it highlights the value of UPBs as tools for identifying strong nonlocality in a more targeted manner, especially in the complex scenarios prevalent in high-dimensional systems. Lastly, our research paves the way for further exploration of strong nonlocality in such scenarios, especially when only partial control over the systems is available. This could have significant implications for the development of strong nonlocal correlations in a more controlled and targeted manner. In doing so, our study may contribute to the advancement of strong nonlocality in quantum systems, a resource that is expected to play a crucial role in various quantum information processing applications in the future. The speed at which massive spectroscopic surveys collect data directly depends on the number of wide-field instruments used. The rise of wide-field spectrographs is being driven by the need for faster data collection. To enhance the efficiency of these instruments, the use of robotically controlled field optimisation is being explored. This paper introduces the concept of assigning targets to astrobots that move in a coordinated manner, resulting in a 0/1 integer programming problem whose solution space is defined by the astrobots' motion constraints. By developing an appropriate metric to evaluate the performance of this coordination, different coordination approaches can be evaluated and compared to a strategy in which the astrobots operate independently. The results of applying this method to the MADEX spectrograph reveal that a coordinated approach can increase observing efficiency by up to 33% compared to random target selection and 13% compared to an independent strategy, depending on the number of available targets. Furthermore, a 10-unit astrobot fleet was able to achieve a 13% better performance than 13 individual astrobots and a 23% better performance than 26 individual astrobots in this scenario. The findings of this research have implications for the optimal design of future wide-field spectrographs and highlight the significance of considering the interplay between the instrument's optical design and its control system. The method presented in this paper is applicable to any instrument that consists of multiple co-moving subunits and can help optimize the spatial distribution of targets by taking into account the specific motion constraints of the instrument's components. The method is available for use at https://github.com/maflex/astrobot_target_assignment. The code has been optimized for the MADEX instrument and uses CPLEX for 0/1 integer programming problems. The method can be adapted for other instruments and different optimization solvers by modifying the relevant scripts. The results of this research have been published in the paper 'Optimizing Wide Field Spectrographs using Robotically Controlled Field Optimization', which is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.10951. Graph transformation rules are a versatile tool for developing program analysis and verification tools. However, the efficiency of these programs can be hindered when using rules that generate extensive subgraphs. To mitigate this issue, employing rooted rules that limit the extent of generated subgraphs is crucial. Yet, the presence of root edges can complicate the matching process. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel matching algorithm capable of efficiently handling rooted rules on large, distributed memory computers. Moreover, the algorithm is designed to accommodate various rule types, including those with nested roots and additional parameters. To demonstrate the efficacy of this algorithm, we develop an example program utilizing a substantial number of rooted rules and demonstrate its execution on a distributed memory computer using the ALF project. Additionally, we explore the implications of our work on the scalability of graph-based program analysis and verification tools. Furthermore, we examine the possibility of extending our algorithm to support concurrent matching on multiple processors. Finally, we outline potential applications and areas for further research in this area. Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by feature extraction techniques. Self-supervised learning methods learn valuable representation features by contrasting similar and dissimilar examples. This study introduces a novel contrastive learning approach, called Local Preserving Contrastive Learning (LPCON, LPCON in short), which utilizes local preserving properties to enhance the learning process. LPCON combines contrastive learning with traditional local preserving methods like Local Preserving Analysis (LPA) to develop a new dimensionality reduction technique. Experimental results show that LPCON outperforms standard contrastive learning and dimensionality reduction methods on various datasets and metrics. The model's performance is particularly notable in reducing the dimensionality of high-dimensional data, achieving superior accuracy and t-principle curves compared to other methods. Furthermore, LPCON exhibits computational efficiency with shorter training times and lower memory requirements. This is attributed to the model's ability to learn compact representation features through contrastive learning. LPCON is versatile and can be applied to various machine learning tasks, including classification, semi-supised learning, and clustering. The code for LPCON is openly available on Caffe2.ai.

We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs. This new infinite collection of examples is derived from a particular framework of twisted star graphs, where vertex connections are arranged in a star-shaped format, combined with the application of group operations that maintain the star shape. Furthermore, we introduce a method to evaluate the quantum complexity of these locally arc-transitive graphs using quantum walks, specifically by determining the quantum entanglement between walk particles and port states. This approach enables us to relate the quantum complexity to graph parameters, including its local transitivity and quasiprimativity properties. As a result, we are able to demonstrate the non-recoverability of the quantum complexity of these graphs from classical measurements, thereby implying these graphs are quantumly expensively designed. Consequently, this indication of quantumly complex construction may serve as a new means of verification for future candidate locally arc-transitive graphs. Lastly, this research introduces a novel context for the study of locally arc-transitive graphs within the broader framework of quantum mechanics. 

Keywords: locally arc-transitive graphs, quasiprimitive groups, quantum complexity, twisted star graphs, finite group theory.
