Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complicated as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making it difficult to identify parsimonious models. Despite its applications, the Generalized Linear Mixed Model (GLMM) is often too restrictive for researchers who need to analyze high-dimensional categorical data. To address this limitation, we developed the Generalized Linear Bayesian Mixed Model (GLBMM) to analyze categorical data under a sparse prior. Specifically, we utilized the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) and the Focused Maximum a Posteriori (fMAP) algorithm to select models and estimate their parameters. To facilitate the computation of these methods, we created an R package called catBIC, which leverages the capabilities of the brms package for Bayesian modeling and the bbmle package for generalized linear models. To enhance catBIC, we also established a set of metrics to evaluate its performance, including the probability of the best model and the probability of models within a certain log-likelihood difference. To assess catBIC, we created a set of simulated scenarios that mimic real-world data sets and included the Clozapine Affective Disorder (CAD) data set as a real-world example. Our results indicate that catBIC is effective in selecting the best model or models with a high degree of accuracy. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been thoroughly explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach generates knowledge graphs specifically tailored for language models that can learn from them through an iterative process of refinement. Unlike traditional methods that rely on descriptive sentences to update the model, our technique directly infuses structured knowledge, outperforming the baseline model that uses similar knowledge graphs but in sentence form. This approach demonstrates the feasibility of using knowledge graphs to feed knowledge into large language models, enabling them to learn from structured information. Moreover, our approach indicates that certain knowledge graphs can serve as a compact knowledge base for multiple language tasks. To facilitate further research, we have released 100 knowledge graphs for 14 OpenBookMM questions at https://github.com/zheng-chen/learning-from-knowledge-graphs. 

Furthermore, our experiments with T5-large and FLAN-1.5B reveal that learning from knowledge graphs results in improved performance on open-book-style few-shot learning for 14 OpenBookMM questions, across both in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations. In-domain evaluations demonstrate that learning from knowledge graphs leads to a significant 12.5% absolute improvement in accuracy, while in experiments with 32-way classification, an 8-way classification task, and 14 OpenBookMM questions, learning from knowledge graphs results in a 5% absolute improvement in accuracy.

This article explores spatially nonlocal diffusion models, where interactions are non-penalized beyond a finite distance and investigates their well-posedness in a fully nonlinear setting, coupled with a given time-dependent parameter. We establish the existence, uniqueness, and regularity of a solution using the theory of Orlicz spaces and an implicit function theorem. Moreover, we examine the dependence of the solution on the nonlocal interaction parameter and prove its continuity in a space of bounded linear operators. Additionally, we discuss the solvability of a related optimal control problem and provide an illustration involving numerical solutions obtained with the DGFEM method. The article concludes with an examination of the asymptotic behavior of the nonlocal diffusion equation and a discussion of open questions regarding the uniqueness of solutions and the optimal control problem.

When capturing panoramic scenes or environments using a single camera, due to the limited field of view, multiple images are often necessary to reconstruct the surroundings comprehensively. This process, known as panoramic image stitching, can be both simple and complex, depending on the approach taken. While basic applications like portrait-oriented photo compilation have minimal geometric intricacies, capturing wide-angle panoramic scenes with significant vertical and horizontal dimensions involve more complex geometry. This complexity arises from the necessity for the camera to be tilted to capture the entire scene, resulting in potential misalignment issues during post-processing. These alignment challenges can introduce significant errors in the reconstruction process, especially when the camera is tilted far from the horizontal axis. This paper delves into the consequences of camera alignment along the vertical axis on the reconstruction process and presents a novel approach to improve stitching accuracy in such scenarios. Through experimental evaluation of multiple wide-angle panoramic scene reconstructions, our approach demonstrated a notable enhancement in accuracy, averaging a 35% reduction in re-projection error when compared to traditional methods. This enhanced performance was further validated by the superior quality of 3D models generated using our approach, as assessed by both automated metrics and human evaluators, outperforming models created with conventional methods in as much as 94%. This improvement in accuracy translates to a more realistic 3D representation of the captured environment, as evident from both quantitative analysis and qualitative visualizations. Furthermore, our approach exhibits scalability, extending beyond the tested 6 to 8 image scenarios. This method is now openly accessible as part of the CMF library on GitHub. This work is particularly relevant to applications such as wide-angle scene monitoring, where accurate 3D reconstructions are crucial, and the approach could be particularly beneficial for further research into mesh-based reconstruction methods. This study presents a novel biophysical model of a midbrain culture, tailored to mimic the key neuronal features of Parkinson's disease pathology. The model incorporates the essential components of a rat substantia nigra pars compacta, incorporating dopaminergic neurons that project to the striatum, and is re-created using rat primary neuronal cultures and a micro-electrode array dish. The model's neural network is observed to exhibit natural degeneration over time, resembling the progression of Parkinson's disease. To study this process, a data-driven approach was employed, building a dynamic model of the network's behavior using a system identification method. The resulting model highlighted the interplay of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs on the survival of dopaminergic neurons, revealing a critical threshold where increased inhibitory input accelerates their death. This finding is consistent with previous clinical and animal studies, suggesting that overactive inhibition may contribute to the degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in Parkinson's disease. The model also predicted that the application of a specific type of electrical stimulation, characterized by low amplitude and slow pulse, could delay the death of these neurons. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific weather types such as rain, snow, and fog.
In this research, a novel approach is presented that utilizes deep learning to identify and classify seven distinct weather conditions: rain, snow, fog, night, day, hail, and freezefog.
A newly created 14-class dataset called RFS, comprising 1000 high-quality images of the seven weather conditions and three corresponding scene types (urban, highway, mountain), has been developed to support this research.
This dataset showcases diverse weather conditions, incorporates scene-specific variations, and is more comprehensive than existing datasets in this field.
A comprehensive evaluation of multiple deep learning architectures, including the impact of scene and weather factors, is also presented, utilizing the newly created dataset.
The results show that a convolutional neural network (CNN) achieves the highest accuracy of 85.16% on the RFS dataset, outperforming alternative approaches that combine CNN and recurrent neural network (RNN) architectures.
Furthermore, an investigation into the effectiveness of adding scene and weather classes to the training dataset revealed that these factors have a significant impact on the accuracy of the model, particularly in cases of limited training data.
Finally, a practical application of this research is presented, where a robust weather detection system is developed and integrated into a self-driving car simulation using the Unity game engine. Experimental results from this evaluation show that the accuracy of this system is directly correlated with the frame rate of the system, indicating potential for real-time performance with further optimization techniques. This research provides a comprehensive foundation for the development of a robust weather detection system that can be utilized in a variety of applications, including autonomous navigation. The newly created RFS dataset is made publicly available to facilitate advancements in this field. It is essential to note that the dataset is not confined to rain, snow, and fog but rather encompasses a broader spectrum of weather conditions, making it a more comprehensive and versatile dataset for this research area. To enhance modeling of long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously introduced by splitting long input sequences into shorter segments and processing them with separate, compact RNNs. System components can then be combined to obtain context-enriched encoder representations. Building on this idea, a Dual-path RNN with Multi-segment Splitting (DMPS) was proposed to further improve modeling of sequences with varying segment lengths by dividing them into equal parts and using multiple sets of splitting strategies. To optimize DMPS, a gradient-based search method was introduced to find optimal encoder combinations. Experimental results show that DMPS achieves better source separation performance compared to the original dual-path RNN model, and it is robust to different batch sizes during training. Moreover, DMPS provides a flexible framework for handling sequences of different lengths, and it can effectively model sequences with similar characteristics in both the time and frequency domains. The method's effectiveness is supported by t-SNE visualizations and spectrogram analyses. Furthermore, DMPS was found to be relatively computation-efficient compared to other sequence splitting methods. The proposed framework can be applied to other sequence-based source separation techniques, such as those employing bidirectional RNNs, and it has the potential to be integrated with external information, such as articulatory features. Experimental evaluations on the LRE18 dataset demonstrate DMPS's superiority over baseline methods, and it achieves a source score of 0.437. The DMPS implementation is available online. Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for the numerical solution of the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The aim of this study is to investigate various numerical solution strategies for the momentum and mass exchange terms present within the multi-fluid equations. A specific, simplified single-column single-fluid model serves as a reference point for the comparison of the different methods. The evaluation criteria include the accuracy of the solution, the frequency of the model, and the model's robustness in the presence of increasing wind shear. The research was conducted using a traditional 1D single-column atmospheric model and comprising 16 different numerical schemes. The results of a 10-day periodic run with weak wind shear revealed that the semi-implicit method yielded the most accurate solution, the largest time step that could be used without divergence, and the least frequent error after divergence. Notably, this method performed significantly better than the traditional quasi-implicit method used in mass-flux schemes. Nonetheless, the research also showed that the choice of method is highly dependent on the model parameters, and no single method emerged as the clear favourite in all scenarios, especially in cases with stronger wind shear. Notably, several of the tested schemes were capable of reproducing the correct frequency with only moderate wind shear, only to fail spectacularly as soon as wind shear increased beyond a certain threshold. The failure of the models under strong wind shear conditions was found to be linked to the magnitude of the momentum flux divergence, and not the wind shear itself. The research highlights the importance of robust numerical schemes that are capable of handling a wide range of atmospheric convection scenarios, and that are not solely based on idealised conditions. We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if it lacks classical connections with any other system. We derive a genuine multipartite entanglement criterion that is applicable to a wider class of Jaynes-Cummings systems, including those with different laser frequencies. Notably, this criterion is achievable even in situations where the system's cavity shares non-classical correlations with another cavity, allowing for the genuine multipartite entanglement of the system with other parties. We illustrate this capability with an example involving two different laser frequencies. Furthermore, we establish that our criterion is sufficient to guarantee the genuine multipartite entanglement of at least one of the system's states, allowing for its unconditional creation through continuous resonant laser pulses. This finding provides a new means of generating genuine multipartite entanglement in the Jaynes-Cummings model. Additionally, we examine the impact of cavity loss on the system's state, revealing that it can still exhibit genuine multipartite entanglement for a limited duration, even in the presence of significant loss. Notably, this duration can be extended through the application of classical fields that counteract the effects of loss. Lastly, our analysis is expanded to include multiple unconnected systems, with a genuine multipartite entanglement criterion derived for a specific scenario involving two separate systems. This is accompanied by numerical simulations demonstrating the ability to generate genuine multipartite entanglement in a wider context. The associated code is made available online. The study's findings are relevant to the experimental generation of genuine multipartite entanglement in cavity-circuit systems. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking the trajectory of particles resulting from high-energy collisions. A vital component of the CMS tracking system is the silicon pixel detector, responsible for pinpointing the position of incoming particles with great accuracy. However, the detector is exposed to harsh radiation conditions due to its proximity to the interaction point, causing lattice damage to its underlying material and significantly impairing the detector's ability to collect reliable data in the long run. As the LHC is set to undergo a series of upgrades in the coming years, including an increase in collision energy and frequency, the silicon pixel detector will be subjected to even more intense levels of radiation, rendering it essential to replace the detector by 2024 to ensure continued effectiveness in data collection. The replacement silicon pixel detector, designed to withstand increased radiation levels for an extended period, features an upgraded readout electronics system known as the readout driver (ROD). The ROD, comprising an integrated circuit known as the digitized pixel front-end (DPFX), will be responsible for converting raw signals from the detector into digital data, performing in-depth signal processing to refine the data, and transmitting the results to other components of the CMS data processing system as part of a custom data link. The DPFX, produced using an advanced 65nm CMOS process, will be the primary focus of this research, detailing the development of the integrated circuit, including its design, functionality, and performance in accordance with its intended purpose. The DPFX design consists of 128 individual channels, each equipped with a unique signal processing algorithm tailored to the characteristics of the associated silicon pixel detector module. The integrated circuit boasts an impressive 5.12-bit effective resolution, achieved through a combination of analog gain, digital refinement, and data transmission techniques. Furthermore, the DPFX features an innovative data compression method, utilizing a variable-length encoding scheme to minimize data volume while maintaining acceptable levels of error, resulting in a compressed data size of approximately 0.5 bytes per channel. The integrated circuit has undergone extensive simulation and testing, yielding positive results in line with its design specifications. The successful development of the DPFX marks a significant milestone in the replacement silicon pixel detector project, paving the way for the creation of a cutting-edge detector capable of withstanding increased radiation levels for an extended period. The DPFX will play a pivotal role in the future of the CMS tracking system, enabling continued precision data collection in the LHC experiments

Farmers rely on crop protection methods like pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing averages from inconsistent field data. 360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences, particularly useful in promoting virtual tourism. However, providing real-time 360-degree video streaming poses significant technical challenges related to data volume, quality degradation, and the need for users to manually navigate videos. In response to these issues, researchers have explored non-blind optimization approaches to improve the quality of real-time 360-degree video streaming. These methods involve training predictive models that anticipate user viewing patterns and prioritize video segments likely to be watched. Although they utilize machine learning to enhance streaming efficiency, they require large datasets and are limited by data quality in actual 360-degree video streaming applications. In contrast, our study proposes a novel blind optimization framework that combines explicit user feedback with implicit cues from streaming data itself to develop a predictive model. This framework enables real-time 360-degree video streaming optimization without relying on complex machine learning models, instead using user feedback to guide the search for optimal streaming sequences. Our results show that this approach leads to significant quality improvements over traditional non-blind optimization methods and is particularly effective in scenarios with limited user feedback. Moreover, our study includes an analysis of user feedback's impact on performance and efficiency, demonstrating that even a single bit of explicit user feedback can result in substantial quality gains. Our findings also highlight the importance of considering the cost of user feedback when designing real-time 360-degree video streaming systems. In scenarios with limited user feedback, our proposed blind framework is shown to be an effective solution, outperforming non-blind optimization methods that require large datasets. Our study's results are applicable to various video streaming applications, including those with limited user feedback, and our code is available for public use. Further research into this topic is seen as valuable for the broader video streaming community.

This type of tensor network, which we call the thermally correlated tensor network, allows for efficient simulation of open quantum systems that are coupled to high entropy environments, described by thermal states. This type of tensor network has significant potential for further research applications in the field of open quantum systems.

Knowledge distillation is a well-known technique that enables the transfer of knowledge from high-performance, resource-intensive deep neural networks to more efficient and compact models. Unlike previous methods that focus on preserving the primary student model's learning ability, our approach simultaneously trains multiple student models with varying parameters, all of which learn the knowledge transferred from a single instructor model. Notably, each of these student models has a specific optimization objective tailored to a particular target dataset, assessment metric, or system constraint. Throughout training, the knowledge transferred from the instructor model is consistent, whereas the student models can learn this shared knowledge through either the standard cross-entropy loss or alternative non-parametric methods such as temperature scaling and matching losses. As a result, our framework reduces memory usage during training and eliminates the need for fine-tuning post-training. Experimental results on multiple datasets and models demonstrate the effectiveness of our multi-student knowledge distillation approach, which outperforms traditional knowledge distillation methods in multiple scenarios. Furthermore, our method's efficiency in reduced parameter count is verified. The code for our multi-student knowledge distillation approach is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengdianchen/Multi-Student-Knowledge-Distillation.

A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a strong geodetic subset with at most~$k$ vertices. This problem was proven NP-complete in 2011, and we now investigate the existence of an NP-certification for SG via the construction of a certificate graph that verifies the correctness of a strong geodetic subset of a graph. The complexity of this certificate construction process is analyzed in terms of the number of vertices~$n$ in the graph. The certificate construction process for SG is demonstrated to require $\Theta(1.644^n)$ computational steps, which represents the worst-case scenario. The applicability of this result is broadened by the identification of a more efficient certificate construction process for a related problem, referred to as the Weak Geodetic problem (WG), which involves $\Theta(1.618^n)$ computational steps. The analysis of the certificate construction process for SG is further expanded to include various graph configurations, such as planar graphs, cubic graphs, and geodetic graphs, as well as the Strong Geodetic degree and Weak Geodetic degree, which are defined as the minimum number of vertices required to strongly geodetically cover all vertices in a graph and its subgraph, respectively. The complexity of the certificate construction process is found to be $\Theta(n)$ in cubic graphs and geodetic graphs, $\Theta(2^n)$ in planar graphs, and $\Theta(1.644^n)$ in general graphs. The analysis of the Strong Geodetic degree and Weak Geodetic degree in terms of the number of vertices~$n$ in a graph reveals the existence of an exponential relationship, which is supported by numerical computations. The investigation of the certificate construction process for SG is further expanded to include various graph families, such as line graphs, power graphs, and Berge graphs, as well as the impact of adding edges to a graph on the Strong Geodetic degree and Weak Geodetic degree. The analysis of the complexity of the certificate construction process for SG is demonstrated to be NP-complete in all the considered graph families, except for line graphs and power graphs, which exhibit a polynomial-time complexity. Imitation learning enables robots to efficiently learn complex tasks by following expert examples. However, relying on perfectly optimized demonstrations can limit the method's potential, as it does not account for the common scenario where subpar initial conditions are met with subpar performance. In many cases, simply using any trajectory, whether good or bad, can be more beneficial than waiting for optimal results. In this research, we build upon the suboptimal imitation learning framework to further expand its capabilities to learn from examples that aren't tailored to specific tasks. This includes using start states that aren't specific to a single task. Our approach involves developing a new loss function that combines cross-entropy losses for multiple tasks. By doing so, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through various experiments, showing it outperforms existing suboptimal imitation learning methods even when applying it to single-task scenarios. Our findings also highlight the benefits of using expert demonstrations that aren't tailored to specific start states or actions, resulting in more generalizable policies. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChenZhF/Generalized-SIL.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this limitation. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both valuable and misleading, our method employs value function expectations to filter out less helpful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, learning from the beneficial knowledge and rejecting the useless knowledge. Through extensive experiments on various games, our findings demonstrate that Co-Imitation Learning outperforms both single-agent imitation learning and cooperative reinforcement learning in a non-imitative setting. Moreover, our analysis reveals that cooperative imitation learning accelerates value function learning and enhances policy optimization. Additionally, we observe that cooperative imitation learning reduces the variance of the value function, thereby enhancing its learning efficiency. The source code for this research is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/Co-Imitation-Learning.

Polarization-adjusted convolutional (PAC) codes possess enhanced error-correction capabilities than conventional convolutional codes, thanks to the added reliability information from an extra convolutional code with complementary polarization properties. By combining the output from a polar code, these codes are capable of tolerating higher convolutional memory sizes without a significant penalty in error-correction performance. Utilizing an optimal metric function for PAC codes, specifically one that considers the likelihood of incorrect symbol detection, facilitates further improvements in their error-correction capabilities, ultimately enabling higher convolutional memory sizes with only a minor deterioration in performance. As a result, the tight bounding gap for the maximum acceptable convolutional memory size $M$ is reduced from $2^{r/2}$ for $r$ bit PAC codes to $12(r-6)/r$ bits for all positive real values of $r$. Consequently, tight bounding gaps are achieved for four distinct PAC code sizes: $4, 6, 7$, and $8$ bits. Furthermore, numerical simulations validate the theoretical findings, confirming that using the optimal metric function results in significant improvements in error-correction performance when the convolutional memory size is high. Moreover, Monte Carlo decoding trials demonstrate the efficacy of the optimal metric function in improving PAC code error-correction performance, particularly for larger memory sizes. In particular, for a specific convolutional memory size of $5$, the error-correction performance of PAC codes is comparable to that of low-density parity-check codes following a uniform distribution, following several decades of decay in the curve. In contrast, conventional convolutional codes exhibit significantly poorer error-correction performance for the same memory size. Consequently, the increased robustness of PAC codes, resulting from incorporating reliability information from a complementary polar code, can effectively compensate for large convolutional memory sizes, thereby providing a compelling rationale for further investigation of these codes in real-world applications. In such scenarios, detailed implementation guidelines are provided to facilitate practical adoption of PAC codes. Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from its substantial computational requirements during multiple iterations of model updates. This paper investigates the premise that the RL algorithm's performance is disproportionately enhanced by a reduced vocabulary when it is explicitly defined, thereby potentially reducing necessary sampling operations and concurrently improving translation precision. Our experimental findings on four evaluation metrics indeed indicate that NMT precision is elevated with a smaller vocabulary and, more importantly, confirm that the RL algorithm's efficiency is indeed optimized when the vocabulary is limited. Building upon these definitions, various properties and characteristics of QFS-spaces are investigated. Key findings include: Firstly, any QFS-space is inherently a quasicontinuous space; secondly, closed subspaces, as well as quasicontinuous reals in QFS-spaces, possess the QFS property; thirdly, the composition of quasi-finitely separating maps is itself quasi-finitely separating; and finally, preadhesive diagrams over QFS-spaces result in QFS-spaces. Moreover, the paper delves into the comparison between QFS-spaces and other types of nonexpansive metric spaces characterized by continuous maps. Specifically, it is proven that closed subspaces of finite-dimensional vector spaces with quasi-isometries correspond to QFS-spaces, and further that there is a one-to-one correspondence between topologically distinct classes of finite-dimensional vector spaces with quasi-isometries and those of QFS-spaces. Lastly, the paper introduces an example of a nonquasicontinuous QFS-space to illustrate the disparity between quasicontinuous and quasi-finitely separating maps. Ultimately, the study of QFS-spaces provides a framework for investigating preadhesive diagrams and quasiapproximate identities within the context of quasicontinuous maps. This framework is then applied to a specific problem involving the convergence of sequences in compact metric spaces. Consequently, the developed techniques give rise to the notion of convergence along quasi-finitely separating maps, a concept that can be viewed as an extension of the classical definition of convergence in metric spaces. Furthermore, it is shown that these redefined sequences and real numbers exhibit the same characteristics as their classical counterparts, and that this redefinition is both unique and universally accepted within the context of QFS-spaces. Between December 2019 and December 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique and comprehensive spectroscopic survey in the Galactic anti-centre region. This data set, which comprises approximately 1.3 million spectra with low to medium resolution, was acquired during 14 nights of observations under the protocol 2020A-040. We analyzed the characteristics of the data, focusing on various aspects such as resolution, signal-to-noise ratio, and radial velocity accuracy. It was found that the majority of the low-resolution spectra have a signal-to-noise ratio greater than 10, while the medium-resolution spectra have a higher signal-to-noise ratio, averaging around 23.4. Furthermore, the radial velocity accuracy was found to be relatively consistent across different resolution levels, ranging from 5.46 to 5.59 km/s. A comparison with previous LAMOST observations revealed a noticeable improvement in data quality, particularly in terms of signal-to-noise ratio. We also compared our data to that from other spectroscopic surveys, including the K2-GAP sample and the APOGEE survey, and found that while the LAMOST data have relatively lower signal-to-noise ratios, they excel in terms of spatial coverage and volume. These data sets offer significant opportunities for studying the movement and distribution of the Milky Way's stars. However, it is essential to exercise caution when utilizing these data due to potential inaccuracies in radial velocity estimates resulting from the survey's protocols. Consequently, these data are best suited for large-scale studies rather than the analysis of individual stars. We have released the data in question, along with associated quality assessments, in the LAMOST Archive. Additionally, we have made available various relevant parameters, including radial velocity templates, in the Vizier database. This comprehensive spectroscopic survey in the Galactic anti-centre region is an important addition to the LAMOST data sets, including those covering the North Galactic Cap and the regions surrounding the Galactic centre and anti-centre, as well as the extensive spectroscopic survey conducted during the prototype stage of the telescope. This study is an integral component of the research being conducted in preparation for the MaTSC, a forthcoming spectroscopic survey that will employ the MaX-CCD spectrograph. This new instrument, featuring 392 science fibres and 3 differential fibre bundles for the measurement of atmospheric properties, will provide radial velocity accuracy as precise as 1.3 km/s and signal-to-noise ratios greater than 30 in medium-resolution spectra. In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Recent breakthroughs in edge learning have demonstrated notable progress, whereas edges are often studied in isolation. Conversely, combined analysis of edges and textures can yield more comprehensive insights, particularly in medical imaging, where texture-based pathology diagnosis holds significant value. Notably, existing methods struggle to effectively manage the interdependence of edges and textures. To address this limitation, we propose an Edge-Texture Coarse-fining Network (ETCN) that systematically refines edges and textures in an iterative, bidirectional process. Initially, an Edge-Texture Coarse-fining Module (ETCM) extracts edges and textures from raw images, producing an initial estimation. These estimates are then fed into a subsequent module, where they are refined in an iterative manner. The output of each iteration is combined with the previous result to produce an updated estimate. This process is repeated multiple times before yielding our final edge and texture maps. To validate our approach, we created a new dataset, namely the Edge-Texture Dataset (ETD), comprising 4000 images from three categories (liver, lung, and breast tissues). Compared to existing methods, our ETNC model achieved superior performance on this dataset, as measured by edge accuracy and texture similarity indices. Moreover, our results on two public medical imaging datasets showed that our approach outperformed state-of-the-art edge learning models in texture prediction tasks. Notably, our method demonstrated a notable 10% gain in edge accuracy and 15% gain in texture similarity when evaluated using the CIEDE2000 color difference formula. Overall, our research indicates that combined analysis of edges and textures leads to a more comprehensive understanding of medical imaging, paving the way for improved texture-based diagnosis. The code and dataset associated with this work are available online at https://github.com/zhengzhengsun/ETCN.

Preliminary findings from the Parker Solar Probe (PSP) regarding solar wind energy flux have been analyzed, specifically at a distance of 1 solar radius from the sun. The data collected from PSP during 19 close approaches in its 4-year orbit were examined by normalizing the energy flux to 1 solar radius of intensity (1 R solar units) and then classifying it into four categories. The designations range from "low" (below 10 times the average value) to "extremely high" (above 100 times the average value) based on the distribution of data. The designations were applied to 145 individual solar wind streams that reached PSP and included 103 observations of fast solar wind, 15 of slow solar wind, and the remaining 27 were undetermined due to a lack of coronal mass ejection information. The results show a significant percentage of solar wind streams that interact with PSP are either "high" (above 50 times the average value) or "extremely high" (above 100 times the average value) energy flux levels when they reach the spacecraft. The data also indicate that energy flux tends to peak at around 1.06 solar radii in the transition region between the solar wind and the coronal mass ejection. The data further indicate that the solar wind energy flux has a tendency to peak earlier than 1 AU and that the peak often occurs inside 1.1 solar radii. The data also show a tendency for solar wind streams with high energy flux levels to have lower densities and similar or higher speeds when they reach 1 AU. The data also indicate that solar wind streams with high energy flux levels at 1 AU tend to have sources with high energy flux levels inside 1 solar radius. Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. However, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition (SER) often falls short in real-world situations due to limited cross-domain models. To bridge this gap, we developed a novel technique called self-emotional distillation (SED) that uses self-supervised learning to extract ser-specific features from data. By combining ser and data-aware attention mechanisms in a multi-head attention network, sed-enabled cross-domain ser models outperformed their baseline competitors in real-world live data settings by achieving a 12.5% absolute improvement in mean class accuracy (MCA). Furthermore, our research demonstrated that sed can effectively enhance the performance of ser models in a data-efficient manner with just 1000 labeled samples. To facilitate further research, we released the ser dataset containing 1000 hours of recordings from 2000 individuals, collected over a period of 18 months, along with the sed code and protocols on GitHub. With sed, we believe we have made significant progress in addressing the ser domain adaptation challenge. To build upon our work, we invite the research community to join us in exploring the sed framework and contributing their findings. The sed project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengzhengchen-ucas/self-emotional-distribution. We present an investigation into the structural, magnetic, and electrical properties of the layered perovskite-related compound Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a material that shares similarities with the high-temperature superconductor Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_8$. BFTO exhibits an intricate structure consisting of bi- and tri-layers of the ABO$_3$ type, arranged in an alternating pattern. When subjected to increasing pressure, the crystal structure of BFTO undergoes a transformation from a non-magnetic monoclinic symmetry to a magnetic orthorhombic symmetry below 1.2 GPa at 1.5 K, accompanied by the onset of a spontaneous magnetic moment. Moreover, our findings indicate that the electrical resistance of BFTO displays non-activated behavior at low temperatures, with the onset of a steep increase in resistance occurring at a temperature that is pressure-dependent, ranging from 0.5 K under 4.5 GPa to 1.1 K under 6.5 GPa. These results suggest that BFTO may be considered a precursor material to the high-temperature superconductors, given its unique layered structure and the similarity of its physical properties to those of the cuprates. However, further research is required to fully explore the potential of BFTO as a high-temperature superconductor. Moreover, our study indicates that the magnetic ordering in BFTO can be controlled through application of pressure, a feature that may be useful for the development of magnetic pressure sensors. Additionally, the findings of our work suggest that BFTO can be an effective material for the study of correlated electron systems under extreme conditions of pressure and temperature. Finally, our research highlights the potential of BFTO as a model system for understanding the complex interplay between structure, magnetism, charge, and superconductivity in the high-temperature superconductors, particularly in the context of the cuprate phase diagram. Consequently, further investigation of BFTO is considered essential to gain a deeper insight into the underlying mechanisms governing the behavior of the high-temperature superconductors. Hybrid methods are commonly employed in graph-based flight planning applications to reduce computational expenses, but they can be challenging to optimize for dense graphs typical of aerial environments. A new approach is proposed for solving continuous shortest path problems within 2D environments by treating the graph as an undirected network with unknown edge weights. A parameterized algorithm estimates the average edge weight based on the graph's density, enabling rapid computation of optimal paths. The algorithm's performance is evaluated against established methods BSPTree and RAPTOR for various graph densities, revealing that its efficiency improves as density increases. Notably, the proposed method outperformed BSPTree and RAPTOR in a representative aerial scenario, highlighting the value of adapting algorithms according to the graph's density. Furthermore, the algorithm's ability to estimate average edge weights provides valuable insights into the graph's structure. As such, the algorithm can be a useful tool for analyzing environment representations used in flight planning applications. However, further research is needed to apply this approach to multi-dimensional environments. The algorithm has been made available online for further study and potential applications in flight planning. 

Keywords: Flight planning, graph algorithms, continuous shortest path problems, hybrid methods.

The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified. These tidal features were identified through a statistical method and were found to be distinct from artifacts. Our findings reveal that a significant proportion, approximately 61%, of these galaxies have notable tidal features with flux percentages exceeding 1%. Furthermore, we discovered that the tidal features are not merely a product of interactions with smaller companions, but rather often stem from collisions with galaxies of similar mass. We also observed that tidal features are common in galaxies with massive counterparts, but are less prevalent in galaxies with less massive counterparts. Additionally, we found that galaxies with notable tidal features tend to have slower rotation rates. We developed two models to simulate the tidal features observed in these galaxies. We utilized these models to gain insights into tidal features and to estimate the mass of these features, which we found to be roughly 5 times more massive than the visible portion of the galaxy. We have developed new techniques to achieve isometric dimension reduction for a variety of functions within the space L_p, meeting specific norm constraints. Given a set of N functions defined across a d-dimensional space and situated within the L_p unit ball, we can successfully limit their representation to a space of (Nd)^{1/2} dimensions while maintaining an almost identical maximum norm. This maximum norm is then bounded by a logarithmic factor in relation to the original maximum norm of the functions. The resulting low-dimensional representation also retains a significant fraction of the original norm across a large subset of the space's unit sphere. Furthermore, our method allows for a degree of flexibility in the choice of dimension reduction method. It is particularly effective for reducing dimensions for functions that are highly correlated with one another. We have demonstrated that a strategy based on random projections can provide comparable results, achieving a maximum norm of a constant factor in relation to the original maximum norm with a sufficiently large number of projections. However, this method has a major limitation in that it is not scalable to large datasets due to its computational requirements. We have also established an upper limit for the achievable maximum norm when using a strategy based on the Restricted Isometric Property (RIP). We have found that the feasibility of isometric dimension reduction is heavily dependent on the specific structure of the dataset. We have explored various strategies for selecting a subset of the most representative functions from the original set, ultimately developing an approach that prioritizes a subset of approximately n^2 functions based on their average norm. We have demonstrated that this approach leads to an improved bound on the maximum norm of the remaining functions. We have also established the applicability of our techniques to a broader range of function spaces, including those defined over compact domains within R^d and the space of continuous functions over [0,1]^d. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, utilizing the detector's natural segmentation. The implementation of this technique led to significant advancements in beam control and feedback systems' performance. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in cosmological research, however the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and carefully controlled experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with high sensitivity and accuracy. To effectively manage the vast amounts of data generated by these experiments in depth, specialized software frameworks have been developed to provide researchers with tools to manage data processing pipelines, detect issues, and make informed decisions. One such framework, known as pipelinet, leverages Python's vast scientific computing libraries to enable researchers to build and execute robust data processing pipelines using probabilistic models to account for uncertainties, even in the absence of expert knowledge in machine learning. In this paper, pipelinet is enhanced to facilitate collaborative research and include features such as reproducibility, issue detection using Bayesian methods, and data visualization using plotnet, a separate tool also introduced here. By utilizing pipelinet in depth, particularly in its application to analyze CMB anisotropies using the HEALPIX pixelization method, this paper demonstrates pipelinet's capabilities to handle large datasets efficiently and provide actionable insights to researchers, ultimately making it an ideal framework for collaborative research and analysis in depth in cosmology and other fields. In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models or the characteristics of word order knowledge they embody. To investigate this, we utilize the BART model to conduct a comprehensive study of word order knowledge. Specifically, we use features from structural knowledge, contextual knowledge, and language knowledge extracted from the BART model via structural saliency and perform a thorough analysis to determine their respective contributions to word order accuracy. Our findings reveal that contextual knowledge plays the most significant role in achieving high scores of word order accuracy. Contextual knowledge is further broken down into its underlying components, including part-of-speech information, semantic dependencies, and sentence syntax, to provide a more in-depth understanding of its mechanisms. Our research provides valuable insights into the characteristics of word order knowledge present in the language network and facilitates the development of more effective methods for learning from pre-trained language models. To facilitate further research, we release the features used in this study, allowing for the comparison of word order knowledge in various models and evaluation protocols. Moreover, our results can be utilized as a benchmark for assessing the capabilities of future models in this domain. Additionally, we introduce a new evaluation metric called structural fidelity that gauges the similarity between the original sentence order and the order produced by machine learning models. With this evaluation metric, we conduct a comprehensive comparison of various models, including linear models, neural networks, and the BART model, to determine their structural fidelity. Our research provides a thorough examination of the capabilities of machine learning models in this domain and raises several key questions for further investigation. For instance, what characterizes word order knowledge present in the network? How do neural models learn this knowledge? To enhance performance, this study proposes an innovative approach, PBDNet, which leverages a dual-path detection network to combine spatial and frequency information. The proposed framework incorporates two distinct detection modules, one processing spectral features derived from the CNN and the other processing spatial features from the CNN. These modules are designed with attention mechanisms and ReLU activation functions to prioritize critical information and promote non-linear decision-making. The fusion of the outputs from both modules is achieved through a dual Decision Fusion Layer. Experimental evaluations using the FACET dataset and additional testing on the Celeb-DF dataset demonstrate the superiority of PBDNet over existing detection methods, with a notable improvement in accuracy of up to 11.5%. The enhanced performance of PBDNet is further validated through rigorous testing on the Celeb-DF dataset, showcasing an accuracy increase of 4.5% without employing data augmentation techniques. A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our research proposes a novel approach utilizing weak coherent states (WCS) and the entanglement-swapping protocol to create a quantum network with high security. By analyzing the impact of imperfect devices on the entire network, we develop an entanglement-based gain per base unit variance formula that effectively predicts the secure transmission distance of quantum hacking resistance. Furthermore, our simulation utilizing weak coherent states demonstrates that the entanglement-based formula accurately estimates the secure transmission variance, enabling the calculation of genuine secure key rates via applying the Holeva-Mayers protocol. Notably, our findings indicate that the entanglement-swapping protocol can achieve genuine secure key rates over five times the distance achievable with conventional weak coherent state WCS-QKD. Consequently, our proposed system offers substantial improvements in achieving high-security levels in extended quantum networks.

Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$. For every positive integer $m$ less than or equal to $n$, denote by $\Lambda_{K,m}$ the set of complex numbers derived from the roots of $x^m - \alpha = 0$, with $\alpha$ being an algebraic integer belonging to the ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$. The set $\Lambda_{K,m}$ is seen as a subset of the lattice generated by $e_1, \ldots, e_{n+m-1}$, where $e_i$ represents the sum of the $i^{th}$ roots of a $d^{th}$ degree polynomial, with $d$ being a divisor of $m$. In this context, our primary objective is to establish an upper bound for the volume of $\Lambda_{K,m}$, denoted as $M_{K,m}$, in a region of the complex plane defined by $[-\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}r, \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}r]$. This upper bound is expressed in terms of the logarithm of the number of orders in $K$ with a specific property, specifically relating to the number of factors they possess. Furthermore, we derive an explicit estimate for a specific volume, namely $\frac{8}{3}\cdot 24^{2}\cdot 3\log{3}$. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between successive minima in orders of number fields and Galois extensions of local fields, establishing upper and lower bounds for ratios of minima in terms of the norm of the Galois group. These bounds are shown to have a significant implication on the behavior of ratios of minima in superpolynomially increasing towers of number fields. Lastly, we explore the connection between the volume of sets derived from roots of polynomials and the distribution of values taken by polynomials over finite fields. This analysis enables us to formulate conjectures related to the behavior of ratios of minima in sets derived from roots of polynomials over finite fields. Consequently, our research provides new insights into various problems concerning minima in number fields and algebraic integers. These results not only shed light on questions posed by several mathematicians but also raise further questions for exploration.

We examine the methods used to model the interaction between light and matter in tight-binding models, which are commonly applied in photonic crystals and photonic integrated circuits. Despite the widespread use of the velocity gauge, we find it more convenient to work with the dipole gauge, which offers a simpler and more direct approach to calculating dipole moments. This choice allows us to derive a novel, straightforward expression for the dipole moment in tight-binding models, which is consistent with the physics of the laser-matter interaction. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive set of dipole moment operators for various atomic and solid-state systems to facilitate numerical simulations of light-matter interaction in tight-binding models. These results are particularly relevant to the study of optical spin Hall effects in solid-state systems. Additionally, we outline the procedure for incorporating the effects of laser photons on tight-binding models, which is essential for accurately modeling systems that involve strong light-matter interaction, such as vacuum Rabi oscillations in cavity quantum electrodynamics. This approach can be applied to a wide range of systems, from atomic gases to solid-state systems and superconducting circuits. By using these results, researchers can perform more accurate numerical simulations of light-matter interaction in tight-binding models, which is crucial for the interpretation of experimental data and the design of future light-matter interaction research. This work is intended to contribute to the advancement of light-matter interaction research by improving the theoretical modeling of these systems. Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks including anomaly detection and process-forecasting. Deep-learning
models are particularly valued for their ability to handle complex, unstructured
data and learn from raw input signals. In this study, a novel approach called
Deep-Signal Learning is introduced to automatize the extraction of meaningful
features from process signals represented as sequences of case IDs, event timestamps,
and attribute values. This is achieved by employing Multi-Layer Neural Networks
that operate directly on signals, eliminating the need for intermediate data
representations such as graphs or neighborhoods. The proposed method is applied
to an industrial supply chain dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness in building
predictive models that rival traditional approaches requiring manual feature
engineering. Furthermore, an intuitive visualization technique called Deep-Path
Learning is also presented to provide insight into the internal workings of DSL.
The introduced framework is available as an open-source R package called RRL. It
facilitates the automation of process signal analysis, making it an ideal solution
for practitioners working with complex, dynamic data processes. It is particularly
beneficial for companies lacking in-house expertise in process analysis by
machine learning methods, such as Deep-Signal Learning. These companies can
efficiently leverage this technology through an industrial cloud service called
DeepMinder. It is designed to monitor processes and detect anomalies in real-time
in return for a paid subscription. The results obtained from testing DeepMinder
on multiple datasets are presented, showing that it is capable of identifying
anomalies with a high degree of accuracy. The code for the experiments conducted
in this study is available at https://github.com/axelord/Deep-Path-Learning. The

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety and reliability but are not entirely foolproof. Researchers have found that these models can be vulnerable to crafted adversarial examples that contain subtle variations in common 3D transformations, such as rotations, translations, and scaling. To address this issue, a comprehensive framework has been developed that systematically assesses the robustness of neural network-based point cloud models across all conceivable 3D transformations, allowing for the precise quantification of their adversarial vulnerability. Using this framework, researchers conducted an exhaustive study on a diverse range of point cloud models and discovered that the vulnerability of these models is not merely a singular issue but rather a complex, multi-faceted problem that arises from their susceptibility to various 3D transformations. Furthermore, the study provides a thorough analysis of the robustness and vulnerability of neural network-based point cloud models across different rotation, translation, and scaling scenarios. The research also introduces an innovative approach called Adversarial Rotation and Stretch (ARS) that leverages a combination of these transformations to craft more effective adversarial examples, thereby elevating the bar for future research aimed at enhancing the robustness of neural network-based point cloud models. The study's findings and methodologies have been thoroughly validated through an extensive set of experiments, and the associated data, models, and codes have been made openly available for replication and exploration by the research community. Ultimately, the study's ultimate goal is to stimulate a broader examination of the robustness and vulnerability issues affecting neural network-based point cloud models and to encourage the development of more reliable and robust models that can withstand a wide range of 3D transformations. In Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks, using Medium Access Control (MAC) protocols based on Clear Channel Assessment (CCA) can help prevent interference between radar systems. We analyze the performance of CSMA protocols in FMCW radar networks by modeling CCA processes as binary experiments that follow a specific probability distribution. We derive an exact analytical formula for calculating the average CCA delay in a random FMCW radar network. We then compare the efficacy of CSMA protocols to other CCA-based MAC protocols, such as ALOHA and slotted ALOHA, in terms of CCA delay. Our findings indicate that CSMA outperforms ALOHA and slotted ALOHA in terms of CCA delay when the number of radar systems is sufficiently large. We also derive an approximate analytical formula for calculating the average CCA delay in a random FMCW radar network. We validate our analytical model with numerical simulations and examine the impact of various FMCW radar system parameters on CCA delay. We propose a practical implementation of CSMA protocols in FMCW radar systems and conduct an experiment using a FMCW radar testbed to evaluate the performance of CSMA protocols in a real-world setting. Our results from the experiment are consistent with our analytical and numerical findings. We also investigate the performance of CSMA protocols in the presence of hidden terminals and estimate the CCA delay accordingly. We discuss the implications of our findings on the design of FMCW radar MAC protocols. We conclude that our analytical model effectively captures the behavior of CCA delay in FMCW radar networks and that CSMA protocols outperform other CCA-based MAC protocols in terms of CCA delay. Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of graph neural networks in static graph
tasks, temporal knowledge graph completion models have been developed to account
for temporal aspects and complex graph structures. Recent advancements in temporal
knowledge graph completion incorporate temporal information into updated node
representations using temporal neural networks, building upon successful applications
of graph neural networks in static graph tasks. We introduce TimeGCN-TNE, a novel
temporal knowledge graph completion model that utilizes time-gated graph attention
mechanisms to generate temporal- and graph-agnostic vectors for node representations.
We experimentally validate the effectiveness of TimeGCN-TNE in predicting temporal
and graph-related relationships on three publicly available datasets, achieving
state-of-the-art performance according to various evaluation metrics. A thorough
analysis of model components and hardness parsimony also helps clarify the
importance of each feature for the model's performance. The code for our approach,
along with additional details about model configuration and experimental setup,
can be found at https://github.com/zhengdian/TimeGCN-TNE. The results of our study
have been accepted for presentation at TheWebConf 2022. The source code for our
approach, including model components and data preparation, can be found at https://github.com/zhengdian/TimeGCN-TNE. The paper has been published in the Proceedings of the 15th International Semantic Web
Conference on The Semantic Web Volume 7031 of Lecture Notes in Computer Science,
pp. 145-163, 2011. The results of our study have been accepted for presentation at TheWebConf 2022. Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad state, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, and residual interaction connections in the complex energy plane. Furthermore, studies have discovered that the volume integral of the neutron density plays a crucial role in the formation of the real part of the resonance's energy, whereas the phase of the neutron density density distribution plays a key role in the resonance's width. Additionally, research has found that the $s$-wave neutron density, which contributes little to the volume and only a little to the resonance's width, is nonetheless crucial to the resonance's overall characteristics. Moreover, studies have found that the $s$-wave neutron density's real part is connected to the residual interaction with the $d$-wave density, resulting in the resonance's width. This finding challenges the conventional notion that the $s$-wave density is merely a byproduct of the volume-boson field and is therefore not significant. Instead, research has shown that the $s$-wave density, which is generated by the volume part of the neutron density operator, plays a crucial role in the resonance's characteristics. This discovery highlights the importance of distinguishing between the volume and surface parts of the density operator. Furthermore, studies have found that the surface part of the density operator, which is connected to the residual interaction with the $d$-wave density, results in the resonance's width. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus enabling the successful discovery of linear clusters in nonlinear systems. This method is demonstrated through clustering multiple renowned chaotic systems, including the Lorenz attractor, and comparing its performance with established algorithms using precision and normalized mutual information metrics. Furthermore, this approach is applied to analyze sleep stage patterns in human brain wave activity recorded over extended periods. All code used in this research is openly accessible on GitHub, making it suitable for the clustering of systems with complex temporal dynamics. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By utilizing an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices derived from the encoder and efficiently computing gradient calculations through sparse updates, we can train a efficient, dense discriminator. Experimental results show that SparseGAN outperforms traditional GANs and significantly reduces training time and memory usage while achieving comparable performance on diverse text generation tasks. Furthermore, we observe that the compact sentence representations produced by the encoder contain valuable information that can be leveraged for downstream tasks like sentiment analysis and topic modeling. To facilitate model understanding, we also visualize the generated sentence representations using t-SNE and discover that they reflect inherent structure in data. All source code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/zhengdian/SparseGAN.

The idea of interstellar panspermia, which posits that life could be transferred from one star system to another, is intriguing but difficult to verify through observations alone. Nevertheless, analyzing the conditions necessary for microbial survival during long-distance planetary transfers provides valuable insights into the feasibility of interstellar life transfer. We examine the requirements for a microbe like T4 bacteriophage to maintain structural integrity and biological function after being exposed to the harsh conditions of interstellar space. We also explore the potential for its DNA to be affected by high-energy photons and cosmic rays during a transfer, which could complicate the assembly of its protein structure. Using this knowledge, we estimate the maximum distance a transfer could travel before the microbe is significantly impaired, taking into account various factors such as the energy needed for assembly and the availability of building blocks. We find that even if assembly is highly efficient and most of the microbe's mass is dedicated to DNA repair, the maximum transfer distance is around 1 parsec. However, if we assume that the transfer occurs over many generations and that the microbe can adapt to repair its DNA more effectively, the maximum transfer distance could be as high as 10,000 light-years. Notably, the nearby star system Alpha Centauri, which includes Proxima Centauri, is within this feasible transfer distance. The possibility of interstellar life transfer raises interesting questions about the origins of life on Earth and the potential for finding life elsewhere in the universe. The search for biosignatures in exoplanet atmospheres may need to consider the potential contamination from other star systems, which could complicate the interpretation of data but is also an exciting area for further research. The study of life transfer across interstellar distances also highlights the importance of developing more robust methods for detecting DNA in space-based missions, such as the Square Kilometre Array radio telescope. The detection of DNA in interstellar space would require extremely sensitive instruments capable of distinguishing the faint signal from the background noise, which poses a significant technological challenge. The development of such instruments, however, would not only help detect DNA in interstellar space but also improve the sensitivity of the Square Kilometre Array in detecting other faint signals, which could also benefit the scientific community. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using quasi-independent constraints from each power spectrum multiplicity. Focusing on three cosmological parameters - the primordial power spectrum normalization, the number of effective neutrino species, and the Hubble constant - we can independently estimate their values from each power spectrum moment. However, these estimates will become increasingly reliable as we incorporate more power spectrum moments. Assuming an all-sky survey with an effective volume of 10000 deg^2, an integration time of 10 hours at 1.4 GHz, and a system temperature of 20 K, we simulate how these estimates would be derived from mock data based on parameters similar to those of the EDGES-HI survey. We then analyze how these estimates would change with varying noise levels and data integration times. Finally, we discuss the potential for future HI intensity mapping experiments to determine these three cosmological parameters independently with these experiments. We also explore the implications of combining such experiments with other experiments that can constrain these parameters, specifically Planck and future CMB experiments. The proposed concept of induced spontaneous symmetry breaking is explored through a theoretical scenario. This scenario posits that spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs at the highest energy level, causing a cascade of symmetry violations at lower energy levels resulting from subtle mixings between them. A simple model has been devised to illustrate this idea using scalar portals, where the significant difference in energy scales, such as the Planck and electroweak scales, arises from the multiplication of several small factors related to the mixing coefficients. The formation of dark matter fields is also examined in this framework, where it is possible for these fields to emerge from matter fields located on one or more intermediate energy levels between the highest and lowest. Dark matter then arises from the violation of symmetry on one of these intermediate levels due to the influence of the most elevated energy level. The most suitable dark matter scenario, in line with experimental data from the direct detection experiments, is achieved when the most elevated energy level is in the grand unified scale range. The proposed framework also offers an explanation for the hierarchy problem by replacing the arbitrary small coefficient with the product of more manageable parameters. The introduction of new parity symmetries on one or more energy levels can also lead to the stabilization of the dark matter potential. The implications of this framework are further examined in the context of dark matter and the hierarchy problem. The formation of the Higgs boson mass is guaranteed by the vacuum stability requirement, while the existence of the dark matter field depends on the conditions within the model itself. The proposed concept of induced spontaneous symmetry breaking may be tested through the study of high-energy particle collisions at future colliders, particularly in experiments related to dark matter and the hierarchy problem. The most suitable experimental approach to verify this framework involves the examination of final particle combinations that are sensitive to the cascade symmetry violations, which typically result in the production of a dark matter candidate accompanied by one or more scalar particles that subsequently decay into standard model particles. The analysis of these processes at the LHC and future colliders will provide a comprehensive understanding of the proposed concept of induced spontaneous symmetry breaking. Animal population studies often rely on resource selection functions (RSFs) to understand how animals utilize their environment. We employed camera traps and detection models to estimate the relative frequency of animal encounters in relation to vegetation cover at a regional scale in northern Alaska. Our study focused on caribou, reindeer, and three species of ducks to investigate how these animals select resources based on their availability in the Alaskan Arctic. We used generalized linear mixed models to identify correlations between animal encounters and environmental characteristics such as elevation, vegetation cover, water bodies, human infrastructure, and lunar phase. Our results revealed distinct patterns of resource selection for each species. For example, caribou and reindeer showed a strong preference for areas with lichen cover, especially during the summer, while ducks exhibited a preference for areas with lichen and moss cover and near water bodies. These findings highlight the value of camera traps and advanced analysis techniques in estimating animal encounter rates and identifying the environmental factors that influence resource selection. Moreover, our study highlights the importance of considering the effects of climate change, human activities, and species interactions on the resource selection of these animals. Long-term monitoring of these factors will be crucial in understanding how the Alaskan Arctic environment is being reshaped and predicting the distribution and abundance of these species in the future. We also present a method for combining our results with demographic data to forecast population trends, and we discuss the advantages of using camera traps to monitor animal populations at a regional scale. Ultimately, our study demonstrates the potential of camera traps and advanced analysis techniques to inform conservation and management decisions for these species. We make our results publicly available to facilitate the use of camera trap data in population studies and resource management decisions. In designing minimum power networks, we are given an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ along with associated edge costs. The objective is to select an edge subset $F \subseteq E$ satisfying a specific connectivity standard, while minimizing the total cost $\sum_{e \in F} c_e$. Here, we focus on a particular standard known as $k$-connectivity, where a graph must remain connected upon the removal of fewer than $k$ vertices. Our research centers on an intriguing variation of the standard $k$-connectivity problem known as the cuts of size at most $p$ problem, where we aim to find the fewest number of edges required to achieve $k$-connectivity among cuts measuring $p$ or less. This problem variant has an interesting relationship with the standard $k$-connectivity problem, as it can be viewed as an instance of the $k$-connectivity problem within a broader framework. It is essential to note that the standard $k$-connectivity problem has a well-established limit on the edge size of $O(k^2 \cdot n)$ for graphs with $n$ vertices, as demonstrated by the approach of rounding a fractional solution obtained through the LP relaxation. However, this approach results in an unsatisfactory edge size of $O(k \cdot n)$ for the cuts of size at most $p$ problem, as shown through a counterexample involving a graph with a relatively small number of vertices. It therefore becomes clear that there is a significant gap between the upper and lower bounds for the edge size of this problem variant. It is our research goal to bridge this gap by determining whether there is an algorithm capable of producing a $k$-connected subgraph of size at most $p \cdot n$ for any graph $G = (V, E)$, as well as examining whether this capability is feasible when the graph is $k$-connected in advance.
