Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. However, this process is labor-intensive and time-sensitive for pathological laboratories to meet clinical deadlines. To address these challenges, several deep learning-based approaches have been proposed in recent years. These models, built with convolutional neural networks (CNN), leverage large datasets to achieve high accuracy levels but often struggle with data scarcity in their native application settings. In contrast to prior work, this study focuses on exploring methods to improve the performance of pre-trained CNN models when dealing with limited data in their native context. Experiments utilizing nine different datasets from the Polyp-12 challenge showed that our proposed techniques yielded models with higher average scores compared to direct application. Notably, employing techniques like data augmentation, ensemble methods, and dimensionality reduction led to notable improvements when data quantities were particularly limited. Ultimately, our findings provide valuable insights for enhancing the effectiveness of pre-trained CNN models in polyp characterization, even with limited data. A novel numerical approach has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered on evaluating the impact of smooth, high-contrast obstacles on plane wave propagation. This method, based on the boundary integral equation (BIE), utilizes a localized non-orthogonal coordinate system to handle the singular operator and obtain a second-order accurate approximation of the solution. The method involves solving a system of equations using a Kaczmarz iterative method and has been shown to have a desirable $O(h^2)$ convergence rate when using the method's residual as the right-hand side. This has been demonstrated through both theoretical analysis and successful numerical examples. It's worth noting that previous methods using the boundary integral equation for scattering problems have typically employed non-local Treelength and format removal techniques to achieve similar $O(h^2)$ accuracy, which can become computationally expensive for large problems. The proposed method's efficiency in scattering applications makes it an attractive alternative to these methods. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches first generate speech features through speech recognition, then employ machine learning to translate these features into the target language. However, these approaches are marred by speech recognition and translation errors. To circumvent this issue, we propose a single-stage speech-to-text translation framework that directly maps spoken language to written language without intermediate features. To facilitate zero-shot translation, we introduce a technique called prosodic token embedding that incorporates phonological elements into token embeddings to capture the rhythmic characteristics of spoken language. To achieve zero-shot translation, we employ a technique called pseudo-labeling that utilizes models trained for few-shot translation to guide zero-shot translation. Through extensive experiments on the Multi-Parallel Corpus dataset, our approach outperforms baseline models in zero-shot translation tasks. Moreover, our method's ability to maintain performance in the face of significant prosodic changes between training and evaluation data is particularly noteworthy. Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we establish a connection between the neutrino oscillation lengths and the mass scales that separate "atmospheric" and "solar" neutrino sectors. This connection is made explicit for both CP-conserving and CP-violating processes. It is shown that the sum of the smallest two neutrino masses can be as low as 0.1 eV, required to meet the conditions set by the Einstein gravitational field equation for a perfect cosmological driver. Lastly, our work highlights the necessity of incorporating all relevant orbital states to achieve a comprehensive understanding of the material's properties.

Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Hocky formula along smooth boundary lines. In this paper, we provide a high-order method that divides each boundary into multiple segments based on the accuracy required and use this method on various domains with irregular boundaries to speed up the computation by up to three orders of magnitude compared to the standard method. In addition, this method can also handle a large number of discrete points within a given domain by reducing the total computational time to a linear increase in domain size. This method has significant implications for solving volume integral equations over complex domains, especially when solving multiple problems for the same domain. In this paper, we also demonstrate this method's effectiveness on a widely studied problem of finding the ground potential caused by dense spherical planets and satellites. The code developed in this research is freely available online for the community to use. Futhermore, this research lays the groundwork for further improving the algorithm to handle three-dimensional domains and boundary points more efficiently. In this research, the algorithms were implemented using C++ and tested with the BLAS and LAPACK linear algebra libraries.
